<meta>This page marks the beginning of the main text, following the dedication page. It introduces the central thesis regarding Leonardo da Vinci's dual legacy as a lost artist and a rediscovered scientist.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION

**L**EONARDO da Vinci is as sharply distinguished from his contemporaries by his mysteriously determined fate as he is by the magical uniqueness of his being. Even if much that other artists of his century planned remained unaccomplished, or much that they created was destroyed—the greatest part of their paintings still glows upon the walls, shines above the altars; their bronze and marble figures still shimmer as before in the squares and in the churches; their buildings still tower victoriously into the blue skies today with their proud facades, graceful arched pillars, and golden domed crowns. From Leonardo’s hand, almost nothing remains to us but the *Mona Lisa*. Whatever else his universal genius <note>original: "Allgenie"</note> created has been lost, spoiled, or perished—existing merely as sketches, doubted into pieces by critics, reduced to a few brushstrokes that might perhaps be authentic.

But while time and the learned gentlemen threaten to snatch Leonardo the artist away from us, until hardly more is left of him than his name and halo, we simultaneously experience in him a joyful Easter miracle. The immense outlines of his being, of which Burckhardt <note>Jacob Burckhardt (1818–1897) was a seminal Swiss historian of the Renaissance.</note> spoke, are filling out and becoming alive; Leonardo the researcher, the thinker, the poet celebrates in our days his resurrection from the grave of the libraries. For thirty years, efforts have been made to decipher and publish his writings. Of the more than 5,000 manuscript pages still preserved for us, more than three-quarters are now available in exemplary facsimile reproductions <note>original: "Faksimilewiedergabe"</note>

<summary>This introductory page contrasts the tragic loss of Leonardo da Vinci's physical artworks with the modern "resurrection" of his intellectual legacy through the publication of his scientific and literary manuscripts.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Mona Lisa, Jacob Burckhardt, Renaissance, universal genius, manuscripts, art history, scientific research</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction, shifting focus from the loss of Leonardo's physical artworks to the profound intellectual wealth found in his rediscovered manuscripts.</meta>

<lang>en</lang>
<sig>II</sig>

available; of the remainder, we have a preliminary understanding through thematically arranged excerpts. One cannot engage with these wonderful records in a superficial manner. They do not reveal themselves easily; but once one begins to penetrate them, they hold one fast in a most divine intoxication. One finds in them—let it be said at once—not a single completed work; yet from these partial treatises—material for books—from the thousandfold ideas, observations, and drafts of these richly illustrated notebooks and journals, there wells up a nearly immeasurable abundance of thought and poetry. Here a spirit is revealed to us whose power and depth were entirely equal to the most monstrous urge to know and to understand that the earth has ever produced. There is hardly a branch of the natural sciences <term>realen Wissenschaften: the "real" or empirical sciences, such as physics and biology</term> in which Leonardo did not gain the most surprising insights. Not only does he teach the experimental method long before Lord Bacon <note>Francis Bacon (1561–1626), often credited as the father of empiricism.</note>, but he also practices it as a master. He anticipated a whole series of the greatest physical discoveries by centuries. Earlier than Copernicus, he relegated the Earth to the modest role of a star among stars and denied the sun its motion <note>original: "der Sonne die Bewegung abgesprochen" — Leonardo intuited that the sun does not revolve around the earth.</note>. His intuitive grasp of the developmental history of our globe, his eye for its primeval past and its future, fills one with amazement; and his errors are just as brilliant as his divinations. He is one of the earliest masters of hydraulic engineering, not merely practically but also theoretically. He founded modern pictorial anatomy and was likely the first to pursue comparative anatomy in the sense that he recognized the common basic blueprint in the bodily structure of humans and animals, studying and depicting it in multiple variations. His manuscript pages are covered with designs and calculations for machines of all kinds. There is nothing he emphasizes with such pride as the fact that he is an inventor. To what extent he truly was—

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction's exploration of Leonardo da Vinci's scientific legacy, contrasting his modern reputation with the lack of understanding from his contemporaries and explaining the purpose of this specific volume of his writings.</meta>

<page-num>III</page-num>
<sig>I*</sig>

modern research establishes with growing admiration. And yet, these deeds of his genius remained for the most part fruitless. His contemporaries, as well as the generation that followed him, speak of Leonardo's discoveries and inventions with that slight shudder one feels toward the supernatural; they use vague words veiled by incidental reproach, which only reveal to us the lack of understanding of men like Vasari and Lomazzo <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574) and Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo (1538–1592) were early art historians whose biographies of Leonardo focused more on his art and eccentricities than his scientific rigor.</note> and mask their rejection of such things. Aside from his writings on painting, whatever else of his astonishing research results entered into the cycle of living development demonstrably did so only through detours and secret paths; in the triumphal march of knowledge, humanity was held back for a few centuries by this misfortune and cheated out of goals that were almost within reach.

Today, the content of Leonardo’s immense life’s work is, of course, largely outdated, expanded, corrected, and has become mere material for the history of the human spirit; nevertheless, there is so much of interest and strangeness in these writings—so much that is superior and world-spanning, such a captivating and luminous charm of personality, so much that provides insight into the nature of genius and the changing of the ages—that even we non-scholars feel cause and invitation to form a clear concept of it for ourselves. The great complete editions of the manuscripts are intended for specialized science; they require slow, attentive study before one can partially uncover Leonardo’s paths of thought within this world of fragmentary and jumbled notes. This gave rise to the plan to select the most beautiful, remarkable, and understandable passages from these writings and to arrange them in such a way that a portrait of Leonardo might emerge in outline. This attempt has been made several times. I know only the still indispensable work by Jean Paul <note>Jean Paul Richter (1847–1937), a German art historian who published the first major compilation of Leonardo's literary works in 1883.</note>

<summary>The author laments how Leonardo's scientific breakthroughs were ignored by his contemporaries, delaying human progress by centuries, and explains that this book aims to make Leonardo's complex manuscripts accessible to the general reader.</summary>

<page-num>IV</page-num>

Richter, which was published in Italian and English in two magnificent volumes by subscription and distributed in about 300 copies throughout the civilized world, and another in duodecimo format <note>A small book size, roughly 5 by 7.5 inches, created by folding a printed sheet into twelve leaves.</note> by Dr. Edmondo Solmi. For the German public, I venture approximately the same as the latter, though with a somewhat different method in the treatment, selection, and grouping of the text. The biography of Leonardo—which I am compiling based on the works of Dr. Paul Müller-Walde, Eugène Müntz, Adolf Rosenberg, E. Solmi, Georg Gronau, Edward Mc Curdy, and many others, as well as the important accounts of Vasari, the anonymous Florentine of the Magliabechiano Codex (edited by Carl Frey), Lomazzo, Amoretti, Giuseppe Bossi, Calvi, etc., yet with the strictest adherence to the documents—will help me, in connection with the characterization of his intellectual nature as it flows from the description of his thinking, his creating, and his working, to supplement the fragmentary quality that unfortunately lies in the nature of Leonardo's texts and in the nature of an extract for <term>the use of the Dauphin</term> <note>original: "usum delphini." A Latin phrase referring to editions of classics prepared for the education of the French prince, meaning a "cleansed" or simplified edition for general readers.</note>. To be sure, we know only a few things with certainty about Leonardo's life; if I therefore wish to renounce imaginative combinations, I will be forced to repeat much that is well-known and to omit all sorts of charming things, often printed and also newly devised, here; yet the truth has its own beauty and eloquence; Leonardo requires no other.

**L**eonardo was born in 1452, according to a tradition still alive today, at Anchiano near Vinci, a mountain hamlet of Monte Albano. For five generations, his ancestors had been notaries, and thus members of one of the higher Florentine guilds; only Antonio, Leonardo's grandfather, followed, it seems, no trade other than perhaps viticulture and gardening. In the house of this grandfather in Vinci, in

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general biographical sources mentioned on page IV to the specific details of Leonardo's early childhood in Vinci and his family background.</meta>

<sig>V</sig>

where the whole family still lived together in 1457, Leonardo spent his first years and had his first intellectual experiences. This rural estate of his grandfather always remained home to him; it later passed to him through inheritance from Francesco, his father's younger brother. "In the earliest memory of my childhood," he says, "it seems to me as if a kite <note>original: "Hühnergeier." While the author uses a term for a hawk or vulture, Leonardo's famous dream refers to the 'nibbio' or kite.</note> came down to me, opened my mouth with its tail, and struck many times with said tail between my lips"; he remarks half-jokingly, half-seriously, in the symbolic manner of the late Middle Ages, that this was likely why it became his destiny to write with such clarity about the kite. In any case, the nature of his native spot made him an early observer of all birds and their flight, of the waters and their course, of the rocks and their origin; it revealed the landscape to him as a vehicle of the deepest atmospheric magic and taught him to paint it as a symbol of a <term>state of soul</term> <note>original: "état d’âme." A French term referring to an emotional or spiritual state reflected in art.</note>.

Leonardo is the natural son of Ser Piero da Vinci and a peasant girl of "good blood," as the <term>Anonymous</term> <note>Referring to the "Anonimo Gaddiano" or "Anonimo Magliabechiano," an unidentified 16th-century author of a manuscript containing biographies of artists.</note> asserts and as we, in view of such a son, are gladly prepared to believe. As early as 1452, Piero married "according to his rank," and Caterina did the same soon after: thus the mother disappears entirely from the history of the son. He grew up in the family of his father; for except in the division of estates, people in those days were not too strict regarding legitimacy, and since Piero's first and second marriages remained childless, all the parents' affection could be centered on Leonardo. When in 1476 a son was finally born from a third marriage, Leonardo no longer required his father's care. —

From a land registry entry, we learn that Ser Piero had moved to Florence before 1469. He inhabited a house that stood on the site of the later Palazzo Gondi

<meta>This page continues the description of Leonardo's family life in Florence and his early education, following the mention of his father Ser Piero's marriage and his mother Caterina's departure from his life.</meta>

<sig>VI</sig>

stood on the Piazza S. Firenze. He supported "four mouths": his wife, his mother, a maidservant, and Leonardo, an "illegitimate son" <note>original: "figlio non legiptimo."</note>. Over the years, his household grew immensely—from a third and a fourth marriage he had nine sons and two daughters—but his prosperity did not lag behind. Skillful and jovial, he knew how to stay on good terms with both secular and spiritual authorities. We soon find him as the procurator of the Monastery of the Santa Annunziata, later as a notary of the Signoria <note>The governing body of Florence.</note>, and as a notary for the House of Medici; by the turn of the century, the most important and numerous contracts in Florence were drafted and signed by him. In any case, the documents speak more of him than of his son.

Of Leonardo's earliest development, we know nothing. Like other sons of citizens, he likely went to the <term>master of the abacus</term> <note>original: "maestro dell’ abbaco." A teacher of practical commercial arithmetic and mathematics.</note>, the reckoning master, before he entered the workshop. In any case, Leonardo often calls himself "without letters" <note>original: "senza lettere."</note>, meaning without an education—that is, without the classical education of the Humanists which was so desired in his time. Whatever he eventually possessed of this, he acquired for himself. His Milanese notebooks show abundant traces of his Latin language studies; he declines, he conjugates, creates word lists, performs grammatical analyses, and progresses so far that he reads his Archimedes and Aristotle in Latin, quotes in Latin, and writes in Latin himself. He likely does not owe his mathematical knowledge to the school in Florence either. In his notebooks from 1480–1500, we read, for example: "have the reckoning master show you how to transform a triangle back into a square," or "learn the multiplication of roots from Master Luca" <note>Referring to Luca Pacioli, the famous mathematician and friend of Leonardo.</note>. According to Vasari's account <note>Giorgio Vasari, the 16th-century biographer of Italian artists.</note>, he had from childhood directed his restless spirit toward too many things and, having barely begun, abandoned each one. "Nevertheless, although he occupied himself with various things, he never ceased drawing and working in...

Academy), the painting in which Leonardo "showed his hand" to the world for the first time. The master had, it is said, painted the main figures with effort, diligence, and faithfulness, and left all the rest, it is believed, to the pupil. Into this, "Leonardo worked an angel who carried some clothes, and although he was so youthful, he executed it in such a way that Leonardo's angel was of much better quality than the figures of Andrea: which became the reason," Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Renaissance artists.</note> tells us, "that Andrea never wanted to touch colors again, because he was incensed that a child understood more of it than he himself." Despite the contrary assertion of Morelli <note>Giovanni Morelli, a 19th-century art critic known for his method of identifying artists by small details like earlobes or fingernails.</note>, most connoisseurs nowadays attribute the angel holding the garments to Leonardo; indeed, following Bayersdorfer, many also wish to recognize the brush of the great pupil in the landscape and in all other parts of the painting where oil paints cover the tempera: as if the style of Verrocchio the painter were already firmly established for us today! The only certain data regarding the young Leonardo were found by Gustavo Uzielli in the "Red Book" (<term>Libro Rosso</term>), the record book of the "Company of Painters" (<term>Compagnia de’ Pittori</term>). Two entries therein prove that in 1472 Leonardo was already a master himself, though likely not a very busy or well-paid one, for he had remained in debt for his membership fee and his share of the sacrificial candles for the day of Saint Luke, the patron saint of the guild; indeed, he probably continued to work in Verrocchio's workshop thereafter; in 1476 he even lived with him. In this year, the "Officers of the Night and the Monasteries" (<term>Ufficiali di Notte e de’ Monasteri</term>), a kind of Florentine vice squad, found in their "drum" (<term>tamburo</term> <note>A wooden box used for anonymous denunciations in Renaissance Florence.</note>), the mailbox for depositing secret accusations, a charge against four young people, among them Leonardo da Vinci, "who lives with Andrea del Verrocchio," stating that they maintained illicit relations with a worthless young fellow. The new re-denunciation <term>Tamburation</term> <note>From the Italian 'tamburo' (drum), referring to the boxes where anonymous accusations were placed.</note> came to a conclusion on June 7th, with a new acquittal for all the accused. At that time, in the era of the blossoming cult of everything considered ancient—and therefore excellent—sodomy was the most elegant of all vices; and this period, in which people had grown accustomed to accusing their neighbors of the most monstrous things without hesitation, was always first at hand with this specific charge. But whoever values that acquittal less than the accusation, and whoever today still sees something other than the purely artistic in Leonardo's cult of beauty—even if intended as praise—reveals themselves to be a poor connoisseur of Leonardo's writings and a bad psychologist regarding the majestic soul from which those writings flowed. Of the works from this era, which Vasari describes for us with graceful art, none have been preserved for us: neither the cartoon for a woven door-curtain with Adam and Eve in Paradise, which he saw at that time "in the happy house" of Ottaviano Medici, nor the round shield with the terrifying mythical creature, whose creation Vasari describes so charmingly and which went to the "Duke of Milan," nor the Medusa head, the description of which has brought so many false Leonardos with the same theme into the museums of Europe. Just as little does the Mother of God with the flower-filled water flask exist, to which the Munich *Madonna with the Carnation* perhaps stands in a certain ancestral relationship. — The earliest authenticated work by Leonardo is a pen drawing kept in the Florentine Uffizi, a landscape with castle-crowned rocks, lovely hills, trees, a plain, and water, all full of delicate, youthful charm. A beautiful study for the head of the Holy Virgin authenticates it as a "Leonardo"; this head certainly belongs to him intellectually, even if the specimen in the Uffizi should happen to be a pupil's copy. And no less belongs to this period the poetic portrait in the Vienna Liechtenstein Gallery, which, being only slightly younger, represents the same personality as the *Bust of a Lady* (Bargello, Florence) created in Verrocchio's workshop — I mean the well-known one with the primroses in her garment and the soulful hands admired by d'Annunzio — hands which prompted one of Verrocchio's latest biographers, Hans Mackowsky, to also attribute this work to Leonardo. Vasari tells of clay busts of laughing women that were still being cast in plaster from Leonardo's models in his day, and likewise of small heads of children that seemed to have come from the hand of a master; the Milanese painter Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo speaks in his treatise on painting of a small <term>clay bust</term> <note>original: "Tonbüste"</note> of a Christ Child which he owned — perhaps the same one to which Leonardo (Codex Atlanticus, Folio 252 r.) alludes: "when I made our Lord as a boy"... but all of that has disappeared without a trace, as if swallowed by the earth. In its place, we have all sorts of interesting combinations, even if they are not entirely removed from the questionable; for example, those of Müller-Waldes, who likely overestimates the <term>stucco relief</term> <note>original: "Stuckrelief"</note> *The Discord* (London, South Kensington) when he claims Leonardo's direct authorship for it, or the better-founded conjectures of Wilhelm Bode. Bode recognizes the soulful hand of the youthful pupil in, among others, the beautiful <term>bronze relief</term> <note>original: "Bronzerelief"</note> *The Lamentation of Christ* (San Maria in Carmine, Venice), which until now had been attributed to Verrocchio.

The *Anonimo Fiorentino* <note>An anonymous Florentine author of a 16th-century manuscript containing biographies of artists</note>, from whom Vasari drew for his *Lives of the Artists*, relates that Lorenzo, as a youth, lived with the "Magnificent" Lorenzo de' Medici, who provided for him and allowed him to work in the garden on the Piazza of San Marco in Florence, where his famous antiquities stood. Nowhere else is Leonardo mentioned among the <term>familiars</term> <note>Close members of a noble household or inner circle</note> of the great Medici, as the younger Michelangelo is mentioned; nor does any personal commission testify to Lorenzo's favor or a pronounced taste for Leonardo's self-willed genius. One fact perhaps illuminates the riddle. When in 1478 Giuliano de' Medici fell victim to the <term>Pazzi Conspiracy</term> <note>A plot by the Pazzi family to displace the Medici as rulers of Florence by assassinating Lorenzo and Giuliano</note> and murderers, suspects, and the innocent alike were cut down with their kin and relatives in seemingly blind rage—hanged, with or without the ceremony of a trial, simply wherever they were found, from the window bars of the <term>Signoria</term> <note>The government palace of Florence, now the Palazzo Vecchio</note> or the Palace of the "Captain of Justice"—it was ordered, according to custom and tradition, that the "executed" be painted on the wall of the Bargello as a deterrent example. The execution of this task was likely granted to someone from the school of Verrocchio, but, as a payment entry of 1478 in the books of the Eight Priors proves, this person was one Sandro Botticelli, whom Lorenzo loved: he was permitted, among others, to depict the escaped murderer of Giuliano, Bernardo Bandini de’ Baroncelli (who was not caught until 1479), in advance as a hanged man. Leonardo seems to have been interested in the task; a pen drawing (in the possession of L. Bonnat in Paris) represents the murderer in the fatal noose; on the same sheet, he has written the exact description of the colors of his clothing, down to the stockings, and he has drawn the head once more, somewhat larger. To be sure, the sketch possesses nothing crude or horror-inducing. Around 1480, it is mentioned that Leonardo had "his own house" <note>original: "casa sua"</note>, which likely means he had a residence and workshop of his own. In July 1481, he entered into a contract with the monks of San Donato in Scopeto, in which he promised to paint a picture for the high altar of their church within a period of no more than 30 months. Whether this was ever begun, we do not know from documents; in any case, there are a few entries in the archives regarding deliveries in kind from the monastery to the painter—the last from September 28, 1481: "to Master Leonardo di Ser Piero da Vinci, on the said day, a bucket of red wine, which he received here in San Donato." In any case, Leonardo did not get very far with his painting. "Time passed, and a disadvantage arose for us," the monks recorded. In 1496, Filippino Lippi then took over the commission and produced an *Adoration of the Magi*, which is today located in the Uffizi. Also located there is the marvel of Leonardo's *Adoration* <note>The *Adoration of the Magi*, left unfinished when Leonardo departed for Milan</note>, which, despite its unfinished state—being merely underpainted—forms a milestone in the development of modern painting along with the associated preparatory studies. That the first sketches were created around 1481 in Florence is undisputed; likewise, it is now almost universally assumed that this painting was intended for San Donato: the somewhat unusual dimensions of the height and width of the picture, which pretty much coincide with those of Filippino’s *Adoration*, encourage this opinion. A favorable fate has preserved for us a great number of drawings for this panel painting. We can follow the transformations from the first thought to the finally established form. And we gain a highly instructive insight into the almost unquenchable abundance of Leonardo’s, one might say, narrative invention, into the entire manner

A drawing in the possession of Mr. Léon Bonnat <note>Léon Bonnat (1833–1922) was a French painter and collector whose drawings are now largely in the Musée Bonnat-Helleu</note> and another in Windsor prove that Leonardo first thought of an *Adoration of the Shepherds*, and according to Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari, the 16th-century biographer of Italian artists</note>, he is said to have executed this theme once in Milan. In the Academy of Venice, there are two delightful sketch sheets for this (No. 256 and 259). On one, Mary kneels, turning fully toward the viewer, before the Holy Child on the ground. The Christ Child <note>original: "Bambino"</note>, lying comfortably on his stomach, has turned his upper body halfway to the left side to stretch out his right hand backward toward the little John <note>St. John the Baptist as a child</note>, who has hurried over and quickly kneels down, folding his hands. The movement of haste is still visible in the posture of his torso and arms. In the foreground on the left sits an older man leaning forward with his legs crossed, turning backward toward a young man who has just stepped up, to whom he stretches out his hand and evidently explains the miracle before him. The second sheet contains variations on the posture of the Child and the boy John. The richness of the motifs of movement is wonderful, combining several moments and giving the composition an immense abundance of lines, expression, and, so to speak, action. Naturally, the theme of the *Adoration* <note>The Adoration of the Magi</note> could be designed even more richly and with more movement, of which we possess the underpainted picture in Florence. Here, Leonardo’s pressing imagination found great scope in sketches. The holiest, most human of all idylls—three kings of different ages, a large retinue, pious shepherds, and indifferent warriors—the rich life he felt in this subject enticed him toward the most extraordinary. He surrounded the scene with an extensive ruined palace, which, with its porticos, stairs, bays, and parapets, offered space and opportunity for manifold designs. The deep emotion—

<sig>XVI</sig>

The purity of feeling found in higher-natured individuals could, through various gradations, stand in contrast to the everyday bustle of the broad, indifferent masses and slowly find its peace. Two drawings—one in the possession of Mr. Galichon in Paris, the other kept in the Uffizi <note>The Uffizi Gallery in Florence, which houses Leonardo's unfinished Adoration of the Magi</note>—represent two fundamentally different compositions of the same idea. But for each of these compositions, there still exists a multitude of detailed studies; Leonardo evidently sees ever-new figures and their relationships to the message of salvation—scenes that must fall entirely outside the frame of a single painting. He envisions people telling one another of the miracle on the street, in the tavern, everywhere where two or more are gathered, until everyone knows, everyone understands—even if one had to trumpet it into the ears of the deaf, just as one figure actually does in the pen drawing that exists in the Malcolm Collection in London <note>The John Malcolm collection, now part of the British Museum</note>. On one of the sheets in the Louvre, several such narrative scenes are sketched: two people who happened to sit next to each other on a bench, and a row of others grouped around a table as if after a meal, listening with the utmost tension to one who shares something momentous. In his descriptive drafts for paintings, Leonardo can never satisfy himself in communicating characteristic detail, which he sees developing further and further still. 

I mention this sheet, however, particularly because of its importance for Leonardo’s biography. Just as a vibrating string causes related strings to sound, the theme of youths, men, and old men sitting around a table at a meal and hearing something great and shattering has evidently caused another internally and externally related theme to resonate in Leonardo’s imagination—the theme of the *Last Supper*. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Josef Strzygowski’s theories regarding the dating of Leonardo’s "Adoration of the Magi" and transitions into an analysis of the social and intellectual climate of Florence that prompted Leonardo's departure for Milan.</meta>

In any case, the designs for this painting were the last things Leonardo produced in Florence. His mind was set on the distance. Florence was too narrow for him; the atmosphere at home too dry; the suspicious and mocking nature of those around him was not conducive to genius. In republics, there is no place for one who openly towers above the others. Julius Caesar paid the price for it; Lorenzo de' Medici, taught by the death of his brother <note>Giuliano de' Medici, assassinated in the Pazzi Conspiracy of 1478</note>, remembered the warning of his wise grandfather Cosimo; like a citizen among citizens, he walked the streets without an escort in an inconspicuous short cloak, and petitioners found him, the <term>Magnifico</term> <note>The Magnificent; a title of honor given to Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, sitting in the courtyard of his house in the evening. In Florence, one simply had to act like one's neighbor, to be like everyone else; otherwise, one fell victim to wit or worse persecution. Even 70 to 80 years later, Vasari says somewhere: "Florence does to its artists as time does to its things, which, hardly made, it destroys again and consumes little by little." A Leonardo, of course, is made by no state; he comes from other expanses—and requires other expanses. At home, he did not find the tasks he craved, nor the understanding he needed. He was more than just a painter, and a painter was, in his eyes, more than a simple craftsman. His century, whose opinions were guided by the <term>Humanists</term> <note>Scholars of the Renaissance who revived classical Greek and Roman studies</note>, thought differently. It placed rhetoric among the <term>seven liberal arts</term> <note>The traditional curriculum of grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy; painting was excluded as a "mechanical" or manual art</note>, but painting not at all. When the young Michelangelo sat as an equal among equals at the <term>Magnifico's</term> table, he sat there as one of knightly birth. He himself writes that only the man of good birth achieves greatness, and the whole era thought so, even if we are taught otherwise today. Even a Baldassare Castiglione believes...

...y felt the need to apologize when it demanded that the perfect courtier <note>A reference to Baldassare Castiglione’s "The Book of the Courtier"</note> should be able to paint: "Do not be surprised if I also require this skill, which today perhaps appears mechanical and little suited for a nobleman." — "You have placed painting among the mechanical arts," Leonardo grumbles. This reflects the entire position of the artist at the end of the <term>Quattrocento</term> <note>The 1400s, or the 15th century in Italian art and culture</note>. Even if one no longer generally addressed the artist with the informal "thou"; even if the times were over when Brunellesco and Donatello ran through the streets in leather aprons and wooden clogs, and David Ghirlandajo was outraged that he and his brother Domenico were given the scraps from the table to eat in the monastery at Passignano—one’s work was still paid for like a daily wage on a monthly basis, or even by the yard, just as Borso d’Este paid Francesco Cossa, who painted the frescoes of Schifanoja. Most often, the artist was still a poor, half-starved fellow, coarse, naive, and often heartily ignorant, though gifted, who had to make do with every task, great and small, and be equal to each—capable of everything and signifying nothing. Leonardo himself, as we know, freshly decorated the clock tower in the monastery of San Donato with gold and ultramarine. He could no longer accommodate himself to such handiwork; he was of a different intellectual race than these magnificent lads—the painters, sculptors, master builders, and carpenters of Florence—with whom he was lumped together and confused, without, however, being found as useful as they were. It was not he who received the great commissions that require trust. He was even surrendered unconditionally to Milan—not merely on loan, as Soderini later gave him to the French, or as Lodovico Moro once requested Perugino from the Baglioni, his rightful masters. In Florence at that time, they had no inkling of what they were losing in Leonardo. He rolled immeasurable plans around in his brain, and others besides merely artistic ones. He

...had already begun to question nature in his own way, in order to understand and to achieve something. Several passages in Leonardo's English manuscripts <note>Refers to the Codex Leicester or other manuscripts held in British collections</note>, which—if the character of the handwriting is not deceptive—were composed before 1480, prove that da Vinci was already occupied with all sorts of earthly problems at that time. He explored the surroundings of Florence; he had his own ideas about the changes that millennia had produced in the physiognomy of this land and about the role of water in the shaping and reshaping of the globe. He observes the vibrant life even of the so-called inorganic world; he sees the cycle of things and their end: the earth will become waterless, wither, and finally go up in ashes, he believes. His research had originated from practical purposes. He was interested in all kinds of questions of mechanics. The original and deep thinker, the inventor, had already stirred within him early on. Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Italian Renaissance artists</note> reports two things relating to Florence. "He was the first," he says, "who, while still quite young, spoke about the river Arno in order to canalize it from Pisa to Florence" . . . "Practice must be built upon good theory," he says, and the "theorist" was listened to with much respect—yet not believed, being dismissed as a schemer, a dreamer, or an ideologue; the names for it change, but the essence remains the same for all eternity.

For the kind of undertakings that enticed him, Leonardo needed a prince, not merely in terms of power, but also in terms of mindset; he needed a realm with virgin soil, where there was something to be achieved for the artist and the inventor. The phantom image of such a prince and such a kingdom lured him from place to place throughout his life, until he reached the one where his grave was dug. Now, he saw the fulfillment of his dreams in Milan.

**O**n December 26, 1476, Galeazzo Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan, had been stabbed to death in church by a few youths whose heads had been filled with the ideas of Plutarch <note>The Greek historian Plutarch wrote "Parallel Lives," which often inspired Renaissance revolutionaries with tales of ancient tyrannicides</note>. His widow, Bona of Savoy, acting as guardian for the eight-year-old Gian Galeazzo, removed her husband's ambitious brothers on the advice of her clever chancellor, Cicco Simonetta. The most significant among them was the eldest, Lodovico, also named Maurus—or *Moro* <note>Italian for "The Moor," a nickname likely given due to his dark complexion</note>—at his baptism. He continued to be called "the Moro" within the family and by the people, even though since his sixth year, following a recovery from a serious illness and a vow made by his mother in honor of the Holy Virgin, he officially bore the name Lodovico Maria.

In 1479, this Moro knew how to persuade his sister-in-law to recall him from Pisa, where he had been exiled. It took only half a year for Simonetta to be beheaded and for Bona to be so compromised that she became impossible; the young Duke fell into the "solicitous" hands of Lodovico, and Lodovico himself became the "Vicar" and Regent of Milan. to power. No sooner had the Moro reached this point than he began to play a different tune. "I am no longer the Lodovico of Pisa," he writes; "I am the son of Francesco Sforza <note>Francesco Sforza (1401–1466) was the founder of the Sforza dynasty and a legendary mercenary commander</note> and I shall prove it." A refined mind with a piercing intellect, he believes he can juggle both people and circumstances. He does not hold himself in low regard; he boasts of having Pope Alexander VI as his chaplain, Emperor Maximilian as his *condottiere* <term>condottiere: a leader of mercenary soldiers</term>, and the King of France as his courier. He once threatened the Venetians that he would throw them into the sea; yet his true methods were not those of violence, so long as he could avoid it. "The said Lord Ludovic was a very wise man," writes Philippe de Comynes <note>original: "Le dict seigneur Ludovic estoit homme très saige... mais fort craintif et bien souple quant il avoit paour... et homme sans foy s’il veoit son prouffit pour la rompre." Comynes was a contemporary French chronicler and diplomat.</note>, "but very fearful and quite flexible when he was afraid (I speak of him as one whom I knew and with whom I transacted many things), and a man without faith if he saw his profit in breaking it." His political principle is to stir up unrest so that he might be left in peace, to muddy foreign waters so that he might fish in them. He was not a villain in the modern sense, but as Burckhardt <note>Jacob Burckhardt (1818–1897), the influential Swiss historian of the Renaissance</note> says of him: "The Moro is the most perfect princely character-figure of this time and thus appears again like a product of nature, with whom one cannot be entirely angry. Despite the deepest immorality of his means, he is completely naive in their application." A man of broad spirit, high education, and great insight, without cruelty or harshness—blood-shy to the point of cowardly weakness, luxury-loving, and pleasure-seeking—he wishes to shape his land into the most flourishing and magnificent in the whole world. He finds great treasures already accumulated; Milan yields 500,000 ducats annually with ease; Lodovico knows how to wring 650,000 from his subjects: after Venice, the city is the richest in Italy—richer than all of Germany, than France, than England; only Spain still surpasses it. concentrated in the hands of the prince, great things could be achieved, and Lodovico the Moor <note>Lodovico "il Moro" Sforza (1452–1508), Duke of Milan and patron of Leonardo da Vinci</note> was the man to undertake great things. There was no lack of intellectual culture in Milan. Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the "Father of Humanism"</note> had lived here, and after him a host of Humanists <term>Humanists: scholars who revived the study of classical Greek and Roman literature and philosophy</term> served as court poets, secretaries of state, teachers, and historians—often parasitic existences who were simultaneously people of dazzling gifts or at least of clever talent, and here and there also men of true merit: the Decembrios, father and son, Antonio Loschi the chancellor, the bold Antonio da Rhò, the two Barzizzas, and above all Filelfo—the insolent and brilliant predecessor of Aretino <note>Pietro Aretino (1492–1556), known for his sharp-tongued satires</note>, whose praise everyone sought and whose blasphemous mockery everyone feared. He bent Popes and Sultans to his will; he extorted princes to provide dowries for his daughters, and believed that the immortality of great deeds hung upon the tip of his pen. Although Filelfo spread the most brilliant polish and the grace of his own spirit throughout the rich, opulent society of Milan, an inferior type of Humanist follower developed after his example—a type that evokes no sympathy at all, and the very type against whom Leonardo <note>Leonardo da Vinci</note> so often turned in resentment . . . Now the times of Lodovico the Moor had arrived, and cultural endeavors had become even more intense. Pavia and Milan swarmed with learned men. Giorgio Merula and Demetrios Chalkondylas were teaching. <page-num>XXIV</page-num>

The brother of the beheaded chancellor Cicco, and Corio, were the elegant historiographers <term>historiographers: official court historians</term> of the Sforza; there was a literal Milky Way of poets and poetasters at court: Bernardo Bellincioni, Lancinus Curtius, Taccone—Gaspare Visconti, il Pistoja, Serafino d’Acquila—to say nothing of highly gifted cavaliers like Niccolò da Correggio. Everyone composed poetry, everyone sang and played the lute. To be sure, poetry and music did not merely serve the need for inner consecration and elevation; yet as the adornment of daily life, they were indispensable. The best virtuosos came streaming to Milan from far and wide: Atalante Migliorotti, the lyre player; Jacopo di Sansecondo, the most excellent violinist of the time; Testagrossa, the superb composer; Franchino Gaffurio, the leader of an entire chapel; singers of great renown, among them Cristoforo Romano, the famous medalist and sculptor, stood in the service of Lodovico the Moor <note>Lodovico "il Moro" Sforza</note>. Regarding the visual arts, however, and consequently regarding its beauty, Milan did not stand at the height of its otherwise aesthetic culture. Since the days of the first Visconti, two gigantic undertakings dominated and consumed all the living artistic power of the Lombard state: the construction of the Cathedral of Milan and that of the Certosa of Pavia <note>A famous Carthusian monastery complex</note>. They occupied all talents and forced every young individuality, imperceptibly but inevitably, into the linear spell of their pre-ordained plans. There was no escape from the weight of the architectural concept which past generations had imposed as an inheritance upon their grandsons in the *Quattrocento* <term>Quattrocento: the 1400s or 15th-century Italian art period</term>. The monumentality of the layout and of that which had already progressed too far in both projects crushed, or at least blurred, the overly personal element in the artists. These projects may be to blame for the fact that in Milan, longer than in other Italian cities, the medieval, corporate practice of art remained in vogue. A family trait also connects the individual, often very rich talents. All this art was, in fact, "bound art"—decoration—despite the thousands of statues scattered across the Cathedral and the Certosa <note>The Carthusian monastery of Pavia</note>, and despite the witty, charming masks and heads of terracotta that looked up to heaven from wreaths of fruit, broke through friezes, enlivened the walls, and seemed to expand the rooms. Educated in an overpowering, often brilliant decorative art, the Milanese taste did not desire any Donatellos; and when new, different types of tasks were set for the sculptor by "the Moor" <note>Lodovico Sforza</note>, the local forces were no longer sufficient—not the Mantegazzas, the Dolcebuonos, the Omodeos, no, not even more independent figures like Cristoforo Solario, called *il Gobbo* <note>The Hunchback</note>, or Cristoforo Foppa, whom the world knows as the famous medalist Caradosso. — Painting was even less developed. The powerful, capable masters Zenale, Vincenzo Foppa, and Butinone, as well as the more delicate, deeply feeling Ambrogio Borgognone, all lagged far behind their contemporaries in technical perfection, artistic taste, and the richness of their personal style. Even for building—insofar as it concerned the drafting of new plans—there had always been a need for foreigners; one had to consult Heinrich von Gmünd, Mignot, Nexenperger—and later, one had to consult Michelozzo and Filarete. The extraordinary was brought in from abroad. Since the seventies of the <term>Quattrocento: the 1400s or 15th century</term>, Bramante of Urbino had been active in Milan. According to the *Anonimo* <note>The "Anonimo Gaddiano," an anonymous 16th-century author of a manuscript on Florentine artists</note> and according to Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari, the famous biographer of Renaissance artists</note>, Leonardo actually came to the court of Sforza as a musician. "And he was thirty years old," said the former, "when he was sent by the said Magnificent Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note> together with Atalante Migliorotti to the Duke of Milan to present him with a lyre, because he was unique in playing such an instrument." — "It happened," says Vasari, "when Giovan Galeazzo, Duke of Milan, had died and Lodovico Sforza was elevated to the same rank in 1494, that Leonardo was led to the Duke in Milan with great reputation, who took great pleasure in the sound of the lyre, so that he might play there; and Leonardo brought that instrument with him, which he had made with his own hand, mostly of silver, in the shape of a horse's skull — a bizarre and new thing — so that the harmony might have a greater resonance <note>original: "Tuba"</note> and sound of the voice; thereby he surpassed all the musicians who were gathered here to play." By 1494, however, Leonardo had already been in Milan for a long time. We possess documents showing that in 1487 he had received several partial payments for the model of a central dome <note>A "tiburio" or crossing tower</note> which he had made for a competition for the Cathedral of Milan, but withdrew in 1490 with the promise to make another drawing, which he then never did. As early as 1810, Giuseppe Bossi demonstrated in his book on the "Last Supper" that Leonardo was already employed at Lodovico's court in 1482, or 1483 at the latest. Be that as it may, the document proves to us in any case how many things Leonardo was already occupying himself with at that time and what he felt confident enough to undertake. Nevertheless, the full unfolding of his genius was only just beginning.

Most of the architectural sketches preserved in Manuscript B of the "Institut" in Paris, in the Codex Trivulzio, the Codex Atlanticus, and the manuscripts of the British Museum in London, etc., likely date to this decade. Despite the works of Baron Henri Geymüller <note>A Swiss art historian (1839–1909) who pioneered the study of Renaissance architecture</note>, these have not yet been sufficiently studied. Even if a portion of these drawings served only for self-instruction — for example, to explore all the possible combinations of a domed building on various floor plans — and even if much was intended only as material for the treatise on architecture which Leonardo planned (just like, alas, so many other things!): it is simply not believable that his practical activity as an architect was limited solely to the model he submitted and then withdrew for the dome of the Milan Cathedral. The history of the buildings erected in Milan between 1472 and 1499 is far from being fully researched. The works of Müller-Walde <note>Paul Müller-Walde, a German art historian who died before completing his major Leonardo biography</note> on Leonardo still await completion. We must be content to cite Geymüller, who says (in J. P. Richter’s *Literary Works of Leonardo*, Vol. II), that there are outstanding buildings from this period in Lombardy whose creators remain unknown and whose artistic merit is so high that the suspicion is not at all improbable that Bramante <note>Donato Bramante, the architect who later designed St. Peter's Basilica in Rome</note> or Leonardo was involved in the construction. Since then, the research into Bramante’s works has been accompanied by the most fortunate and surprising success; yet Leonardo the architect remains a dark mystery to us. We can only hold fast to Leonardo the architectural theorist, who enjoyed so much prestige that his expert opinion was sought — in Milan, in Pavia (1490), and later in

Most interesting to us, however, are his ideas on **urban planning**. Were they ever allowed to be formulated into precise proposals? And the city makes beauty the companion of its name, and makes itself useful to you through its gifts and the eternal glory of its growth” . . . The completely modern simplicity and elegance of the solution characterizing these mechanisms—as with all of Leonardo's—is astonishing. And yet, Leonardo is not a practitioner in the ordinary sense. He arrives at his inventions through a theoretical path. His mind is directed toward the investigation of nature and its laws. He wants to comprehend them before he attempts to make them useful. This applies to art as well. For art shall no longer be disparaged as merely a manual skill <note>original: "Handfertigkeit"; refers to the medieval classification of painting as a "mechanical art" rather than a "liberal art."</note>. It shall receive a firm scientific foundation. Leonardo is already planning his great treatise on painting. He begins the preliminary work by occupying himself with studies on light and shadow, but above all with the exploration of the human structure. Even less difficult matters imperiously demanded his time—matters, to be sure, which were then considered serious and very worthy, because in life nothing was as important as beauty in every form. One need only remember the role that clothing played—with what precision letters, diaries, chronicles, and poems report what this person and that (and their horse and his servant) had worn on such and such a day. In 1489–1490, magnificent festivals were celebrated in the Milanese territory. Lodovico <note>Lodovico Sforza (1452–1508), known as "Il Moro," the de facto ruler of Milan and Leonardo's primary patron.</note> married off his nephew, Duke Gian Galeazzo—from whom he was firmly determined to withhold the government—to Isabella of Aragon, daughter of Crown Prince Alfonso of Naples, and thus granddaughter of the powerful King Ferrante. It was a childhood betrothal concluded in 1480, which "the Moor" <note>original: "der Moro"; Lodovico's nickname, likely due to his dark complexion.</note> had not dared to cancel despite the dangers it held for his plans: he trusted in his resourceful spirit and in chance, to which he was always eager to open all too many doors in his house. The death of Lodovico’s sister Ippolita Sforza, who was the mother of the young bride, interrupted the wedding festivities; only a year later were they resumed, culminating in a performance which, as Dr. E. Solmi has established, took place on January 13, 1490. It was called "Paradise," "because with great ingenuity and art, Master Leonardo Vinci the Florentine built the heavens with all the seven planets, which rotates, and the planets were represented by men, in form and dress as the poets describe them; which planets all speak in praise of the aforementioned Duchess Isabella, as you will see when you read it" (Introduction to the verses of Bernardo Bellincioni, cited by Carlo Amoretti, page 35).

The artistic activity of Leonardo during this entire time was, however, especially dedicated to the Sforza monument <note>The "Gran Cavallo," a massive bronze equestrian statue intended to honor Francesco Sforza, which was never cast in bronze.</note>. <page-num>XXXVII</page-num>

> “is a portrait of Francesco, Duke of Milan, and beneath the horse, which is galloping to the left, we see a warrior lying struck down on the ground—exactly the same idea as we find in some of Leonardo’s drawings for the monument. Since it is impossible to explain this remarkable coincidence by assuming that one of these artists borrowed from the other, we can only conclude that the conditions for the competition included the proposal to represent the Duke on a horse at full gallop, with a fallen enemy beneath its hooves.”

If this conclusion is correct, then those sketches by Leonardo—in which the rider intends to leap over the fallen enemy, before whom the horse rears up or looks down with shy pity, while the cavalier sometimes throws his arm back with the commander’s staff to announce triumph, and at other times seems to storm forward wildly swinging a weapon, etc.—would be brilliant solutions to a prescribed theme whose unprecedented nature must have tempted him. Which of these sketches Leonardo shaped into the first model, we do not know. It seems, however, that the thought of casting such daring poses into such colossal masses of bronze eventually filled him with anxious skepticism.

Manuscript Ashburnham I <note>original: "Ms. Ash. I." — part of the collection of Leonardo's notebooks now in the Institut de France.</note>, which dates from the years 1489–90, contains a remark on Folio 16 r. that likely refers to this: 

> “Figures in raised work” (<term>rilievo</term> <note>Leonardo uses this term to refer to free-standing three-dimensional sculpture rather than low-relief.</note>), “which appear to be in motion—if you try to set them on their feet, they will, according to reason (<term>per ragione</term> <note>meaning according to the laws of physics or proportions.</note>), fall forward.”

The purpose of this drawing for Leonardo was certainly to convince himself of what the correct armature <note>The internal metal framework used to support a large sculpture.</note> for a model so constructed must be, and a remark regarding all the “heads of the large screw-nails” confirms this. <meta>This page continues the analysis of Leonardo da Vinci's second model for the Sforza monument, specifically focusing on his inspirations from antiquity and his transition from a galloping horse to a more stable, walking pose.</meta>

<page-num>XXXIX</page-num>

with the preliminary work for the Last Supper; therefore, it is not a matter of the first, abandoned model. In this horse, conceived so sculpturally, one has wanted to feel the influence of antiquity and felt reminded of the statue of Marcus Aurelius <note>The famous Roman equestrian statue on the Capitoline Hill.</note>, the bronze horses of Venice <note>The four ancient horses on St. Mark's Basilica.</note>, and even Donatello's Gattamelata monument in Padua. However, as far as is known to date, Leonardo was not in Padua, nor Venice, nor Rome before 1499; he did, however, visit Pavia in 1490 regarding cathedral construction matters, where indeed—as Müller-Walde demonstrates (see *Yearbook of the Prussian Art Collections*, 1897)—an admirable ancient equestrian statue of gilded bronze stood until 1796: Petrarch had already praised it to Boccaccio in 1346. Allegedly, it represented the Gothic King Gisulf—it was popularly called the *Regisole* <note>The "Sun King," an ancient bronze statue destroyed during the French Revolution.</note>—it originated from Ravenna and was destroyed in 1796 by the republican French as the glorification of a king. Leonardo's words from the *Codex Atlanticus* Fol. 147 r. evidently refer to the horse of the *Regisole*:

> "In that one of Pavia, the movement is more praiseworthy than anything else. The imitation of ancient things is more praiseworthy than that of modern ones. Beauty and utility cannot be united, as is visible in fortresses and in men. The whole is almost of the quality of a free horse. Where natural liveliness is lacking, one must make an artificial (<term>accidentale</term> <note>In this context, Leonardo refers to "accidental" or "contrived" motion to simulate life.</note>) one."

One can almost hear Leonardo talking himself into it. For the sake of the useful and the possible, he must renounce something so beautiful, bold, and unprecedented as the design of the galloping, rearing horse with the warrior thrown to the ground beneath it—he must renounce the "<term>terribilità</term>" <note>A quality of emotional intensity and "terrible" grandeur, often associated with Michelangelo.</note>, that power which had grown so deep into the heart of the Renaissance and was its highest ideal. He, whose artistic principle it is never to repeat anything, not even himself, feels...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci's second model for the Sforza equestrian monument, specifically how he balanced the "utility" of ancient models with his own intense studies of living horses.</meta>

<page-num>XL</page-num>

forced by common "utility" to fall back on the old, yet proven methods, and consoles himself with the fact that the imitation of ancient things is less blameworthy, especially where the object to be imitated has almost the quality of a living horse in freedom. What it lacked, in comparison to what Leonardo had first intended, and what the motif of movement in a sculptural execution necessarily lacked, had to be replaced by something artificial—one simply had to heighten everything, movement and expression, a trace beyond the possible, beyond nature: then one obtained life. From the perspective of this observation, one should study Leonardo's drawings for this monument, as they are published in Courajod's and in J. P. Richter's work, and in volumes 18 and 20 of the *Yearbook of the Prussian Art Collections*; see how heavily and reluctantly Leonardo parts from the bolder design; see how he worked the ancient model and the studies from nature into one another—studies from nature that are evidenced for us by countless sheets and by notes such as: "The great Barbary horse <note>original: "Berber"</note> of Messer Galeazzo" (referring to Galeazzo Sanseverino, who had been married since 1490 to Madonna Bianca, a natural daughter of Lodovico, the same woman who is held—without reason, I must say—to be the original model for the so-called "Milanese Princess" in Room IV of the Brera <note>The Pinacoteca di Brera, a major public museum in Milan.</note>); "The Sicilian of Messer Galeazzo" (this Neapolitan breed of horse was a beautiful cross of Spanish and Moorish steeds); "Measurement of the Sicilian, the hind leg, seen from the back, raised and extended"; — "Morel the Florentine of Messer Mariolo, a strong horse with a beautiful neck and a truly very beautiful head"; — "The white stallion of the falconer has beautiful hind thighs," etc. — all notes from the notebooks of the years 1490–1495, from a time, therefore, when the model was evidently still unfinished, which is also confirmed by Bandello <note>Matteo Bandello (1485–1561), a writer and monk who observed Leonardo at work.</note>, who speaks of the simultaneity of the

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the timeline and technical challenges of Leonardo da Vinci’s Sforza monument, specifically debunking the myth of its public display in 1493 and detailing the immense scale of the bronze casting requirements.</meta>

<sig>XLI</sig>

work on the Sforza design and on the *Last Supper* speaks most convincingly. All of this, however, makes what has been believed for over a hundred years increasingly implausible: namely, that in 1493, at the wedding of Emperor Maximilian to Bianca Maria Sforza, the finished model paraded under a triumphal arch. Which one? Perhaps the small wax model mentioned by Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Italian Renaissance artists.</note>? Or surely not the one made of clay, in natural size, 7½ meters high, without the rider? This one likely never left the *Corte Vecchia* <note>The Old Court, the ducal palace in Milan where Leonardo had his workshop.</note> where Leonardo shaped it and was intended to cast it. The description by Pietro Lazzarone—"At the very front stood Francesco Sforza, ruler of the Ligurians and of upper Insubria <note>Historical regions in Northern Italy.</note>, carried by a horse, known to the whole world"—has been misleadingly applied to Leonardo's work. The equestrian image under the triumphal arch, which shone during the procession, was merely painted on simple canvas—perhaps the same one used in 1491 for the decoration of a hall at Lodovico's wedding; for such things were, as Müller-Walde has proven (*Yearbook of the Prussian Art Collections*, 1897), customary in the House of Sforza. By 1497, the model was in any case ready for casting. At that moment, Lodovico "the Moor" <note>Lodovico Sforza (1452–1508), Leonardo's patron in Milan.</note> was harassing the artist and had him admonished, among other things, regarding the *Last Supper*; he remains silent about the monument. Leonardo was ready; the statue simply could not be cast. The commission was missing. The horse was to be 7½ meters high; that required 80,000 kilograms of bronze, which Leonardo intended to melt in 3–4 furnaces in order to bring the casting out of a single mold—that is, in one piece—perfectly. What he planned for the pedestal, and what it would have required, we do not hear. By no means could the Sforza monument have used a hollow substructure, such as Leonardo proposed for the Trivulzio funerary monument; how could such a substructure have been able to bear the weight of the bronze colossus!

<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the failure to cast the Sforza monument, shifting focus from technical difficulties to the financial and political collapse of the Sforza court, and the eventual fate of the clay model.</meta>

<page-num>XLII</page-num>

Therefore, the sketches cannot have been intended for the equestrian statue of Francesco Sforza <note>The founder of the Sforza dynasty and father of Leonardo’s patron, Lodovico.</note> whose pedestal arches over the sarcophagus with the recumbent figure of the deceased in the manner of an open, column-supported chapel—unless it were for a version of more modest dimensions. However, since a large number of drawings showing the horse rearing over or leaping across a fallen soldier—drawings that still bear the mark of a more youthful precision—show such a tomb sheltered within its pedestal, I can only assume that a monument in bold movement and rich execution was first planned for Sforza, though of moderate size and intended for a church. When a second model later proposed the calm gait of the horse, the <term>terribilità</term> <note>original: "terribilità" — a quality of emotional intensity and awe-inspiring power, often associated with the works of Michelangelo and Leonardo.</note>, the sheer grandeur, was to be transferred into the unprecedented scale of the horse and rider.

If the monument was not executed, despite all concessions to feasibility and to the patron, the reason certainly does not lie in Leonardo’s will or ability. Around this time, Leonardo complains that he must earn his living in other ways; for two years, he and his assistants had remained entirely without salary. From all sides, enemies and wars beset "the Moor" <note>Lodovico Sforza, nicknamed Il Moro.</note>; ruin threatened him; there was no money left for great artistic endeavors. And that is likely where the Sforza monument foundered. What follows is merely the end without song or fanfare—the neglect and decay of the model in the <term>Corte vecchia</term> <note>The Old Court in Milan, where Leonardo's workshop was located.</note>; the archers who, in 1500, shot at it out of sheer wantonness; but even this was not the very final end. On September 19, 1501, Ercole d’Este, Duke of Ferrara, wrote to his Milanese agent: “Knowing that there exists in Milan a model of a horse, by a certain Master Leonardo, a master very skilled in such matters, a model which Duke Lodovico...”

<sig>XLVII</sig>

This work was to consist of "a panel in oil featuring Our Dear Lady" by Leonardo, along with side panels depicting two angels, set within an "altar-frame <note>original: "Ancona"; a large, carved wooden frame for an altarpiece.</note> with figures in relief covered in the finest gold," the production of which had been undertaken by Ambrogio da Predis. However, the brotherhood refused to pay the 300 ducats which the two artists demanded for their labor and high expenses. They valued the painting of the Mother of God at no more than 25 ducats, even though—"as is evident from a list provided by said petitioners"—its value amounted to at least one hundred ducats, for which price several persons were already prepared to buy it. Consequently, da Predis and Leonardo addressed a petition to the authorities—it is assumed between 1491 and 1494—so that "without further delay of time," an appraisal of the painting might be conducted by two persons "experienced in such matters <note>original: "in talibus erfahren"</note>." They requested that, following this appraisal, the Confraternity of the Holy Conception be forced to fulfill their duty or "leave the aforementioned Our Dear Lady in oil to the named exponents."

This "Our Dear Lady" is the famous "Virgin of the Rocks" <note>original: "Vierge aux Rochers"</note>. As is well known, it exists in several versions, and connoisseurs have argued long enough over which is the original: the version in the Louvre or the one in the English National Gallery. The London painting originates from the church of San Francesco in Milan itself; it is the same one described by Lomazzo in 1584, which in 1777 passed directly from the church into the possession of the English collector Gavin Hamilton for 30 ducats. The French version, however, is said to have been owned by Francis I; in any case, Cassiano del Pozzo (1625) and Father le Dan (1642) mention it as one of the paintings they admired in the royal gallery at Fontainebleau. Despite multiple "restorations"—that is, despite the overpaintings which, for example, have rendered the angel's posture entirely incomprehensible—scholars have spoken out unconditionally in favor of the Paris Madonna. Not only do the heads of the angel and the infant John correspond exactly in form and turn to the magnificent studies that we possess (some provided with pouncing holes <note>original: "Durchpauselöchern"; small holes pricked into a drawing to transfer the design to a panel by dusting it with charcoal powder.</note>) in the Louvre and in the Royal Library of Turin; but what proves more is the quality of the painting. 

There emanates from the wonderful grace of this Holy Virgin, from the profound earnestness of the two children, from the beauty of the angel with eyes intoxicated by paradise; there emanates from the divine invention of this scenery—the dark rocky grotto through whose crevices the delicate light of heaven trickles down silver upon the holy figures from above, and which allows one to sense the earthly world in the background as if at a distance from the world; there emanates from the somewhat archaic constraint in the appearance of this sweetly-mature Mother of God, from the mysteriousness in the sign language <note>original: "Gebärdensprache"; the symbolic gestures and hand positions.</note> of Mary and the angel; there emanates from every stone and every flowering herb and the dead luster of the pool of water, into which the Christ Child would glide if the arm of his guardian spirit did not hold him; there emanates from the interplay of these elements in a magical alternation of light and dark an inexplicably compelling poetry, against which the London painting—with its greater clarity and intelligibility, with its "prettier" qualities, with all its skillfulness in the arrangement of structural lines, in the greater speed of a brush that knows no reflection, but also in its greater generality and the soulless emptiness of so many parts—cannot compete at all. The coloring on the associated side panels matches perfectly, leading us to believe that the entire altarpiece <note>original: "Ancona"; a large, multi-paneled altarpiece common in the Italian Renaissance.</note>, even if under Leonardo's supervision, was painted by Ambrogio da Predis. According to the documents, the altar work for Saint Francis <note>San Francesco Grande in Milan.</note> was created between 1491 and 1494. Regarding the Louvre painting, one would like to assume it was painted not too long after the Florentine "Adoration." Anyone who knows Leonardo's hesitant way of working cannot possibly fit such a novel, grandiose work—with its solution to so many painterly problems of lighting, composition, and the treatment of form—into the timeframe of 1490–99, which was entirely occupied by the Sforza monument <note>The "Gran Cavallo," a massive bronze horse intended for Francesco Sforza.</note> and the "Last Supper." The varied repetition for the church of Saint Francis, in which Leonardo primarily utilized the hand of da Predis, may then indeed have fallen into the nineties and is precisely the London version of the "Virgin of the Rocks" <note>original: "Vierge aux rochers".</note>. In recent years, a third, smaller version of the "Holy Virgin of the Grotto" has been discovered in Saint Ambrose at Affori near Milan, which was demonstrably in the possession of the noble families Corbella, Litta, and d’Adda, and came to that village church through inheritance in 1844. Naturally, this work has also found its "prophets" who declared it to be the actual original prototype; however, it is quite obviously a repetition by a master's hand—that of Sodoma, say some, or that of Luini, say others.

In the "Virgin of the Rocks," Leonardo finally expresses himself fully as an artist, and indeed with a mastery at the first great attempt that cannot be explained by the incessant study of nature in its appearances and laws alone, but only through something inexplicable: through his genius. Now he had attained mastery over all his means and thus a freedom of ability, such as would find overwhelming expression in the "Last Supper."

<summary>The author argues that the London version of the "Virgin of the Rocks" was likely executed by Ambrogio da Predis under Leonardo's guidance, while the Louvre version represents Leonardo's earlier, original genius. A third version in Affori is dismissed as a high-quality copy by a follower like Sodoma or Luini.</summary>

We do not know when Leonardo received the actual commission to decorate the wall of the refectory <note>The dining hall of a monastery.</note> in the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie; however, from a faded inscription in the refectory, Müller-Walde <note>Paul Müller-Walde (1858–1931), an art historian known for his studies on Leonardo.</note> concludes that Leonardo began painting between 1490 and 1494, because Beatrice is mentioned in this legend and is called the Duchess of Bari. On October 21, 1495, however, Lodovico ceased to use the title Duke of Bari—at that fateful and yet, for him, fortunate moment that made him the Duke of Milan. Since his marriage to the energetic, ambitious Princess of Este <note>Beatrice d'Este.</note>, a driving force had entered his politics. Beatrice found it intolerable that she should play a secondary role, and that the incapable Gian Galeazzo, held in a state of legal minority, should receive the honors of a ruler. She urged her husband toward ruthlessness and severity; she incessantly insulted Isabella, the wife of Gian Galeazzo, who complained most bitterly in Naples about the unworthy treatment she received, as well as the force with which her husband was still kept away from state affairs. King Ferrante grew angry and issued threats. Lodovico sought a distraction for him. He encouraged the King of France to come to Italy and conquer Naples for himself as the inheritance of the House of Anjou. While Charles VIII still wavered and alliances were forming for and against him, Lodovico attempted to bind the German Emperor to himself as a counterweight by giving him Gian Galeazzo’s sister as a wife with a truly princely dowry, and by securing for himself, in any event, a document from the Emperor that invested him with the Duchy of Milan. He claimed this because he was "born in the purple" <note>A term signifying a child born to a reigning monarch, used here to argue his legitimacy over his nephew.</note> and thus the only rightful claimant to the throne: his older brother, the father of Gian Galeazzo, had come into the world before Francesco Sforza had risen from a <term>Condottiere</term> <note>A leader of mercenary soldiers in Renaissance Italy.</note> to a prince. He had imagined the French enterprise quite differently: in an Italian and contemporary fashion, more polite, more diplomatic. In the <term>Condottieri war</term> <note>A style of mercenary warfare common in Renaissance Italy, characterized by strategic maneuvering and financial leverage rather than total destruction.</note> which he knew, the one who could pay best and longest was in the right, and that would always have been him. When a powerful league finally formed against Charles VIII—whose luck quickly aroused misgivings and envy—it was through the anxious efforts of the Duke, despite the cool hesitation of the Venetians, and despite the open resistance of Emperor Maximilian, who, now that he had brought home his bride <note>Bianca Maria Sforza.</note> and perhaps under her influence, saw in Lodovico a poisoner and a usurper of the throne. The <term>Moro</term> <note>Lodovico Sforza's nickname, "The Moor," likely due to his dark complexion.</note> joined this league, and the King had to be glad to escape with his life and honor from that Italy which a few months earlier had lain at his feet. But the Italian turmoils and the French danger did not cease. And when Charles VIII died in 1498, his successor Louis XII, a grandson of Valentine Visconti, threateningly called himself King of the Two Sicilies and Duke of Milan.

The great work of these years was, alongside the Sforza Colossus <note>The massive bronze horse monument intended for Francesco Sforza, which was never cast.</note>, the mural in the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie. The compositional sketches we possess date from the twilight hours in which the first thought gradually takes shape; likewise the notes in the manuscripts of the South Kensington Museum <note>Now the Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A).</note> (see pp. 186, 187). Nothing, almost nothing else of it remains to us! However, the overwhelming impression the work made on the imagination of the time is reflected in the anecdotes linked to the painting, in the novellas <note>Short stories or tales, a popular literary form in the Renaissance.</note> that take it as their starting point; and to these we owe traits that make Leonardo’s nature, genius, and way of working more vivid to us than many a learned treatise. Matteo Bandello, a nephew of the Prior of Santa Maria delle Grazie, who was a novice in the monastery during the last decade of the Quattrocento <note>The 1400s (15th century).</note>, recounts in the famous introduction to his 58th Novella: "There were in Milan at the time of Lodovico Sforza Visconti, Duke of Milan, several noblemen in the monastery of the Grazie..."

I also saw him (if the mood or whim took him) at midday, when the sun is in the sign of Leo <note>Referring to the height of summer heat in July or August.</note>, leave the Old Court <note>original: "Corte Vecchia," the ducal residence in Milan where Leonardo worked on his sculpture.</note> where he was composing that stupendous horse of clay, and come directly to Saint Mary of the Graces <note>Santa Maria delle Grazie.</note> and, having climbed the scaffolding, seize the brush, give one of those figures two or three brushstrokes, and immediately go away again elsewhere. The Cardinal asked how much salary he received from Duke Ludovico <note>Ludovico Sforza, "Il Moro," Duke of Milan and Leonardo's patron.</note>. Leonardo replied that he usually had a pension of 2,000 ducats <note>A gold coin used as a standard currency across Europe.</note>, not counting the gifts and presents the Duke gave him all day long.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci's artistic methods, specifically how he observed real-life models to inform his compositions, transitioning from Giraldi's account to those of Vasari and the author's own analysis.</meta>

<page-num>LVI</page-num>

...it with every possible diligence in that panel which he painted in Milan in the monastery of the Preaching Friars <note>The Dominican Order; the painting referenced is the *Last Supper* at Santa Maria delle Grazie.</note>, in which our Savior is depicted with his disciples sitting at the table.” This narrative is certainly correct. Leonardo recommends to the painter himself to always have a little book with him and to note down with a few strokes whatever seemed remarkable to him. “It pleased him so much,” says Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Italian Renaissance artists.</note>, “when he saw certain bizarre heads, either with beards or with the hair of natural men, that he could have followed one who pleased him for an entire day; and he fixed him so firmly in his memory that afterwards, having arrived home, he drew him as if he had him before his eyes.” And notes such as: “Giovannina, fantastic face—lives in <term>Sta Caterina</term> <note>Saint Catherine</note>, in the hospital”—“Cristofano da Castiglione lives in the <term>Pietà</term>, has a good head” confirm this just as much as his drawings, especially the so-called <term>caricatures</term> <note>Exaggerated portraits emphasizing grotesque or unique features.</note>, which for the most part are only studies after the grotesque formations which nature produces and art ignores. But whoever assumes from this that Leonardo ever used nature exactly as it presented itself to him, or that he—as even Goethe <note>Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, the German polymath who wrote extensively on Leonardo's *Last Supper*.</note> was still permitted to believe—had “sought an approximate figure” for the idea that hovered before him in order to place it into the position which the composition required (in a sense, to work a portrait into the compositional scheme), has not grasped this artist. Leonardo studied reality incessantly in order to supply his imagination with an ever-new treasury of forms; but he copied in order to compose from it. What he found useful in nature first had to go into the melting pot of his spirit and did not come out until it looked as if it were entirely Leonardo and born freely out of his own idea—a work, “to which,” as in Dante <note>A reference to Dante Alighieri's *Paradiso* (Canto XXV), describing his poem.</note>, “both heaven and earth have set their hand” <note>original: "al quale han posto mano e cielo e terra"</note>, upon which heaven and earth have labored until a thing resulted...

The author argues that Leonardo did not simply copy these models into his paintings, but transformed them through his own creative "melting pot."</summary>
