<meta>This page continues the analysis of Leonardo da Vinci’s artistic philosophy, moving from his use of real-life models to the technical and spiritual reasons behind the physical decay of the Last Supper and his preference for oil painting over fresco.</meta>

<page-num>LVII</page-num>

was created, which signifies something great, “a fiction that signifies a great thing” <note>original: "una finzione che significa cosa grande"</note>. We can follow this process down to the smallest detail in the sketches for the equestrian monument <note>The "Gran Cavallo," a massive bronze monument intended for Francesco Sforza that was never completed.</note>. Why the *Last Supper*, this summation of the highest wisdom and highest skill, has perished, while the wall paintings of the first available fool of that time survive, we know: the condition of the wall, which Leonardo sought in vain to remedy; added to that, various misfortunes and the technique in which it was executed. But let us remember: as Lomazzo <note>Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo (1538–1592), a painter and theorist who wrote extensively on Leonardo.</note> tells us, Leonardo was one of the first in Italy to exchange tempera painting for oil painting; he still lacked much experience, and he was enticed to seek what no other had done. Above all, however: it is not the line, not the rounding, not the color, not the group, not the light, indeed, not even the subject matter itself which he represents—all mere means—that are the center of his art: he is a painter of expression <note>original: "Ausdrucksmaler"</note>; he wants, like nature, to reveal the soulful in the appearance, and to present every emotion intensely, yet in the most subtle manner, so that it does not violate the modesty of nature, which achieves greatness with inconspicuous means, yet often affects us as if with the highest richness and the highest beauty of selective art. This cannot be achieved with the abbreviated process of fresco <note>Fresco requires rapid painting onto wet plaster, which does not allow for the slow, layered "sfumato" technique Leonardo preferred.</note>. Extremely selective amidst the most exuberant springs of invention, convinced that only one form can be the perfect one, he said—like Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE known for his realism.</note> in the Greek anecdote—that he lingered long over each of his works so that it might live long. A man of the deepest considerations, it had to remain possible for him to still apply a "stroke of repentance" <note>original: "Reuezug"; a pentimento, or an alteration made by the artist during the painting process.</note>, as Goethe calls it, to his picture. He did not fall upon his work like a lion upon its prey: but that is what the fresco painter must do. It is described to us time and again that he was unable to approach a great task other than trembling in his whole body: he could not...

<summary>The author explains that Leonardo's *Last Supper* decayed because he prioritized psychological expression and technical experimentation with oil over the durable but restrictive fresco technique. Leonardo's perfectionism required a slow, contemplative process that allowed for constant revisions, which was incompatible with the rapid pace of traditional wall painting.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s technical struggles with fresco versus oil painting, specifically regarding the Last Supper, before transitioning to an analysis of his Saint Jerome and his decorative work in the Sforza Castle in Milan.</meta>

<page-num>LVIII</page-num>

employ a different technique than that of oil, which necessitates interruptions and gives full scope to the "finest considerations," as Leonardo says. Thus, the greatest artist, thinker, and inventor of the Renaissance was bound to fail, by the very nature of his genius, in things that the least of his pupils knew how to avoid; and so we are poorer by a masterpiece that remained unparalleled in every direction.

Strzygowski <note>Josef Strzygowski (1862–1941), an influential and controversial art historian.</note> likewise places the only partially painted image of *Saint Jerome*—with the wonderfully large and decorative lion lying in the foreground (Vatikan)—in the 1490s, in contrast to Müller-Walde <note>Paul Müller-Walde (1858–1931), a Leonardo scholar known for his archival research.</note>, who believes it was created in Florence. Supporting the former view are the mastery of the chiaroscuro <term>chiaroscuro: the treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting</term> treatment, the distribution of light, and the thorough knowledge of anatomy. The neck and shoulder sections in particular have a great affinity with a few drawings that Leonardo made for his book on the human figure.

Furthermore, Leonardo participated in the decoration of the Castle <note>The Castello Sforzesco in Milan.</note>—his work in the *Saletta negra* <note>The "Little Black Room."</note> has unfortunately fallen victim to a lack of understanding, though it is documented; his painting in the *Sala della Torre* or *delle Asse* <note>The "Room of the Wooden Boards."</note> has not only been uncovered and exposed with the greatest care, but has also been restored in full beauty and fidelity, as Luca Beltrami <note>An architect and historian who led the restoration of the Castello Sforzesco.</note> assures us: an ingenious and graceful decoration in the style of a pergola <note>original: "Pergolata"</note>, mighty trunks whose densely foliated branches intertwine and are tied together by means of gilded cords in a play of the most wonderful entanglements. Studies for this can be found in the pages of the *Codex Atlanticus* (Fol. 261 r., Fol. 273 v.) and the Windsor Collection (see, for example, Edouard Rouveyre’s edition, *Notes and Sketches on the Anatomy of the Horse* <note>original: "Notes et Croquis sur l’Anatomie du Cheval"</note>, Vol. II., Fol. 57 r.).

<page-num>LIX</page-num>

Beltrami's <note>Luca Beltrami (1854–1933), the architect and historian who led the restoration of the Castello Sforzesco.</note> findings are intertwined with an interesting episode which casts a sharp light on the allegedly brilliant existence of Leonardo at the court of "Il Moro" <note>Lodovico Sforza (1452–1508), nicknamed "The Moor," Duke of Milan and Leonardo's patron.</note>. In the autumn of 1495, doors were broken through in the "Camerini" <note>Small private chambers or cabinets.</note>—which were located near the castle garden next to the tower—and the painting ground was prepared; the Duke wished to see these rooms finished quickly. However, there exists a draft of a letter that Lodovico Moro had written on June 8, 1496, to the Archbishop of Milan in Venice:

> "The painter who was painting our Camerini today caused a certain scandal, because of which he departed; and since we must now think of another painter to deliver the work and to satisfy that for which we employed the labor of the one who has absented himself, and since we hear that Master Petro Perusino <note>Pietro Perugino (c. 1446–1523), a famous Umbrian painter and teacher of Raphael.</note> is there (in Venice), it seems right to us to charge you to speak with the said Perugino and hear from him if he wishes to come to serve us, telling him that if he came, we would make such conditions for him that he could be satisfied"...

However, Perugino had already left Venice, and it was not known there where he was now. The Duke then made inquiries regarding other painters; a document exists that is interesting for its characterization of those proposed—Botticelli, Filippino Lippi, Domenico Ghirlandajo, and again Perugino—between whom the palm of victory "is almost ambiguous" <note>original: "è quasi ambigua"</note>—that is, it wavers quite a bit. On March 28, 1497, Lodovico turned—likewise in vain—to Guido and Rodolfo di Baglioni, lords of Perugia, to ask them to persuade Perugino to come to Milan "to satisfy some matters" that he had planned, and to make the master understand that "if he came here, he would receive such treatment <term>treatment: "Traktament" here refers to salary, board, and general reception</term> from us that he would always be satisfied to have come."

— But who was the painter who, after a certain scandal, abandoned the work on the *Camerini* <note>Small private chambers in the Castello Sforzesco.</note> and whom the Duke felt could only be replaced by the best artist in Tuscany? Müller-Walde <note>Paul Müller-Walde (1858–1931), a German art historian and Leonardo specialist.</note> decides in favor of Leonardo. On June 29, 1497, the Duke gave the order to Marchesino Stanga <note>A high-ranking courtier and diplomat for the Sforza family.</note> to remind "Leonardo the Florentine" <note>original: "Leonardo Fiorentino"</note> that he must finish the work begun in the Refectory of the *Grazie* <note>The dining hall of the Santa Maria delle Grazie convent, home to "The Last Supper."</note>, so that he might afterwards "apply himself" to the other wall of the same Refectory (on which he painted the portraits of Lodovico, his wife, and his sons). And a second time, on November 29, he wrote to the same gentlemen to ensure that he "had" Perugino, either to remain permanently in his service or only for a limited time: the Duke would take him exactly as he wished... This too remained without result. — But had a rupture really occurred between "The Moor" <note>Lodovico Sforza.</note> and Leonardo? — If the Prince had reason to complain, the artist had much more. A few half-words, which Müller-Walde believes may be referred to the Duke, betray a deep-seated resentment: "first the benefices and afterwards the works, and then the ingratitude, and following this the unworthy complaints".... We have two letter drafts by Leonardo (pages 206 and 207), which, although preserved only in fragments, are nevertheless of great importance and provide an insight into the hardships of his existence. It seems that instead of money, he had been assigned "benefices" <note>term: Benefizien; here referring to the right to collect specific taxes or fees rather than receiving a direct salary.</note> such as gate tolls, water taxes, etc. — these were the "gifts" with which the Duke overwhelmed him "all day long." For two years he had remained without a salary, yet he had to feed six people. Against this background, the differences had developed to such an extent that Leonardo broke off his work, and Lodovico sought a replacement for him. Now, Leonardo nevertheless relents. <meta>This page continues the narrative of Leonardo da Vinci’s final years in Milan under the patronage of Duke Lodovico Sforza, transitioning from his financial distress to the political collapse of the Sforza dynasty.</meta>

LXII

The author of "On the Divine Proportion" <note>original: "De divina proportione" — a famous mathematical treatise by Luca Pacioli.</note>, whom the Moor <note>Lodovico Sforza, nicknamed "Il Moro" for his dark complexion.</note> had drawn to Milan in 1496 and who quickly became friends with Leonardo, reports that on February 8, 1499, "in the invincible castle of the illustrious city of Milan," a "praiseworthy and scientific duel" <note>A formal intellectual debate or scholarly competition common in Renaissance courts.</note> took place in the presence of the Duke, which he attended in the company of "the most ingenious architect and engineer and diligent inventor of new things, Leonardo da Vinci, our Florentine countryman." On April 26, the Duke presented Leonardo with a vineyard outside the Vercelliana Gate, measuring 16 rods <note>A traditional unit of land measurement.</note>, with words of the highest honor and with the acknowledgment of "having so much obligation toward him that, if we did not give him some gift, we would believe ourselves to be failing in our duty".... Favor and grace could rise no higher; yet it was no longer able to achieve anything effective. Pope Alexander VI, Louis XII, and Venice had formed an alliance against Milan. "Fine, you have shared my state with the King," said the Moor to the ambassadors of the Most Serene Republic <note>original: "Serenissima" — the formal title for the Republic of Venice.</note>; "but by God! I will send you out to the sea to fish, and you shall not keep a hand’s breadth of earth on the mainland" <note>original: "per Dio! vi farò andare a pescare a la marina, e non avrete in terra ferma un palmo di terra"</note>. He concluded a counter-alliance with the Emperor, the Sultan, and the King of Naples; but when Louis XII crossed the Alps in July 1499, as one fortress after another fell "before the impetuosity of the Swiss and the children of France," Maximilian <note>Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I.</note> was naturally just then involved in war-dealings with the Cantons <note>The Swiss Confederacy.</note>, and Federigo <note>King Frederick of Naples.</note> seized the moment and remained inactive until it was too late: then Lodovico the Moor gave way and fled with all his treasures to Tyrol, while Milan opened its gates to Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, the French commander. On October 6, Louis XII entered in triumph and was jubilantly greeted by the people.

LXIII

welcomed. However, the French rule was even harsher than that of the Sforzas. Therefore, when Lodovico approached from Como with an army of Swiss and Germans, Milan—which had been incited by the followers of the Moor <note>Lodovico Sforza's nickname</note>, including Jacopo Andrea da Ferrara—rose up, and on February 5, 1500, the Duke returned to his capital. But the French arrived in forced marches from the Romagna, where they had been assisting the plans of Cesare Borgia; new troops moved in from France. When the Moor confronted the enemy at Novara on April 10, the Swiss mercenaries refused to fight and surrendered the Duke. He was taken to France and died in 1510 in the dungeon at Loches. "A man of singular wisdom," says Paolo Giovio <note>A 16th-century Italian physician, historian, and biographer</note>, "yet of an ambition without limits—born for the ruin of Italy." France now imposes a harsh punitive judgment upon the fickle city; the partisans of the Sforza are stripped of their property, and Jacopo Andrea is captured, beheaded, and quartered.

Leonardo da Vinci had left Milan before the catastrophe broke. Whether it was foresight, caution, or a specific commission that prompted him to do so cannot be determined; yet loyalty, patriotism, and similar general civic virtues would never have held or bound him. Leonardo, like Faust <note>The legendary German scholar who makes a pact with the devil; here used to represent a restless, wandering spirit</note>, belongs to the "homeless"; he exists without a fixed relationship to his contemporary world. He loves all creatures; he is full of kindness for all who are dependent on him; his students are as close to his heart as sons; nevertheless, it must be emphasized—and it should come as no surprise—that nothing and no one could bind Leonardo, except for a problem that he was pursuing; that he could not have lived for any prince, any country, any friend, or any woman, but rather that his entire being and existence stood in the service of the overpowering passion of his mind and was entirely [driven] by the goals

To be able to belong to no one but himself and his work—this is the innate law of genius and thus its destiny; it turns the extraordinary man, in the Faustian sense <note>Referring to the restless, striving spirit of Goethe's Faust</note>, into a solitary figure, a superman, an "un-man." While the French approach, Leonardo continues to work undeterred. "On August 1, 1499, I wrote here of motion and weight," he notes (<term>Codex Atlanticus</term> <note>A twelve-volume set of drawings and writings by Leonardo</note> Folio 104 r.) and seven drawings: "Of the bath of Duchess Isabella. — A is placed so that the pin does not turn at the same time as the screw. — Pen" — a final memory of the last commissions of Lodovico, who gladly accommodated all the indifferent wishes of the unhappy widow of Gian Galeazzo, "Isabella of Aragon Sforza, unique in misfortune," as she signed her name.

Another record (<term>Codex Atlanticus</term> Folio 284 r.), however, shows that Leonardo did not face events blindly. He makes an inventory of his monetary holdings, according to the types of coins, which he kept in various hiding places in his home.

On December 29, he then deposited his surplus cash through a Milanese banking house in the Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, the Florentine savings bank of that time: 600 <term>gold florins</term> <note>original: "Goldgulden"; a standard gold coin used throughout Europe</note> in total—the result of seventeen years of immense activity.

Leonardo himself likely left Milan long before. LXVI

The Louvre cartoon, of which a smaller and much less lively repetition exists in the Uffizi, represents Isabella d’Este Gonzaga, Margravine of Mantua. No other of her portraits paints her essence for us better than this wonderful sketch, with the gentle greeting of the smiling eyes and the animated play of the witty, spiritedly pursed lips. Leonardo never sought a common "striking likeness"; yet the study resembles her in its features—and even more through the movement of those features—sufficiently to match the portraits in the Vienna Court Museum, which are considered valuable in terms of likeness: the medals by Cristoforo Romano and the miniature from Ambras Castle, a copy of that portrait which the Gonzaga family regarded as the most faithful... Leonardo awaited the outcome of the fates of Milan in Venice, in the company of Luca Pacioli, who had also left Lombardy "due to certain events in those parts" <note>original: "certi successi in questa parte"</note>, where the famous mathematician was well known through his works. On March 13, 1500, the musical instrument maker Lorenzo Gusnasco wrote to Isabella of Mantua: "Leonardo Vinci is in Venice, who has shown me a likeness of Your Highness which is entirely natural, as well made as is hardly possible" <note>original: "molto naturale a quella, sta tanto bene facto non è possibile"</note>. And while in Milan the ground upon which he built his existence collapses, Leonardo pursues mathematical and geological studies, observing the ebb and flow of the tide and the life of the rivers; "for," he says, "this kind nature provides in such a way that everywhere in the world you find something to learn." Milan falls definitively into the hands of the French; his hopes are destroyed, his greatest works are threatened. **I**n April 1500, Leonardo da Vinci is back home in Florence. He withdraws 50 gold guilders from his deposit at Santa Maria Nuova <note>A major hospital in Florence that also functioned as a bank for citizens</note>. He lives with Luca Pacioli, to whom he owes much in mathematics and who, in turn, owes much to him: besides a wealth of intellectual stimulation, also the perspective drawings and sculptural models of regular and semi-regular bodies for his work "On the Divine Proportion" and "On Architecture" (printed 1509 in Venice) — "crafted and shaped by that <term>ineffabile sinistra</term> <note>original: "unbeschreibliche Linke"</note>, the indescribable left hand, adapted to all mathematical disciplines, of the prince and foremost among mortals today, our Leonardo da Vinci of Florence, in that blessed time when we found ourselves together in the same service in the truly wondrous city of Milan," as the good Friar <note>Referring to Pacioli, who was a Franciscan monk</note> expresses it in his bombastic enthusiasm — works which Leonardo continued independently in 1508–1509. In the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, he carries on his beloved anatomical studies unhindered. He resumed his investigations regarding making the Arno navigable and a canal system that regulated the water flow, served the irrigation of the land, and the drainage of the marshes. He submits an expert opinion to the consuls of the Merchant’s Guild regarding the reasons why the Franciscan church of San Salvadore (on the hill of San Miniato) — "the beautiful peasant girl," <note>original: "la bella villanella"</note> as Michelangelo called it — was in danger of collapsing; he notes a movement of the earth and explains how to remedy it. — Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari, the 16th-century biographer of Italian artists</note> relates that Filippino Lippi, being the amiable person he was, had at Leonardo's request ceded the commission given to him by the monks of the <term>Servi</term> <note>The Servite Order at the Santissima Annunziata</note> to paint a panel for the high altar of the Nun-

The clergyman replied on April 3rd: "As far as I can see, Leonardo's life is highly inconsistent and so uncertain that he seems to live from one day to the next. Since he has been in Florence, he has merely made the sketch for a cartoon. He represents a Christ as a child, about a year old, who, slipping from his mother's (<term>mamma</term>) arms, grasps a lamb and, it seems, squeezes it. The mother, almost rising from the lap of Saint Anne, takes the boy to detach him from the little lamb—the sacrificial animal that signifies the Passion <note>The suffering and death of Jesus Christ</note>. Saint Anne, rising slightly from her seat, seems to want to hold her daughter back so that she does not pull the child away from the lamb; she perhaps represents the Church, which would not wish the Passion of Christ to be prevented. And these figures are life-sized, but are contained in a small cartoon because they are all either sitting or standing hunched, and one is a little behind the other toward the left hand. And this sketch is not yet finished. He has done nothing else, except that two of his pupils are painting portraits and he occasionally puts his hand to one of them. He devotes intense labor to geometry and is extremely impatient with the brush." This valuable letter gives us the certainty that the cartoon for the painting of *The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne* <note>original: "h. Anna selbdritt" — a traditional German term for a depiction of St. Anne, the Virgin Mary, and the Christ Child together</note> in the Louvre dates to the beginning of this second Florentine period of the master

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s shifting priorities in 1501, moving from the specific commissions mentioned on the previous page to his evolving theoretical disdain for the physical labor of sculpture compared to the intellectual nature of painting.</meta>

<page-num>LXXIII</page-num>

could still entice Leonardo at this time. He held the conviction that an art form was lower the more mechanical it was. He had already written down by then that the sculptor, "in the execution of his work through the strength of his arm and the impact of the blow, consumes the marble or other prominent stone—which in its dimensions exceeds the figure enclosed within it—through a highly mechanical exercise (<term>esercizio</term> <note>original: "esercizio" — practice or physical exertion</note>)," and he describes the sculptor and his dwelling as covered in filth; in contrast to the painter, "who sits with great ease and well-dressed before his work and moves the feather-light brush with lovely colors. He is adorned with garments as it pleases him, and the dwelling is full of charming paintings and is clean, and often he is accompanied by musicians or by readers of diverse and beautiful works, which—without the noise of hammers or other mixed sounds—are then heard with great pleasure." Regarding sculpture, he now only praises the casting of bronze, which sets the mind in motion rather than the arm, and the way he strives to arrange his life is no longer far from his maxim: that designing is the work of a master, but execution is the work of a servant. One must not confuse this view—which in Leonardo was the result of growing spirituality and an almost morbid sensitivity toward the unlovely—with the self-image of younger artists who, during the <term>Cinquecento</term> <note>The 1500s, or the High Renaissance in Italy</note>, desired and attained a semi-princely status—such as a Raphael, who never went out without an entourage; a Titian, for whom Charles V picked up a dropped brush; or a Michelangelo, who indignantly rejected a commission from a Florentine acquaintance: "I do not keep a shop for the people." Leonardo was interested in a commission only insofar as a new problem beckoned to him within it. The rest was a burden to him. Even as an artist, he is primarily a researcher and inventor. perfection of his revenge, a multitude of arrests and incomprehensible deaths—such as that of the imprisoned Cardinal Orsini—provoke a true panic in Rome. The Orsini, the Colonna, and the Savelli <note>Three of the most powerful noble families in Renaissance Rome, usually bitter rivals</note> reconcile for once, and the Pope falls into fear and distress. He fortifies himself in the Vatican, the Cardinals barricade themselves in their palaces, and Alexander summons "his" Duke <note>Cesare Borgia, the Pope's son</note> in haste to Rome (late February 1503). Not a single word in the manuscripts betrays that Leonardo had been a witness to such terrible things. He sees and hears; but to an artist, life is merely material—often far more shadowy than that which he creates from it. Thus Leonardo, as Walter Pater <note>An influential 19th-century English essayist and art critic</note> says, moves unmoved through the most tragic fates, like one who, on some secret mission, strides through events as if only by chance. His secret mission was: to learn, to perceive, to create. He stood under the harsh command of his genius, and common humanity lay at times deep beneath him. Anyone who has read Goethe’s "Campaign in France" <note>original: "Campagne in Frankreich"; Goethe's account of the 1792 war, noted for his detached, scientific observations amidst the horrors of battle</note> knows what I mean. One would have to say that this episode in Leonardo’s life had also dissolved into nothing tangible, were it not for the wonderful geographical surveys that Leonardo made for the Borgia, some of which Richter <note>Jean Paul Richter, a scholar who compiled Leonardo's literary works</note> was permitted to publish. But these months bore good fruit in other ways as well. Leonardo had seen war up close.

In his house, meat is eaten two or three times a week; otherwise, they nourish themselves on eggs, vegetables, fruit, cheese (<term>ricotta</term> <note>A soft Italian whey cheese</note>), bread, and wine. The <term>Codex Atlanticus</term> <note>original: "Cod. atl."; Leonardo's largest collection of drawings and writings</note> (Folio 74 r.) contains a description of the Battle of Anghiari, with precise details of names and locations, taken from some chronicle or narrative. However advantageous that might have been for the Florentines—as a salvation and simultaneously as a warning to all future enemies never to touch those under heavenly protection—the Florentines appeared greater when they had helped themselves. Of what Leonardo drew from books or tradition, he could use nothing for his battle. The *Battle for the Standard* was therefore perhaps only the central main group of the painting, which, unfortunately, can hardly be reconstructed from the existing sketches. However, the cartoon—which, as Cellini (1558) says in his biography, was "the school of the whole world" <note>original: "la scuola del mondo"</note> as long as it hung in the Pope’s Hall—has vanished without a trace. While working on the cavalry battle (in which, according to Machiavelli, only a single man had fallen), Leonardo continued his scientific studies without pause. He had conceived of an Arno canal that would connect Florence with Prato, Pistoia, Serravalle, the Lake of Bientina, Lucca, and Pisa; through sufficient "cataracts" <note>term: cataracts — here meaning locks or weirs used to control water levels</note> it would revitalize all the stagnant "ponds" and have a water flow in all seasons to carry ships, drive mills and other works, and irrigate meadows and gardens. Initially, he thought this could be done without basins and locks, the construction and maintenance of which cost too much; with more thorough investigations of the terrain, more complicated plans emerged; but they would improve the land and bring the whole region 200,000 ducats. (Further details on this in the compilations by Mario Baratta, *Leonardo da Vinci in the studies for the navigation of the Arno*, Rome, Italian Geographical Society, 1905.) "They do not know why the Arno never remains in its channel, namely because the rivers that pour into it deposit earth upon their entry and take it away from the opposite bank, thus bending the river." He questioned a Sienese merchant about Flemish hydraulic engineering and learned from him that a river whose course is diverted from one place to another "must be flattered, rather than provoked by violence," and now he teaches how one can gradually move the river away from the place it damages by using fishing weirs, or lead it through a whole system of dams into a new, regulated bed with regulated junctions of the tribu—

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Leonardo da Vinci’s engineering projects during the war between Florence and Pisa, specifically his plan to divert the Arno River, and transitions into his scientific studies on flight.</meta>

<page-num>LXXXVI</page-num>

...should lead rivers into it. The Florentines were at that time involved in a long-drawn-out war with Pisa, and to defeat them completely was a matter of life and death. Even when the city was kept under the tightest siege, provisions were smuggled into the fortress from the sea via the river. The old proposals therefore gained new life: to divert the Arno away from Pisa and lead it toward Livorno; the Gonfaloniere <note>term: Gonfaloniere — the "Standard-bearer of Justice," the highest office in the Florentine Republic</note> Soderini and Machiavelli supported the plan. They turned to Leonardo. In July 1503, commissioned by the Signoria <note>term: Signoria — the governing body or council of the Florentine Republic</note>, he traveled out to the camp at Pisa with drawings and surveyed the terrain. The Priors approved the project; however, the execution was fragmented, thereby failing its purpose and falling victim to bitter criticism. Leonardo had likely hoped that these works—which, undertaken for war purposes, could only be temporary—would be the beginning of a magnificent, comprehensive work that he intended to develop based on his Lombard experiences. All the great cities of Tuscany would have been connected to Florence by canals and would have had their marketplace in the Florentine port of Livorno; great reservoirs with weirs to regulate the water flow; lock systems to help ships overcome differences in ground elevation. The *Codex Atlanticus* <note>original: "Cod. atl."</note> and the Windsor manuscripts contain countless designs that remained only designs. Florence had become a narrow-minded, very petty-bourgeois republic, in which they even attempted to pay a salary to an artist like Leonardo in copper coins—the anecdote is characteristic of the stingy mindset that prevailed in the Signoria at the beginning of the *Cinquecento* <note>term: Cinquecento — the 1500s or the High Renaissance period</note>.

At the same time as these, the mathematical, astronomical, and physical works were pursued with increasing intensity; observations on flight were collected and shaped into a theory, and attempts were made to construct a flying machine.

On July 12, 1505, a new notebook was begun (South Kensington Museum): "On the transformation of one body into another, without reduction or enlargement of matter," <note>original: "Von der Verwandlung eines Körpers in einen andern, ohne Verkleinerung oder Vergrößerung von Materie"</note> in which Leonardo intended to record all manner of geometrical problems.

When in May 1504 Isabella Gonzaga <note>Isabella d'Este, Marchioness of Mantua, one of the leading women of the Italian Renaissance</note>, having "come into good hope" of obtaining something from him, wrote personally to Leonardo and asked him for a youthful Christ, "who would be of that age he was when he disputed with the doctors, and with that sweetness and grace in appearance (*sweetness and softness of air* <note>original: "dolcezza e suavità di aere"</note>), which you possess in excellence as a special art," he gave nothing but promises. Once more Isabella tried and inquired in October whether he might not, if he were "bored (*wearied*) <note>original: "fastidito"</note> by the Florentine history," wish to create the requested thing for her as a recreation; yet even this so amiable reminder of his promise, *the obligation of faith* <note>original: "l’obbligo della fede"</note>, could not seduce Leonardo. His servant <note>term: Familiar — a close member of a household or an intimate assistant</note> and pupil Salai had offered himself for a work, says Dr. Solmi, but was not accepted in place of Leonardo.

If Leonardo felt bored and fatigued by the Florentine history <note>referring to the massive "Battle of Anghiari" fresco commission</note>, he had another work for his recreation. During these years, there stood on his easel that portrait which has become the epitome of the highest art and whose fame seems to grow continually. Just as the great books of humanity are never finished things, but rather every century, every epoch, every person continues to compose them, so is the *Gioconda* <note>The Mona Lisa</note>, in which Leonardo sang his highest song of woman, of...

What else Leonardo experienced in Florence was not very pleasant: “On the 7th day of July 1504, Wednesday at 7 o'clock, Ser Piero da Vinci died, notary of the Palace of the Podestà <note>The Palazzo del Podestà, now the Bargello, was the seat of the high magistrate in Florence.</note>, my father. That era did not yet know the modern, sentimental diary. One let the facts speak for themselves and attached, at most, a pious reflection to them. However, pious reflections of a practical kind did not suit the masculine, upright, and self-contained nature of Leonardo. In the face of the everyday sad things that happen to man, he left God out of the matter. Not because he was irreverent, but because his piety came from a different, higher disposition and flowed from a spirit that admires and adores the power and reason of what happens, but asks nothing for itself from it, except the strength to comprehend it and to teach it. Moreover, the death of his father brought him grief and a disappointment. He, the great one, the fame and pride of the house, remained only the natural <note>Meaning "illegitimate" or born out of wedlock.</note> son and came away without an inheritance. Vexation also grew for him from the poor relationship with the most brilliant younger artist of Florence, the bitter, violent, and suspicious Michelangelo. It was a subtle antipathy, I think, by nature between them, a repulsion caused by the contrast of temperament. <meta>This page continues the account of the rivalry between Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, moving from their intellectual disputes over Dante to Michelangelo's personal insults and Leonardo's scientific pursuit of human flight.</meta>

<page-num>XCII</page-num>

Agnolo <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti</note>, in order to deal Leonardo a blow, said: "And those capon-brained Milanese who actually believed in you!"

This occurred even before the failure of the Battle of the Anghiari <note>Leonardo's experimental mural in the Palazzo Vecchio which famously failed to dry correctly.</note>. According to Solmi <note>Edmondo Solmi (1874–1912), a pioneering scholar of Leonardo’s scientific manuscripts.</note>, Leonardo would have suffered another great disappointment around this time. His observations on the flight of birds have already been mentioned several times. The manuscripts contain drawings for flying machines, all of which are based on the same fundamental principle of action and reaction.

> "The object which strikes against the air evokes in it as much counter-force as the air evokes in the object itself <note>original: "Tanta forza si fa colla cosa incontro all’aria, quanto l’aria alla cosa"</note>. You see that the beating of wings against the air sustains the heavy eagle in the highest and thinnest air. Conversely, you see the air moving over the sea, filling the swelling sails and making the heavily laden ship run. From these proofs you may recognize that man, with his great wings, by generating force against the resisting air, will be able to victoriously subdue it and rise up upon it."

The main feature of the apparatus consists, therefore, of enormous wings which ingeniously transform the shape of <term>bat wings</term> <note>Leonardo preferred the structure of bat wings over feathered bird wings because the membrane provided a continuous surface without gaps.</note> into a movable mechanism. When these wings rose, they allowed the air to pass through, much like the feathers of birds; when they were lowered, the openings closed, and the air, compressed downward by the wingbeat, would support the weight like a cushion—or so Leonardo hoped. He had also thought of a double pair of wings with opposing motion: as the upper pair rose, the lower pair simultaneously descended. The apparatus itself was intended to imitate the body of a bird as closely as possible—indeed, to turn the human body itself into a bird's body. The manuscripts B and CA <note>Codex Atlanticus</note> contain interesting drawings of this. Sometimes the wings are attached to the limbs of the man, sometimes to a board that resembles an inverted

"Test your instrument over water," he writes, "so that in falling you do not hurt yourself." "You shall have a long tube girded about you, so that in falling you do not drown." Thus equipped, the father of the most modern <term>aeronautics</term> <note>The science or practice of travel through the air.</note>—one thinks of Lilienthal <note>Otto Lilienthal (1848–1896), the German "Flying Man" who successfully pioneered glider flights.</note>—believed himself equal to all airy adventures, and he intended to venture a serious attempt around this time. "The great bird will take its first flight from the back of a giant swan (cecero), filling the universe with amazement, all writings with its fame, and bringing eternal glory to the place where it was born," he prophesies in two variations (Ms. "On the Flight of Birds," *Sul volo degli uccelli*, Sabaschnikoff Edition, inside cover 2 and Fol. 18 v.). Now, it is documented that Leonardo was in Fiesole for a time in the year 1506, which possesses a long, bare hill, Monte Ceceri <note>The name "Monte Ceceri" translates to "Swan Mountain," which explains Leonardo's poetic wordplay.</note>. And in that region, a legend persists, as Solmi reports, that from the "naked mountain near Florence" a great swan took flight, which then disappeared, and no one ever saw it again. Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), the famous scholar whose father Fazio was an intimate friend of Leonardo—and who therefore could have known much about the artist and might have been the heir to some of Leonardo's scientific insights—writes (I quote according to Solmi) in "On Subtlety" <note>original: *De subtilitate*</note> with quiet irony: "Leonardo da Vinci also tried to fly; but it turned out badly for him: he was a great painter."

We desire no further requests, for the work must satisfy the public, and we cannot, without our own burden, allow him to be kept by Your Lordship any longer." "When he was once accused of deception and Piero Soderini grumbled against him," as **Vasari** <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Renaissance artists.</note> relates, he is said to have collected money with the help of his friends and returned it to the state treasury, though Soderini did not accept it. **Solmi** <note>Edmondo Solmi (1874–1912), a prominent Leonardo scholar.</note> would very much like this to have been a fact and to have occurred around this time. Finally, Chaumont released Leonardo on December 15th. The Republic of Florence had nothing to refuse the powerful King and ally. It finally gives up its claims on Leonardo.

What works Chaumont <note>Charles d'Amboise, Seigneur de Chaumont, the French governor of Milan.</note> commissioned from Leonardo, we do not know. The artist spent most of the waiting period until the King's arrival in Vaprio, the country estate of the noble Melzi family, whose son Francesco, born in 1493, became his pupil and remained as tenderly attached to him as a son. The fresco painting on the front of the Casa Melzi, a giant Madonna and Child, has been attributed to Leonardo, but is by no means worthy of his master hand. Various notes in manuscripts mention Vaprio, preserving the memory of the studies, experiments, and observations he made here.

On April 27, the master received back through Chaumont the vineyard outside the Porta Vercelliana, which Lodovico Sforza had once gifted to him. Now he grows his own wine there, plants trees and flowers, and has vegetable seeds sent to him from Florence . . .

On May 24, Louis XII entered Milan with great pomp. Around this time, Leonardo was appointed court painter, <term>peintre du Roy</term> <note>French: "Painter to the King."</note>. It was not difficult for him to completely win over the King. Indeed, Paul Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio, a contemporary historian and biographer.</note> says of him:

> "He was a charming spirit, most brilliant, of a magnificent nature (generous); his countenance was the most beautiful in the world. Since he was a wonderful inventor

The King gave him commissions, including one for a painting of the Madonna; he took an interest in Leonardo's hydraulic works and not only granted him the title of his engineer, but also gifted him—the date is disputed—a quantity of water from the canal of San Cristofano which, according to Venturi <note>Giovanni Battista Venturi (1746–1822), a physicist and historian who rediscovered many of Leonardo's scientific manuscripts.</note>, equals that of a small Lombard canal.

Then Francesco da Vinci, Leonardo's uncle, died; he had always held much affection for this nephew. Over the inheritance—a small house and a piece of land that yielded about 500 lire annually—a legal dispute broke out between Leonardo and his brothers. This dispute also reached back to the father's estate, insofar as Leonardo believed there must at least be a deed of gift for him, the illegitimate son. Equipped with recommendations from Chaumont dated August 15, 1507, and supported by a letter from the King and the protection of Cardinal Ippolito d'Este (Leonardo's letter to the latter is preserved in Modena), he began his lawsuit, which, however, dragged on immeasurably. The artist lived for half a year in the house of Piero Martelli, with the sculptor Giovanni Francesco Rustici. He occupied himself as usual. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci's life and work habits during his time in Florence, specifically focusing on his method of recording observations and his struggle to complete his vast scientific projects.</meta>

<page-num>XCVIII</page-num>

> I am, I will have to repeat the same thing in it several times, so that, O reader, you do not blame me because the things are many, and memory cannot preserve them, and say: — "this I will not write, because I wrote it before." — And if I did not wish to fall into such error, it would be necessary that for every case I copied, I would always have to read through everything past in order not to repeat, and especially since I go to writing at long intervals from one time to the next."

This entry shows us the working method of <term>Leonardo</term> <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), the polymath of the High Renaissance.</note>. Into small notebooks, such as he always carried with him—the French manuscripts contain some of these—he sketched and wrote everything that struck him or occurred to him; then from these he made unordered excerpts, whereupon he arranged the excerpts by subject matter—for example, Ms. C. in Paris, "On Light and Shadow," Ms. D., which contains compilations on the eye, the English manuscripts in Windsor (W. An. I, II, III, IV) on anatomy: from these he then intended one day to make treatises, regular books. He constantly cites these books of his on <term>mechanics</term> <note>The branch of physics dealing with the motion of objects and the forces acting upon them.</note>, on water—they were to form a giant work on the "things of nature"; if he ever completed one of them other than in his imagination, it has unfortunately been lost to us. However, as long as Leonardo possessed a breath of life, he much rather hesitated to conclude that which is infinite; when could a spirit like his and a pioneer like him, who found hardly any useful preliminary work in any field—his last predecessor is <term>Archimedes</term> <note>Ancient Greek mathematician and engineer (c. 287–212 BC) whose works Leonardo studied deeply.</note>—have been able to say he had completely explored any area? For the <term>scholastic</term> <note>A follower of Scholasticism, the medieval method of learning that relied on dogma and fixed authorities like Aristotle.</note>, of course, it had been different. For him, as <term>Gabriel Séailles</term> <note>French philosopher and art historian (1852–1922) who wrote a significant biography of Leonardo.</note> so beautifully says, "science is finished <note>original: "la science est faite"</note>. The world—the man who thinks it—God who creates it—that is the matter of a few folio volumes. His spirit, like his universe, is

--- Page 117 ---
<meta>This page continues the contrast between the rigid systems of the past and Leonardo da Vinci's expansive, boundary-pushing scientific method, moving into his collaborative work in Florence and his potential projects for the French King.</meta>

<page-num>XCIX</page-num>
<sig>VII*</sig>

a closed system <note>original: "système clos"</note>. He knows where science begins, where it ends, its divisions and their order; he knows after how many heavenly spheres one finally reaches Paradise and enters the Kingdom of God. Leonardo discovers a world whose boundaries constantly recede before him. He looks, and the phenomena multiply before his eyes." He is lured from step to step, from practice to theory, from science to science. His method forbids him "hasty ambitions" <note>original: "les ambitions hâtives"</note>, the rush of vanity. The system could not be at the beginning; and where did he find the end? —

Fortunately, Leonardo was one of those rare spirits who love the truth so much that for its sake they also love the path to it — as he himself expresses it, fame flies in the arms of labor, which almost disappears in the process. "No work is able to tire me. By nature, Nature has fashioned me so."

From science, this most perfect human talent recovered in art.

Giovanni Francesco Rustici, with whom he lived, was at that time occupied with a group of statues which had been commissioned from him in 1506 for the <term>Baptistery</term> <note>The octagonal religious building standing in front of the Florence Cathedral, famous for its bronze doors.</note>: Christ between the Pharisee and the Levite. One attributes to Leonardo more than a mere influence on this masterful work. The sculptor may have been strongly alive in him again at that time. It is even possible that one of the works which Louis XII discussed with him in Milan in 1507 was the equestrian monument for the Marshal of France, Trivulzio. The King may have wished to honor the conqueror of Lombardy, and Leonardo wished to see his old plans realized, even if on a more modest scale. <sig>C III</sig>

turned outward, the raised right arm with the commander’s staff pointing forward across the neck of the noble animal—the whole possessed of an indescribable natural nobility, of the most beautiful <term>eurhythmy</term> <note>original: "Eurhythmie"; a harmonious proportion or pleasing rhythm in artistic lines.</note> of lines, serving as a substitute for the boldness and passion of the former type. The substructure also consists of two basic forms. It opens above the <term>sarcophagus</term> <note>original: "Sarkophag"; a stone coffin, typically adorned with sculpture.</note> containing the deceased in the form of a triumphal arch or in the form of a hall. The eight figures of the monument were intended to be captives—(small sketches for these are found several times in the manuscripts; once Leonardo writes regarding such a figure: “make him out of wax, a finger long”—), a strange meeting of two geniuses in the same artistic thought: as is well known, prisoners were also intended to decorate Michelangelo’s tomb for Pope Julius II, which unfortunately remained a mutilated torso. Of the Trivulzio monument, less remains to us—nothing but this magnificent design on paper, which, one must hope, research will yet be able to bring into a clearer light. —

In the years between 1508 and 1513, everything in Leonardo’s life fluctuates. Into this period are crowded the works and designs of the master that one does not know how to place elsewhere; other works again, of which documents speak, have disappeared or were only planned; one can hardly date anything with certainty, not even the outcome of the legal dispute with his brothers. Did the decision or a settlement come in 1508, or in 1511? Certainly, Leonardo was mostly in Milan during this epoch. Which Madonnas he brought with him from Florence in a fairly advanced state in 1511 (or 1508?, as Solmi claims)—he solemnly announces the paintings to Marshal Chaumont in a draft letter which I reproduce on page 207—we do not know. Perhaps one of them was the <term>St. Anne with the Virgin and Child</term> <note>original: "h. Anna selbdritt"; a traditional motif in Christian art showing St. Anne, her daughter the Virgin Mary, and the infant Jesus.</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo's Milanese period, moving from the lost Trivulzio monument to his surviving and attributed paintings, specifically the Virgin and Child with Saint Anne, the Bacchus, and Saint John the Baptist.</meta>

<sig>CIV</sig>

...g this time, as evidenced by the many Lombard school replicas of this magnificent composition. What unity it possesses, and what abundance at the same time! An infinite content of movement in the smallest space, as H. Wölfflin <note>Heinrich Wölfflin (1864–1945), a highly influential Swiss art historian who defined principles of art analysis.</note> says; the entire wealth of contrasting lines tamed into exquisite beauty, with a sea of tenderness poured over it. That most perfect specimen possessed by the Louvre, which is nevertheless very spoiled in its colors, seems to be partly by the master's own hand—which one believes to recognize, for example, in the head of Saint Anne and in the wonderfully soul-infused feet. Furthermore, the *Bacchus* originated in Milan as a cartoon—the painting itself was likely executed by one of the pupils under the master's eyes. That this poetic composition was always intended as a *Bacchus* is no longer in doubt today, because an epigram by a contemporary, Flavio Antonio Giraldi, titled "Leonardo da Vinci's Bacchus," has been found celebrating this painting. The divine spirit of rich nature, saturated with beauty, has never been more wonderfully embodied. The formally related half-figure of *Saint John* was also conceived here—certainly not that of the locust-eater of the desert, but of the herald of a joyful message, of a kingdom of justice, of love for humanity and one's neighbor, the religion of the forgiving Father of all men instead of the punishing God—the seductive messenger of a high happiness that would bathe heaven and earth in bliss. There is no other work by Leonardo in which the subject matter becomes so much a secondary concern as here. Once more, Leonardo summarized everything that his art possessed in terms of magic. He painted once more truly for the sake of painting—to model with <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: "Helldunkel"; the use of strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of three-dimensional volume.</note>, to breathe the wonderful smile onto gracious features through the play of shadow and light, revealing the most secret beauty of a soul; he has

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo's artistic output and engineering projects during his second Milanese period, following the analysis of his Saint John the Baptist.</meta>

<sig>CV</sig>

...nardo has shown the perfection of the most perfect creation of nature—a human body—using the means of the highest artistic skill, and he intended nothing else. The name that one might choose to give to this creature of his imagination was to him "sound and smoke" <note>A German idiom (Schall und Rauch) meaning something empty or insignificant; the artist cared for the form more than the specific mythological label.</note>.

Another composition by Leonardo is authenticated for us, and perhaps the master even gave it several versions—I mean the *Leda and the Swan*. Lomazzo <note>Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo (1538–1592), a painter and art theorist who wrote extensively on Leonardo.</note> speaks of a seated Leda; it may be that such a version was drafted in Milan: its last echo would have been the now-lost *Leda* by Correggio. However, the true *Leda* of Leonardo is in any case a standing naked figure, with her head turned sideways and a modest smile; beside her is the swan, whose powerful wing nestles against her magnificently formed hip like a large oval shield. Oxford preserves a drawing by Raphael after this composition, which was repeated so often in the Roman school that the theory has been proposed whether the painting might have come to Rome with Leonardo or was even executed there for Giuliano Medici.

A large part of Leonardo's practical activity during this second Milanese stay was devoted to hydraulic works. Whether the joining of the Martesana Canal with the old Ticino Canal—which only became possible by leveling the difference in height by means of several lock devices, a work that Lodovico "the Moor" Sforza <note>Lodovico Sforza (1452–1508), Duke of Milan and Leonardo’s great patron.</note> had already ordered to be carried out—whether Leonardo executed that has been doubted in recent times. Around 1508, Leonardo worked out plans to make the Adda navigable as far as Lake Como by developing the short stretch from Trezzo to Brivio and installing two locks. This project was indeed carried out in 1519, though not exactly according to Leonardo's proposals, and it failed. On the other hand, Leonardo directed the construction of the lock of the Naviglio Grande near San Cristoforo, and

--- Page 124 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of Leonardo's engineering and scientific pursuits during his second stay in Milan, transitioning from hydraulic engineering to his groundbreaking work in anatomy, natural sciences, and linguistics.</meta>

<page-num>CVI</page-num>

through a large basin, it was possible to protect Milan from flooding, as well as to better preserve the canal itself from debris (See the works of Luca Beltrami <note>Luca Beltrami (1854–1933) was an architect and historian known for restoring the Sforza Castle in Milan.</note> etc.).

Leonardo's anatomical studies were now significantly deepened. "This winter of 1510, I hope to settle the whole of anatomy," he writes. A supportive friendship connects him with Marcantonio della Torre (born 1481, died 1511 of the plague), who teaches anatomy in Pavia and who has likewise dared to break away from the authority of the Ancients <note>Refers to the traditional medical teachings of Galen and Aristotle which dominated the Middle Ages.</note>. Leonardo is the first to draw anatomical plates based on human preparations <note>Dissected cadavers.</note>, the first to practice comparative anatomy.

Likewise, during this second Milanese period, Leonardo's views on the sun, moon, and stars mature, as do his thoughts on the history of the earth, the role of water in the formation of mountain and valley, stratified rocks, and fossils. He observes and experiments. The phenomenon of the ebb and flow of the tide occupies him; he studies it wherever he can—even at the mills of Vaprio; he cannot reach an agreement with himself about it. It interests him whether heat is something material. "Make a scale with one arm and weigh a glowing object, and then weigh it again when cold." The manuscripts F., G., and M. <note>References to Leonardo's notebooks, categorized by later scholars.</note> fill up with notes on all the real sciences.

To these are added investigations into language. At first, Leonardo seems to have recorded only rarer expressions, seeking definitions for his scientific nomenclature <term>nomenclature: a system of names or terms used in a particular field of study</term>. This expanded, however, and finally, he created word lists that suggest the idea that he intended to compile a dictionary of the Italian language.

In mathematics, he never ceases to learn; around this time, he also makes his best discoveries in this field.

<meta>This page follows the account of Leonardo's scientific and anatomical studies in Milan, shifting the narrative toward the political upheavals that forced his departure and his subsequent move to Rome under the patronage of the Medici.</meta>

<page-num>CVII</page-num>

However, the beautiful, peaceful, and productive Milanese working period was already coming to an end. Pope Julius II <note>Giuliano della Rovere (reigned 1503–1513), known as the "Warrior Pope."</note> no longer wished to tolerate the French in Italy once he himself no longer had need of them. To cast out the "barbarians" <note>A term used by Italians of the Renaissance to refer to foreign invaders, particularly the French, Germans, and Spanish.</note> was the final dream of his grand life. He assembled an overwhelming League <note>The Holy League of 1511, an alliance formed to oppose the expansionism of France.</note> against Louis XII. War flared up. Twice the Pope was on the brink of ruin, in danger of becoming a French prisoner. Neither illness nor misfortune was able to bend him. Fate was ultimately with him. The bloody victory of the French at Ravenna (on April 11, 1512) was offset by the death of their magnificent leader Gaston de Foix (Chaumont <note>Charles II d'Amboise, Seigneur de Chaumont, Leonardo's patron and the French governor of Milan.</note> had already fallen before Bologna in March 1511); his successor La Palice was weak and incapable; the Swiss invaded; the Milanese rose up; by the end of June, the French had evacuated Italy. The League installed Massimiliano Sforza, son of "Il Moro" <note>Ludovico Sforza, Leonardo's former patron who died in a French prison.</note>, in Milan; but this weak, insignificant boy was no prince, no master according to Leonardo’s mind.

On May 13, 1513, Giovanni Medici, the second son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, ascended the papal throne under the name Leo X. In Rome, an Augustan Age <note>A period of great cultural and artistic achievement, named after the Roman Emperor Augustus.</note> seemed to be dawning, which was intended to surpass even the era of Julius II. The greatest artists of Italy worked there, were overwhelmed with commissions, and gained riches and honors.

On Folio 1 r. of Manuscript E., Leonardo records: “I departed from Milan for Rome on the 24th day of September 1513, with Giovan Francesco de Melzi, Salai, Lorenzo, and Fanfoja (?)” <note>These were Leonardo's pupils and servants; Melzi was his most devoted companion and heir.</note>. He is said to have traveled via Florence and deposited 300 gold guilders in Santa Maria Nuova, where his treasure had dwindled to 150 ducats between the years 1500 and 1507. In Rome, Giuliano Medici, the youngest brother of the Pope, had prepared an apartment for Leonardo in the Belvedere <note>A villa within the Vatican complex.</note>, where

Giuliano loved the arts; however, he was particularly interested in mathematics and mechanics; Leonardo could therefore once again devote himself to his scientific investigations and hope to be permitted to carry out his inventions. It is perhaps a misunderstanding on the part of Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Renaissance artists.</note> if he considers what was an experiment to be a mere trifle—namely, that Leonardo, in "walking, made the thinnest possible animals out of wax, filled with air," which flew in the wind; in any case, there was a sense of grim humor rather than a foolish whim in the fact that he carefully eviscerated sheep intestines, which he was able to hide in the palm of his hand, and inflated them by means of a bellows so that they filled his room up to the ceiling and drove the people away. If he truly took a strange lizard, brought to him by the "vinedresser" of the Belvedere <note>The Cortile del Belvedere in the Vatican, where Leonardo had his workshop.</note>, and attached horns to it, glued on a beard, and manufactured wings from lizard scales which he fastened to its shoulders by means of a mercury mixture and which trembled strangely whenever the animal moved; if he accustomed this little monster to a box in order to frighten his visitors into flight, then this was an invention to delight a Pope who, while he valued artists, valued jugglers, alchemists, jokers, and dwarves not much less (See Arturo Graf, *Through the Sixteenth Century* <note>original: "Attraverso il Cinquecento"</note> and others). — A passage in the Windsor Manuscripts, which Richter cites in § 726, proves that Leonardo occupied himself with devising better minting methods for the coinage in Rome—whether at the behest of the Pope is unproven, just as it is uncertain whether he only planned or actually executed certain works in the harbor of Civita Vecchia. <page-num>CIX</page-num>

This is not a man who will accomplish anything, if he begins by thinking about the end of the work before he has even started." Otto Sachs rightly remarks in his work on Leonardo—which unfortunately did not progress beyond a sketch (*Vienna Review* <note>original: "Wiener Rundschau"</note>, Vol. IV, Issues 4 and 6)—that for Leonardo, this small, inconspicuous matter, which the great lords in Rome and all artists down to the days of Vasari laughed at, namely the preparation of a varnish <term>varnish: a protective finish applied to a painting to enhance colors and preserve the surface</term> which would give the colors increased luminosity, was perhaps the most important thing and the very motive that prompted him to paint this picture. But how was it possible that in an era of ascending art, in which every painter added something new to the inherited treasury of technical knowledge, a man like Leonardo—the greatest innovator and inventor in this field, from whom they had all learned the most important and greatest lessons—in composition, in the grouping of figures, in perspective, in the treatment of light and shadow, in modeling through <term>chiaroscuro: the use of strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of three-dimensional volume</term> <note>original: "Helldunkel"</note>, in coloring, in drawing—not to mention the deepening of expression, the variety in poses, the motifs of movement, the treatment of drapery, and even the intangible values of gracious poetry and divine beauty—that a man whose fame had already flown across the world could become a laughingstock in the center of the culture of that time? How? Unless he was truly ever understood except by a very few individuals, who were often not artists themselves? Vasari is merely the echo of the opinion of all those who were permitted to have an opinion, when he constantly speaks of the "follies," "foolish whims," "eccentricities," "caprices"—of the inconstancy, unreliability, eccentricity, and the eternal fiasco of Leonardo, and implies that Leonardo achieved more in words than in deeds. Of the greatest significance...

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Leonardo da Vinci’s isolation in Rome during the High Renaissance, contrasting his scientific and experimental temperament with the more productive and socially integrated careers of Michelangelo and Raphael.</meta>

mixed into everyone’s wonder was always a grain of mocking disregard—that same disregard which the swan in the duck pond can always be certain of receiving. If Michelangelo set the tone for this, as is always told and as the little story from Florence proves in a concentrated example, it is not because he was small or petty, but because he was so utterly different and lacked the key to this completely contrary spirit—"there was a very great disdain between Michelangelo Buonarroti and him" <note>original: "era sdegno grandissimo fra Michelagnolo Buonarroti e lui"</note>. Raphael, of course, with his nature so far from envy, loving and adaptable, who guessed with such spiritual delicacy what he perhaps could not understand with his head, Raphael might have still bowed in his heart before the master to whom he owed something quite immense; yet in these years he was occupied with his own fame and far too much with his own perfection through the absorption of Michelangelesque elements into his art to sacrifice time and thought to others.

So Leonardo remained in Rome entirely apart and, as it were, excluded from the rich life of the time and place. He wandered about by himself, seeking traces of prehistoric life in the countryside: "let yourself be informed where the (fossil) shells of Monte Mario are" <note>original: "laß dich unterrichten, wo die (fossilen) Muscheln des Monte Mario sind"</note> (Codex Atlanticus, Folio 92 v.); he made acoustic observations during the excavation of the Castel Sant'Angelo; he completed a geometric work "on July 9th at 11 o'clock at night." Otherwise, he made a few "small pictures" for the treasurer of ecclesiastical benefices (<term>datario: a high-ranking official in the papal curia responsible for dates and grants</term>) Baldassare Turini, which are lost—some believe also the fresco in the monastery of Sant’ Onofrio in Rome, which however more likely stems from his pupil Boltraffio, who used a drawing by the master for the Christ Child—for the rest, he had a German mechanic construct "the oval lathe" <note>original: "il tornio ovale"</note>, which he had invented, as well as other secret things for Giuliano de' Medici—what they were, we do not know; we learn of them through the draft letters (page 211 and following),

He has also been ill. The times are over when he, as Vasari reports to us, "with his strength could withstand any violent force and with his right hand could bend a <term>wall-bell</term> <note>A heavy iron bell-pull or clapper used in fortifications.</note> or a horseshoe as if it were pure lead."

"On the 9th day of January 1515, at sunrise, the illustrious Giuliano de' Medici left Rome to go and marry his wife in Savoy. And on the same day, the death of the King of France was (made known) to us," writes Leonardo (Ms. G., inside cover). Giuliano, who receives the title Duke of Nemours and for whom the Pope has great plans—Naples would have been just right for him—Giuliano Medici marries Philiberta—*neither beautiful nor charming* <note>original Latin: "nec pulchra, nec venusta"</note>, says a contemporary—the aging sister of that eternally youthful Louise of Savoy, whose son had just ascended the throne of France on January 1, 1515, as the successor to Louis XII. With this young, ambitious, fiery king, a more violent tempo enters the affairs of the world. Tired of the intrigue of a policy in which it became the rule to secure oneself against one's own allies through a counter-alliance, Francis resumes the plans of his predecessors Charles VIII and Louis XII, in order to prevent a great coalition between the Pope, the Emperor, the Spanish King, Milan, Genoa, and the Swiss through the renewed conquest of Milan (See Ludwig Pastor, *History of the Popes*, Vol. IV, 1906). Accompanied by the brilliance of Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, Trémouille, Lautrec, and Bayard <note>Famous military commanders of the French army.</note>, he breaks into Italy by bypassing the well-guarded Alpine passes via the Col d’Argentière, which was considered impassable. Prospero Colonna is taken prisoner, the Swiss retreat toward Milan, and Lorenzo de’ Medici—who has taken command of the papal troops in place of the ailing Giuliano—stalls for time. However, on September 13, the Swiss, under Cardinal Schinner, attack the fortified camp of King Francis at Marignano; only on the second day does the bloody struggle end with a complete victory for the French. Milan opens its gates; Massimiliano Sforza renounces his troublesome duchy with a thousand joys in exchange for a handsome annual pension. This time, France is not faced with the fiery spirit of a Julius II. The deeply terrified Pope seeks a meeting with King Francis in Bologna (December 1515).

Regarding Leonardo, we do not know much that is fully authenticated during this entire period. He had been "on September 25, 1514, at Parma, in the countryside," perhaps with Giuliano, whose household he belonged to for a time; in December, he seems to have been in Rome again, for Alessandra da Vinci, in a letter, asks her husband Ser Giuliano, who is staying there, to remind his brother Leonardo—an "excellent and most singular man" <note>original: "uomo eccellentissimo e singhu-larissimo"</note>—of her. On March 31, 1515, the Duke of Nemours <note>Giuliano de' Medici.</note> had made a festive entry into Rome with his wife Philiberta; on June 29, as the standard-bearer of the Church, he was given supreme command over the Pope's army; yet as early as August 8, Lorenzo Medici had to take his place, as Giuliano had fallen seriously ill and had withdrawn to Florence, where he succumbed to a lingering malady on March 17, 1516. Although the documents do not mention his name in connection with these, he likely would have been the leading spirit of these games. In Amboise, the King wanted to build a new palace: thus, Leonardo was once again permitted to indulge in magnificent architectural designs. In the royal castle at Blois, during Leonardo’s presence in the Touraine, a wonderful spiral staircase was created, for which the first construction installment was paid in July 1516. It is reminiscent of a certain snail, called *Voluta vespertilio* <note>The "Bat Volute," a species of sea snail known for its spiral shell.</note>, which is frequently found in the Mediterranean Sea and of which an occasional specimen carries its spiral upward, turned from left to right: so too this staircase, which is conceived as if by a left-handed person; therefore, Mr. Theodore Andrea Cook put forward the beautiful hypothesis that Leonardo perhaps created the plan for this magnificent staircase (see *The National Review*, April 1 and 15, 1902). Other works of the aging artist are more certain. In the vicinity of Amboise, there stretched at that time a desolate swampland, which was only reclaimed in the 19th century. Leonardo studied the terrain, the small and large watercourses, the Loire and its tributaries, and then drafted a plan to connect the Touraine with the Lyonnais by way of the Saône by means of a canal system, which would serve trade, assist in land cultivation, and make the country healthy. Mr. Charles Ravaisson-Mollien, the excellent editor of Leonardo’s French manuscripts, says that the canals which exist there today correspond to Leonardo’s traces and ideas and prove their excellence. The death of such a man is lamented by everyone, for his like is no longer within the power of Nature. Now may God grant him eternal rest. He passed over from this present life on the 2nd day of May with all the comforts of Holy Mother Church, and well prepared . . .”

<meta>This page follows the announcement of Leonardo da Vinci's death and the letter from his pupil Melzi to Leonardo's brothers. It concludes the biographical narrative by discussing his burial and the philosophical weight of his legacy.</meta>

<page-num>CXIX</page-num>

a document tells us:
> “Was interred in the cloister of this church Master Lionard de Vincy, Milanese nobleman, first painter and engineer and architect to the King, state mechanician <note>original: "meschasnischien d’estat"</note> and former director of painting for the Duke of Milan. This was done on the twelfth day of August 1519.”

He was not entombed like Raphael and Michelangelo; the place where he sleeps in death was soon abandoned and forgotten. Greater than the others, despite all his failures, he had remained a solitary figure, one who walked apart; thus it is only fitting that he rests apart and alone. Just as his body has been scattered—to the earth, the water, the air, which is common to us all, secretly mingled—so the essence of his spirit and creation vibrates invisibly within us, even where its traces are not recognizable to everyone: in lines, colors, gestures—in the rhythm of spatial animation, in all that is artistically beautiful, and in our entire way of thinking and feeling; it can never be lost to us.

There is a tremendous melancholy in the life and death of this man. It was his tragedy to be so great and yet only a finite human being. What he desired, the work of generations had first to achieve: “truth is the daughter of time alone.” He had no numerous predecessors, he had no sufficient assistants, he had no dazzling pupils. As an artist, as a researcher, as an inventor, he aimed for things so immense, so irreconcilable, that he was bound to fail as an individual. He broke under the weight of his own greatness. He attempted what we are still searching for today, and yet he was a child of the <term>Quattrocento</term> <note>The 1400s, or the 15th-century period of the Italian Renaissance.</note>. He wrestled for the gigantic; in art, he wanted to compete with nature when she is at her most divine and grand; in science, he wanted to capture in laws the infinite “<term>ragioni</term>” <note>Italian for "reasons" or "principles"; Leonardo used the term to describe the underlying mathematical or logical laws of nature.</note> which rest hidden within her “and never entered into experience.” In the feeling of the brevity of existence and the inadequacy of the human spirit, he was driven from place to place to find the climate where his work might flourish—not inner-

<meta>This page continues the philosophical reflection on Leonardo da Vinci’s character, transitioning from the tragedy of his death to his inner composure and his foundational role in the history of art.</meta>

<page-num>CXX</page-num>

He sought, as he long believed, the conditions where he could quietly bring his plans to maturity—happiness—as we all do, and one day he saw through what drives us all, without melancholy, but as the philosopher <note>original: "Weltweise," literally a "world-wise man" or sage</note> that he was, with a faint smile:

> “The man who, with constant desires, always awaits the new spring with great festivity, and always the new summer, and always the new months and new years—while it seems to him as if the longed-for things are too slow in coming—does not realize that he is wishing for his own dissolution!
>
> But this wish is the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth element" or purest essence beyond earth, air, fire, and water</note>, the true spirit of the elements, which feel themselves enclosed by the soul within the human body and always desire to return to their sender. And I want you to know that this very same wish is that <term>Quintessence</term>, the companion of nature, and man is the model of the whole world.”

It is not within the plan of this book, nor within the scope of my ability, to speak with authority on what Leonardo achieved for art—that is, for the development of artistic vision and artistic skill. Regarding him as an architect, and even as a sculptor, judgment can only be passed with great caution. Volumes have been written about Leonardo the painter; nevertheless, I would like to refer to only a single one, to Heinrich Wölfflin’s beautiful work: “Classical Art,” in which it is shown with so much spirit—even if not with a strong enough emphasis for all readers—how much Leonardo was the inventor in all aspects of great art, a guide and model for the later masters.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s influence on the history of art, specifically focusing on how his technical innovations and compositional structures were adopted by later masters like Dürer, Raphael, and Botticelli.</meta>

<sig>CXXI</sig>

In his hand-drawings, there is also no turn of phrase, hardly a single line, that has not been used and imitated a hundredfold. The magnificent trotting horse of the <term>Sforza Monument</term> <note>Leonardo's ambitious, never-completed equestrian statue for Francesco Sforza</note> design lives on in Dürer’s “Knight, Death and the Devil”; the rearing horse of other sketches from Windsor has varied after-images in Fernkorn’s “Archduke Charles” (Vienna) and in Falconet’s “Peter the Great” (Petersburg). “The unheard-of elegance of the seating” of the Holy Virgin and the “charming motif of the figure’s rotation with the boy turning sideways,” which Leonardo found for his “Adoration of the Magi,” was “literally repeated” by Raphael as late as 1512 in his *Madonna di Foligno*, as Wölfflin says. From this same important early work, Botticelli—and after him the mature <term>Cinquecento</term> <note>The 1500s, or the High Renaissance period in Italian art</note>—learned how to use corner figures as framing supports and as a firm conclusion to a composition. Here, for the first time since the great Masaccio and with richer means, the attempt is made to subject the masses, clearly grouped, to a formal idea.

To seek the secret of all beauty in the necessary and the lawful, and to bring the lawfulness of every appearance down to measure and number—to express it in proportion and geometric body-schemes—a mind of Leonardo’s nature was bound to hit upon this sooner or later. Just as he spent his life tracing fixed proportions in human and animal forms, he was also soon striving to lay the outline of some simple, regular figure as a scaffold beneath the composition of a work of art. And indeed, already in the “Adoration” <note>original: "Adorazione"</note>, modeled out of the mass by the guidance of light, an isosceles triangle emerges as the compositional ground plan for the main group—an experiment which he takes up again and develops better in the *Virgin of the Rocks* <note>original: "Vierge aux rochers"</note> and which then, in the magnificent pyramid of the structure of the *Virgin and Child with Saint Anne*...
