The **Leonardo school** has repeated and modified this masterpiece a hundred times; it has been picked apart into its compositional elements a hundred times, and each became the core of a new, though less beautiful, creation; one recognizes its motifs of movement, its outlines in **Raphael’s** *Madonna in the Meadow*, and the *Alba Madonna*; even **Michelangelo** was unable to escape its influence; it is believable when **Wölfflin** <note>Heinrich Wölfflin (1864–1945), a highly influential Swiss art historian</note> suggests that his *Holy Family* in the **Tribuna in Florence** <note>The Doni Tondo</note> was created in conflict with Leonardo’s painting, in order to surpass it, to extinguish it . . . It is the only form, conceived and useful for the only content; but the instruction that can be drawn, for example, from the use of all painterly means, through which **Christ**, the motionless individual in the midst of four groups of passionately excited people, becomes clear as the one to whom everything relates—because every line leads to him, because all light is there to shine around him—the instruction of such things has worked directly and indirectly into the distance of all times. And what atmosphere and charm Leonardo, the first great teacher of <term>aerial perspective</term> <note>The technique of creating an illusion of depth by depicting distant objects as paler, greener, or bluer</note>, gives to the delicately tinted distances of his landscapes! How he knows how to use light and line to fuse man and all creatures, the world of plants, rock and water, heaven and earth, into an all-encompassing harmony! It is not for nothing that Corot <note>Camille Corot (1796–1875), a pivotal French landscape painter</note> calls him the creator of the modern landscape. He does not exalt man by placing him outside of nature, as the <term>Cinquecento</term> <note>The 1500s, or High Renaissance period in Italy</note> did—for whom the human figure alone was everything—and as his great antipode in art, Michelangelo, especially did. 

Leonardo is also the most "universal" painter, the "all-rounder" of his time. No one studied the horse as much as he did. His *Saint Jerome* and many beautiful study sheets show how familiar he was with the lion. His plant drawings are those of a learned botanist. He wants to be able to reproduce everything living. He knows that the mastery of the line is not enough for this; one must master the <term>management of light and shadow</term> <note>original: "Licht- und Schattenführung," often referred to by the Italian term chiaroscuro</note>, the mixing of light and dark, the sharp contrasts as well as the "smoky" transitions. He made rounding—the <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensional physical volume on a flat surface</note>—the most important element in painting. In the treatment of light, only Correggio <note>Antonio da Correggio (1489–1534), known for his use of soft light and dynamic composition</note> led the way beyond him. "He is the born noble painter," says Wölfflin, "sensitive to the delicate. He has a feeling for fine hands, for transparent fabrics, for tender skin. He especially loves beautiful, soft, wavy hair... The strong and the soft are equally familiar to him. When he paints a battle, he surpasses everyone in the expression of unleashed passion and immense movement, and yet alongside this, he knows how to steal upon the most delicate sensations and the..."

<page-num>CXXV</page-num>

**T**he manuscripts of Leonardo fared no better than his other works, although he wrote more than he built, modeled, or painted. He speaks once (see p. 90) of the 120 books that he composed; another time he cites the 114th book. Among these, however, one should probably only understand scrapbooks or notebooks; we no longer believe in the existence of finished, polished works. All reports about them sound too vague in the face of the fact that none of them exist. "The Book of Painting" <note>original: "Das Buch von der Malerei," commonly known today as the *Trattato della Pittura*</note>? In its richest, most complete form, Heinrich Ludwig (in the Eitelberger source writings on art history) published an exemplary edition, without concealing the fact that it is likely nothing more than a careful compilation dating from the 16th century—a time, therefore, when Leonardo's notes were still all collected together. If it were a copy, it would only prove that the work had not been a cohesive whole ready for printing in the modern sense. The much-cited work by Leonardo "On the Nature, Motion, and Weight of Water" (published under the title "Of the motion and measurement of water" <note>original Latin/Italian: "Del moto e misura dell'acqua"</note> as Vol. X of a collection of Italian authors who wrote on hydraulics, Bologna, 1824) is likewise an excerpt from the manuscripts, which the learned Dominican Lodovico Maria Arconati personally prepared for the art-loving Cardinal Francesco Barberini (1643). Just as about two-thirds of the content of the *Book of Painting* has been found scattered throughout the still-existing manuscripts, so too does one possess a large part of the important work on water fragmentarily in the preserved <term>Codices</term> <note>Manuscript volumes or notebooks</note>. Manuscript D, containing the compilations on the eye, and the Windsor notebooks on anatomy, differ from the two large, previously mentioned compilations only by their degree of aimless disorder and by the fact that they were prepared by Leonardo himself—as material for a final revision and only as material. Yet even of this material, the largest part has unfortunately completely disappeared, and of what remains, the majority has again been barbarically dismembered. When Leonardo left Italy, much that was irreplaceable remained at Santa Maria Nuova in Florence and elsewhere. According to the wording of his will, Francesco Melzi inherited only those writings, books, drawings, instruments, and portraits that Leonardo had "present," that is, with him in France; these "are dear to him, and he keeps such papers as relics, just like the portrait of the happy memory of Leonardo," says Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Italian Renaissance artists</note>; but he also recounts that he himself owned hand drawings by the master; he further speaks of a painter, whose name he indicates with dots <note>Vasari likely omitted the name to avoid scandal or legal issues regarding the ownership of the papers</note>, who "possessed several of Leonardo's writings dealing with painting and the ways of drawing and coloring," and who went to Rome to publish them. Until Francesco Melzi died, that is, until 1570, at least a portion of these treasures was well-guarded; however, his son Orazio had no understanding of their value. The items gathered dust in the attic at Vaprio; anyone who pleased could take from them: thus a certain Lelio Gavardi had 13 volumes of the manuscripts in his possession on loan, and since the owner cared so little about them, Gavardi kept them; indeed, he even entered into negotiations with Grand Duke Francesco of Tuscany regarding a sale. Gianambrogio Mazzenta, a Milanese nobleman, reproached him for the dishonesty of his actions, and since the Grand Duke died before the deal was finalized, it was less difficult to convince Gavardi. The largest part of it was acquired by a pupil of Michelangelo, Pompeo Leoni, sculptor to Philip II of Spain; and he so inflamed Orazio Melzi's head with the representation of what offices, honors, and titles he (Orazio) could have obtained from the King if he had laid the 13 volumes at his feet instead of Mazzenta's, that the poor fool went out of his mind, went to Mazzenta, and on bended knee implored him to return the manuscripts. Guido Mazzenta, however, gave him back only 7 volumes; of the remaining six, he made use of three. One volume was received by Duke Charles Emmanuel of Savoy; it was likely charred in one of the Turin library fires. A third was in the possession of the English consul Joseph Smith in Venice in 1775 and has since been lost. Volumes 4, 5, and 6, however, came into Leoni's hands after Mazzenta's death in 1613: whether Melzi gave all seven of the others to Pompeo has not been clarified. The Mazzenta volumes (4, 5, 6) were cut up by Pompeo Leoni—who nevertheless boasted of being an artist—and, along with other acquired manuscripts, drawings, etc., were given to a bookbinder to be beautifully bound: which the latter indeed did, though certainly from the spi- <note>The text ends mid-word "Ge-", likely "Gesichtspunkt" (point of view) or "Geist" (spirit)</note>

Is it perhaps the atomized volume of Joseph Smith, which was considered lost? The history of the English Leonardo manuscripts has not yet been cleared up.

After the death of Pompeo Leoni, Count Galeazzo Arconati acquired the Codex Atlanticus; he succeeded in acquiring ten other notebooks of smaller scope; yet despite being offered thousands from England, he rejected it all and gifted the immeasurable treasure to the Milanese Ambrosiana <note>The Biblioteca Ambrosiana, a historic library in Milan</note> in 1637. Count Archinti gave Codex K to the library, which now, with Cardinal Borromeo’s Codex C, possessed 13 codices of very different sizes, but which are not identical with the 13 large volumes of Melzi. — The Codex of the Casa Trivulzi <note>The Trivulziano Collection</note> comes from the possession of Arconati.

When one speaks of Leonardo, one is always in danger of attributing to him much that one or another of his contemporaries also knew; however, one can certainly never describe the scope of his being largely enough. He is so great, not because he was a completely modern man, but because he still stands so firmly rooted in the Middle Ages and yet, with his thinking, researching, and willing, grows formally into the very heart of our own day: that is what gives him his giant stature. He came to science like so many of the best artists of the *Quattrocento* <note>the 1400s/15th century in Italy</note>, who, in order to become masters of their art, had to concern themselves with more than just their paint pots. What we have—or imagine we have—had to first be sought and invented back then. We laypeople have no proper conception of how much ingenuity, reflection, labor, and experimentation it cost alone to create a deep space out of a flat surface and to animate it with form and fullness. First, a few brilliantly simple aids had to be devised to support the hand and eye; much had to be experimented with in lines and colors; with incessant observation, nature had to be pressed closely, and not least of all, geometry had to be practiced. They practiced all sorts of things, those good artists of the *Quattrocento*—such as Piero della Francesca, the great master of perspective; Antonio da San Gallo, the military engineer; Leone Battista Alberti, the universal man and inventor of the *camera obscura* <note>a darkened box with a lens or hole for projecting an image of external objects onto a screen inside</note>; as empiricists <note>those who rely on observation and experience</note>, they were equal to many tasks. <page-num>CXXXII</page-num>

the modern age begins, modern science. He places experience in the stead of inner speculation; an artist, he appeals to the senses. He dethrones blind faith in authority; he places every truth, no matter how recognized and old it may be, under the control of observation and reason; for in order to shine, the truth must first have passed through the thousand fires of doubt. How highly he prizes it is revealed by his beautiful words:
> “If falsehood spoke well of the things of God, it would rob their divinity of grace, and of such distinction is the truth, that even humble things which it praises become most noble.”

With these humble things he wishes to occupy himself and leave the others to the “wandering geniuses.” He studies above all the phenomena of nature; he does not just look, he sees, he notices; he observes simultaneously with the eye and the intellect (<term>speculare</term> <note>to investigate or observe intellectually</note> in contrast to mere <term>vedere</term> <note>to see</note>). The sea with its movements, the river which eats away at the bank; the tree, its branch arrangement, the foliage, the sun that shines through it; the bird which cleaves the air, a bell that rings, a fantastic face—everything awakens his interest, is noted down. Just as he finally distills the one typical movement he seeks and needs from a thousand movements held fast in memory and on paper, so he extracts from a thousand recorded facts the typical, the general, the rule, the law, or as he calls it: the <term>cause</term> <note>original: "Ursache"; Leonardo used the term "ragione" or "causa" to mean the underlying physical law</note>. But the well-conducted experiment must first confirm the observation; for
> “experience does not err; only your judgments err.”

He teaches again and again to ascend from the correctly established phenomenon to the <term>cause</term> (the law), although nature proceeds differently, because within her the rational cause is the primary element which calls forth the phenomenon. However, he by no means censures those who for once do not proceed inductively, but rather a rule from a

In order to give them that precision which turns knowledge into a science, he seeks to introduce measure and number into them. “No human investigation can be called true science if it has not passed through mathematical demonstrations.” ... “Proportion is not only to be found in numbers and measurements, but also in sounds, weights, times, and places, and in every force, whatever it may be.” ... “He who disdains the supreme certainty of mathematics feeds on confusion and will never impose silence upon the sophistical sciences, which produce nothing but an eternal clamor (<term>gridore</term> <note>Italian for "shouting" or "outcry"</note>).” From these concise sentences, it is not a long way to Galileo, who says that the book of nature is written in mathematical language, and to Kant, who believes there is only as much actual science in the study of nature as there is mathematics to be found in it; and indeed, our entire era still thinks this way.

By means of such methods, Leonardo attempts to get a grip on nature and to re-establish the science “of natural things” (<term>delle cose naturali</term>). He has to struggle with difficulties that we cannot imagine today. Not only did nature lie before him like a book of hieroglyphics of which barely a few pages had been deciphered; he first had to learn how to make what he read therein communicable to others; he had to formally create both the real science and, at the same time, the language for it. Humanistic science was still handed down in Latin; in Italian, the short, sharp expression for clear, cold, scientific thoughts had yet to be found. Thinking itself was figurative, anthropomorphic <note>attributing human characteristics to non-human things</note>, and the argumentation was cumbersome, full of scholastic <note>referring to the medieval school of philosophy that relied heavily on tradition and dogma</note> ballast. Even in Leonardo’s work, a definition sometimes resembles an episode in a novel, and a fall, an impact, every kind of force or violence (<term>violentia</term> <note>Latin/Italian term for physical force or impetus</note>) experiences between birth and death

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Leonardo da Vinci’s scientific philosophy, specifically his struggle to articulate natural laws and his pioneering theories on mechanics and motion.</meta>

<page-num>CXXXIV</page-num>

with him, the most wonderful adventures. Everything is more seen than merely thought out and possesses the charm of a naive poetry, which richly compensates the modern reader for occasional obscurity, awkwardness, or the length of the deduction. The struggle for the most precise expression is often touching. Leonardo shaped and reshaped many a sentence ten times over.

Above all, he establishes the inviolability of the laws that live "infused" (<term>infuso</term> <note>original: "infuso," meaning poured into or permeated</note>) within nature, melted into it—the outflow of a necessity that is rational. Whatever goes against these laws cannot exist, "unless one were to accept the miracle," as he says several times: therefore, in an age where people conjure the dead and consult the stars, practice magic and pursue secret arts, he fights the belief in spirits most extensively with arguments drawn from physics.

At the head of Leonardo’s scientific insights stand other weighty and fundamental principles. He knows that all worldly existence, that every phenomenon of life, is motion; he directly calls motion "the cause of all being" and says that every "action is exercised through motion." He knows the law of inertia and declares that no motion arises by itself, nor ends by itself; admittedly, the state of rest seems to him the natural one. Motion is disturbed equilibrium. It is brought about by an energy or force that Leonardo calls a spiritual essence, because it changes nothing in the mass or weight of the body. It communicates itself to the body through the "impetus" (<term>impeto</term>) as an "impressed virtue" (<term>virtù impressa</term> <note>A medieval and Renaissance concept of kinetic energy as a quality "impressed" into a moving object</note>), as an impression, an impulse that indeed "desires eternity," but consumes itself in the motion: a train of thought from which even Galileo could not yet free himself. All motion is measurable and calculable. Its cause—that is, the initiating force—is always a sensory one. The ultimate source of all force, however, and thus of all motion,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s scientific philosophy, moving from his general concepts of motion and inertia to his specific understanding of the "First Mover" and his pioneering work in mechanics, including friction and the laws of the lever.</meta>

<page-num>CXXXV</page-num>

is for Leonardo "the first mover" <note>original: "der erste Beweger"; a reference to the Prime Mover or *Primum Mobile*</note>, whom the Florentine Platonists of the <term>Quattrocento</term> <note>The 1400s, or the Italian Renaissance period</note> had adopted from the Arabian philosophers and <term>Aristotelians</term> <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Aristotle</note>. What could be more deeply moving than 그 outburst of delight with which Leonardo, at the dawning intuition of the law of the conservation of energy, calls upon "the wonderful justice of the <term>first mover</term>" <note>original: "primo Motore"</note>, because he recognizes and reveres in this law a kind of moral foundation for the world order (p. 22). Séailles <note>Gabriel Séailles, a French philosopher and art historian</note> recalls the conception of the world that Leibniz taught us: "Everywhere there is geometry and everywhere there is morality." Leonardo, to be sure, considered his task to be merely the geometry—that is, if possible, the mathematical formula for every law of the world. He seeks the relationship between force and motion; he seeks to establish the increasing speed of a fall through experimentation. He studied friction in all its details; therefore his machines work; therefore he fights against perpetual motion and the music of the spheres <note>The ancient philosophical concept that celestial bodies created a divine harmony through their movements</note>. As Wilhelm Elsässer states ("The Significance of L. d. V. for the Exact Natural Sciences," Prussian Yearbooks, July-Sept. 1899), Leonardo is the first who expresses the law of virtual velocities with some precision and essentially understands it quite correctly. Regarding free fall, he is likely in error, as he believes the speed of the falling body is proportional to its weight; but he is the first to take the influence of air resistance into account during a fall. Particularly successful are his investigations and observations regarding impact, which he knows how to make effective through excellent drawings. Neither Galileo nor Descartes reached his level of knowledge on this point.

As the first since Archimedes, and with expanded knowledge, he occupies himself with the laws of the lever. He shows what lawful relationships exist between the magnitude of the force and the length of the lever arm—

<meta>This page continues the detailed analysis of Leonardo da Vinci’s contributions to physics, specifically transitioning from his work on virtual velocities to his mastery of the lever and his foundational role in hydraulics and wave theory.</meta>

<page-num>CXXXVI</page-num>

stand; he knows, draws, and explains the **angled lever** in all its forms; he investigates the pressure and weight ratios of every lever point with the utmost precision; he traces the pulley, the block and tackle, and the wheel and axle back to the effect of the simple and compound lever. He sees in the movements of humans and animals nothing other than the movement of lever arms, and he does not forget to connect the self-weight of the lever arm as an active factor with the other forces and to include it in his observations. Not Ubaldi <note>Guido Ubaldo del Monte (1545–1607), an Italian mathematician who studied mechanics</note>, not Stevinus <note>Simon Stevin (1548–1620), a Flemish mathematician and engineer</note>, nor Benedetti <note>Giovanni Battista Benedetti (1530–1590), an Italian physicist</note>, but Leonardo has the great merit of being the first to have recognized and applied the laws of the lever in all directions: thus he appears as the founder of modern mechanics.

Leonardo is considered no less the father of the hydraulic sciences. He knows the laws of the propagation of pressure in water, which he was the first to study and understand since Archimedes <note>The ancient Greek mathematician and inventor</note>. He is a peerless predecessor to Stevinus and Galileo in hydrostatics <term>hydrostatics</term> <note>The branch of physics that deals with fluids at rest and the pressure they exert</note>. He understands the molecular properties of water. He knows the reason for the buoyancy of a body. He knows the law of communicating vessels; he knows that liquids that do not mix will arrange themselves in such vessels in proportion to their weight to one another. He conducts experiments on the outflow of water through various openings; he investigates the causes of the vortex, the whirlpool, etc., etc., long before Castelli <note>Benedetto Castelli (1578–1643), a student of Galileo and a pioneer in hydraulics</note>. He was the first to study the wave movements of the sea, in their causes and in their appearance. He knows that the wave flees the place of its origin while the water itself does not move from its spot, much like the waves one sees rushing across a cornfield without the grain moving from its place. He knows that two waves can cross through each other without destroying one another. He applies the laws—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s scientific foresight, moving from his foundational work in hydraulics and hydrostatics to his broader theories on wave motion, atmospheric science, and acoustics.</meta>

<page-num>CXXXVII</page-num>

Apply the concept of wave motion—its propagation in circles and in all directions, and the way waves cross one another without canceling each other out—to sound, to light, to magnetism, and indeed, even to human thought: in truth, I believe nothing more or higher can be said of Leonardo’s brilliant intuition and of his need to recognize a single great principle within the diversity of things. This remains true even if we must admit, along with Wilhelm Elsässer <note>A 19th-century German scholar of Leonardo's scientific manuscripts</note>, that there is still a long way from these premonitions to the modern <term>undulation theory</term> <note>The wave theory of light and energy</note>.

Leonardo transfers his experiences regarding the movement of water to the air in order to study the wind. He is interested in meteorology. He occupies himself with fog, clouds, rain, snow, and hail. Some things he perceives through simple observation, such as the flame; although he cannot explain it, he observes it so correctly that he invents the lamp with a cylinder and globe. And 250 years before Lavoisier <note>Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794), the father of modern chemistry who identified oxygen</note>, he already had a slight inkling of that component of the air which alone is fit for burning and breathing. Regarding his underwater boats and diving apparatuses—alas, who could even list his inventions within such a narrow framework!—he speaks of pumping out air and taking <term>alito</term> <note>original: "alito"; Italian for breath or breathing air</note>, breathing air, down into the depths with him. His observations of bird flight, which are said to have been surpassed by no one as of yet, his flying machines, and his invention of the parachute have already been discussed previously.

His achievements in the field of acoustics are full of surprising starts. In almost every instance, one finds him on the right path. He compares the propagation of sound with the wave motion that arises when one throws a stone into the water, which always keeps its center at the point of origin. He seeks to measure the speed of sound. He senses what the pitch—

<page-num>CXXXVIII</page-num>

In addition to the laws of mechanics, the painter is naturally most occupied by light, sight, and the eye—optics, which at that time was included under the term <term>perspective</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "perspectiva" referred to the science of optics and vision as well as artistic depth.</note>. In this field, too, his ideas are brilliant. There is nothing of material theories here. He recognizes rectilinear propagation in all directions, reflection, and refraction; here, too, he applies the comparison with wave motion; one hears only of motion and the laws of motion. The entire world, including the living world, is subject to the laws of mechanics; the earth is a machine, and man is one as well. Although Leone Battista Alberti <note>An influential Italian Renaissance architect and polymath (1404–1472)</note> was already familiar with the <term>camera obscura</term> <note>A darkened box with a hole that projects an inverted image of the outside world onto an inside surface.</note>, Leonardo experiments with it and finds the correct reason for the formation of the inverted image on its back wall. He also considers the eye to be a *camera obscura* and struggles to understand why we nevertheless see upright. He assumes that a second inversion of the image occurs during the passage of rays through the crystalline lens (he does not reach clarity regarding where the first and second crossing points are located); thus, the image appears upright on the back wall of the eye; the optic nerve endings receive it and convey it to the internal, "common sense," where it is first understood. Some passages, which are admittedly not very precise, even allow for the interpretation that Leonardo intended to leave the upright perception of the inverted image entirely to this understanding "common sense": but these are matters whose clarification is not yet possible today, despite the compilations of Dr. Edmondo Solmi <note>original: "Nuovi Studi sulla Filosofia naturale di L. d. Vinci, 1905"; New Studies on the Natural Philosophy of Leonardo da Vinci</note>. In general, it causes Leonardo enormous difficulty to understand how things become visible; what is certain is that he saw nothing in the eye but a receiving apparatus; whether he...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s optical studies, specifically his experiments with the eye and light, before transitioning into his investigations of heat and steam power.</meta>

<page-num>CXXXIX</page-num>

Whether he regarded light as an exciter of images or merely as the carrier of "species"—illusory images of things that are spread throughout the entire universe—must remain undecided for the time being. In any case, his optical works are full of ingenious experiments and beautiful results. Elsässer <note>Likely referring to a 19th-century historian of science or medicine.</note> credits him with the merit of being the first to attempt a methodical representation of the path of light rays in the eye and a geometrical construction of the image. He understands physical vision; he manufactures an artificial eye in order to learn how the natural one functions. He occupies himself with the phenomena of irradiation <note>The apparent enlargement of a bright object against a dark background.</note> and with negative afterimages; he explains with great success the halo of rays around luminous bodies; he recognizes moonlight—and admittedly also the light of fixed stars—as reflected light from the sun; he finds the correct reason for the <term>ashy light</term> <note>original: "Lumen cinereum." This refers to "earthshine," where the dark part of the moon is faintly illuminated by sunlight reflected from the Earth.</note>. He teaches how to manufacture concave, convex, parabolic, and spherical mirrors; he determines the point where the reflected rays intersect. His theory of colored shadows was long considered the only true one; it, along with his theories on color, will soon be made more easily accessible to German readers through a translation of the *Treatise on Painting* than was previously possible in the voluminous, scholarly edition by Ludwig Heinrich.

Leonardo investigates heat in its many effects and makes attempts to use steam as a motor. He draws a steam-powered launch; he describes a roasting spit driven by hot air; he constructs a steam cannon, the <term>Architronito</term> <note>A steam-powered cannon described by Leonardo, which he attributed to the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes.</note>, the invention of which he admittedly ascribes to Archimedes—perhaps because he feared being burned as a sorcerer. Leonardo, it seems, had no desire to die for any conviction; he likely thought it more valuable to live for his ideas. Martyrdom is only for those who are filled by a single thought. Leonardo had too many thoughts.

Just as decisively as Leonardo speaks out against the "gold-makers" <note>A derogatory term for alchemists who claimed they could transmute base metals into gold.</note>, he nevertheless places alchemy in sharp contrast to astrology and necromancy, and he recognizes the utility it provides. He himself teaches how to manufacture powders, he constructs a glass furnace, and he draws an excellent distillation apparatus.

For Leonardo's achievements as an inventor of machines, I must refer to Dr. Hermann Grothe's "Leonardo da Vinci as Engineer and Philosopher" (Berlin, 1874). This author praises the precise knowledge that Leonardo possessed of all machine parts, their properties, and their possible applications. Indeed, a treatise by the master was to be dedicated to the <term>mechanical elements</term> <note>original: "elementi macchinali"</note>, apparently as part of the book "on applications," <term>on the benefits</term> <note>original: "dei giovamenti"</note>, which was intended to follow the theory of mechanics. Additionally, hydraulic machines, a hydraulic press, pumping stations—I believe that suffices.

Without sound mathematical knowledge, all of this would not have been possible. Leonardo also added several things to the science itself. If one wishes to truly appreciate the insights that Leonardo gained regarding astronomy, one must remember that his era had scarcely moved beyond the ideas of Aristotle and <term>Scholasticism</term> <note>The medieval school of philosophy that sought to reconcile Christian theology with classical Greek philosophy, particularly that of Aristotle.</note>, which we know from Dante. I wish to convey this with the beautiful words of Gabriel Séailles:
> "The stars are incorruptible, divine, without relation to our sublunary world <note>The region of the cosmos below the moon, which in ancient physics was the only place subject to change and decay.</note>, whose law is generation, change, and death. The Earth teaches us nothing about the heavens, which belong to a different order . . . Boldly, Leonardo shatters this hierarchy; he places the Earth in the heavens."

—
> "You have to show in your treatise that the Earth is a star, like the moon or nearly so, and thus prove the nobility of our world,"

Leonardo therefore says. The same laws as on Earth prevail throughout the entire world; the same necessity encompasses the universe. Everything is subject to motion, to measure, and to number. The heavens no longer revolve around a fixed center, moved by heavenly spirits who inhabit the stars, and no music accompanies their movement (see page 24) <note>A reference to the "Music of the Spheres," an ancient philosophical concept that the movements of celestial bodies created a divine harmony.</note>. And the stars are not glittering diamonds, fixed into the individual heavens according to nobility and dignity. The celestial bodies float freely in space, in the equilibrium of their elements. And the Earth is not at the center of the solar circle, nor is it the center and heart of the world. It is a star to the stars and a moon to the moon; its brilliance, like that of the moon, is a reflection of the sun, whose light is cast back to the celestial bodies in a strong glow by the thousandfold reflections of the wave-furrowed sea. Leonardo's conception is strange, yet full of fairytale charm and conceived quite realistically. The moon resembles the Earth and behaves like the Earth, [composed] of water, air, and...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Leonardo da Vinci’s cosmology, transitioning from his rejection of the medieval hierarchy of the heavens to his specific theories on the elements and the central role of the sun.</meta>

<page-num>CXLII</page-num>

...clothed in fire, elements that it draws to itself just as the earth draws its own, "just as the magnet draws iron." Leonardo clings strangely to the four elements; yet he no longer knows what to do with the element of fire. It is not exactly the burning thing; at most, it is drawn in by the flame. It is dark if it does not mix with something else; even whether it is hot seems sometimes questionable to him: how else would the air border the fire and yet be colder in the heights than in the depths—? It is the thinnest element, and perhaps Leonardo needs it to fill the space of the universe, since, as he emphasizes, there is no vacuum <note>original: "kein Leeres." Leonardo followed the Aristotelian belief that nature abhors a vacuum, requiring a substance to fill all space.</note>. The source of all light, the source of all warmth is the sun. He sings a hymn to it. It is more divine than the gods, is more powerful than they. From it, along with warmth, comes all life, all animation—that animation which is life, which was called at times <term>vital force</term> <note>original: "Lebenskraft." A hypothetical force or energy that gives life to living organisms.</note>, at times the <term>blood-soul</term> <note>original: "Blutseele." A concept of a physical soul tied to the blood and bodily functions, distinct from the spiritual mind.</note>, a physical, mortal, or at least volatile soul, such as the Platonists in Florence knew alongside the immortal spirit. In one of his manuscripts, Leonardo recorded in large letters amidst mathematical formulas the words: "The sun does not move." <note>original: "Il sole non si muove." This famous note in Leonardo's notebooks predates the widespread acceptance of the heliocentric model.</note> Was that a late-won conviction, or did Leonardo always know this dangerous truth? If we still say today, "the sun rises, the sun sets," why should Leonardo not speak of the twenty-four-hour course of the sun while having the correct state of affairs in mind? In those times, it was not advisable to want to know more than was approved by high authorities. Even the mere presumption of it made one highly suspicious.

More than with the sun, Leonardo occupied himself with the earth, and indeed with it not as a celestial body, but as the human home. Just as it does not stand still, so nothing stands still upon it. It is

in eternal becoming and dissolving—to use a phrase of Angelus Silesius <note>A 17th-century German priest and mystic poet known for his paradoxical verses on the nature of God and the soul.</note>—a creature of water. No seabed is so deep that it has not already seen the light of the sun, and no mountain peak so high that schools of fish did not formerly pass over it. The salt deposits of the earth are the <term>residues</term> <note>Remnants or leftovers of a process.</note> of earlier seas, and the seawater is salty because it leaches out old continents. Water eternally carries earth from the heights to the valley, eats away its banks, saws itself deeper and deeper, tears away and hollows out and creates mountains and heights; and the lightened mainland rises more and more out of the immense seas. And the water flows turbid from the earth it carries with it and deposits it—at the mouths, in the sea. And slowly the floor of the ocean rises and will emerge and become mainland, and where the fish passed, birds will fly. Through the <term>alluvium</term> <note>original: "Anschwemmungen." Deposits of clay, silt, and sand left by flowing water.</note>, through the <term>sedimentation</term> <note>original: "Ablagerungen." The process of particles settling to the bottom of a liquid.</note> of mud on the shores, which grew upward slowly, slowly over infinite ages, the <term>fossils</term> <note>original: "Fossilien." Leonardo was one of the first to correctly identify fossils as the remains of ancient living organisms rather than "tricks of nature."</note> were created, which we find layer by layer up to the summits of the mountains. Not the influence of the stars formed them; the tide did not bring them up, nor any <term>Great Flood</term> <note>original: "Sintflut." The biblical Deluge of Noah.</note> which covered the whole earth; such a thing never existed, could never have existed—"unless you believed in miracles"—which Leonardo does not do. He does not believe in violent interventions by God into the ordered world; he believes in transformations, not in upheavals—in <term>evolution</term> <note>The gradual development of something over time.</note>, despite the most modern thinkers. He reckons with millions of years; the wildly catastrophic is, to him as it was to Goethe, against his taste. The Florentine, who lived in the flat, water-rich Milan, never saw the subterranean forces of fire at work and never correctly recognized them. Thus, he also studies no primary rock. He knows only of <term>neptunistic formations</term> <note>original: "neptunischem Gebilde." Referring to Neptunism, the superseded geological theory that rocks formed from the crystallization of minerals in the early Earth's oceans.</note>. Regarding the tides, he does not reach a clear conclusion. Is the ebb and flow an effect of the moon, of the sun? he asks.

The answer varies. At times he believes it to be the breathing of the earth, which for a long time—and not merely as a play of fantasy—he considered to be a living being, formed in the likeness of an animal. In this view, the mountains were the bones and the rivers were the veins, fed from subterranean waters as if from a lake of blood; waters that rose to the peaks just as blood rises to the brain, and thus broke through the rock crevices like a burst vein to become the source of all rivers. In this way, the waters circulated and nourished the earth, just as blood circulates in the veins and nourishes the body. But just as Leonardo eventually argues against himself regarding the ebb and flow of the tide as the "breathing of the earth"—unfortunately, I have not reproduced that passage in the text—he also moves away from the belief that watercourses within the earth lead to the heights. It would be interesting to know if he realized that the earth possesses no pumping mechanism similar to the animal heart. He scolds himself and advises himself to "learn natural science <note>original: "Naturales." Referring to the study of the physical world and natural laws.</note> again" in order to rid himself of such opinions, of which he had accumulated a great store alongside the "capital of the fruit" that he possessed (p. 65)—I believe Leonardo means to say, alongside the fruitful knowledge he had acquired. As Mario Baratta <note>An Italian geographer and historian (1868–1935) who was a pioneer in the study of Leonardo’s scientific manuscripts.</note> rightly remarks in his fine book *Leonardo da Vinci and the Problems of the Earth*, the great researcher abandoned such theories in his later notes; he calls the clouds the "sowers of rivers" and clarifies this opinion more than once. The images that Leonardo draws of the changes in the face of the earth are extraordinarily magnificent, such as his conceptions of the past and future of the lands of the Mediterranean basin. However, it is not necessary for me to elaborate on this; the texts speak clearly for themselves.

knowledge went far beyond what he needed to know as an artist; however, it also went far beyond what the learned world of his time knew, or indeed, could even dream of. After all, in the Middle Ages, dissection was a practice as good as forbidden by the Church—at most a tolerated matter that was overlooked as long as possible. The medical schools were occasionally provided with the body of a criminal—under the rule of the Bentivogli <note>The noble family that ruled Bologna during the 15th century.</note>, the University of Bologna even had two executed persons at its disposal annually. Furthermore, a Bolognese professor, Mondino dei Luzzi, was the first to dissect human corpses and perform public anatomical demonstrations. His writing, which had been in circulation since 1316 in numerous, often highly distorted copies and was printed repeatedly from 1478 until the 16th century, contains on 44 pages brief descriptions of the contents of the head, chest, and abdomen, and adheres more to Galen <note>Aelius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), a Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years.</note> and the Arabists than to nature. Galen himself, however, the great authority of the ancients, never dissected anything other than monkeys and dogs. He congratulates himself that he was once able to examine human bones to his heart's content when a flooded river, which had destroyed a grave, left skeletons behind on a marshy spot. Mondino’s work was without illustrations; it was not until Berengar of Carpi, who taught in Bologna, attempted in 1521 to produce text and images based on his own incomplete research—both of which were meager and erroneous enough. The 30 corpses alone that Leonardo anatomically dissected were an unheard-of case: equally unheard-of was the result of this intensive study. Dr. Fritz Raab, in his "Leonardo da Vinci as a Natural Scientist" (*Collection of Popular Lectures*, edited by Virchow and Helmholtz, 1880), speaks of the anatomical work of Prof. Magnus Hundt, which proves the strange ideas that science held regarding the human entrails <term>entrails: internal organs, specifically the intestines</term> around 1501. With regard to the latter, to cite just one example, it should be mentioned that the pelvic tilt—the representation of the correct position of the pelvis in the body—was only pointed out in modern times through the investigations of Nägele, although Leonardo already knew and depicted it exactly." Leonardo is also the first, and for a long time the only one, who understood how to correctly draw the rib cage with the proper slant of the ribs, the curvature of the spine—in short, everything connected with this pelvic tilt. Likewise, the representation of the skull is masterful and always oriented according to the plane that we recognize as correct today. If I, as a layman, correctly understand Leonardo’s anatomical research, he never pursued anatomy purely for the sake of anatomy, as Vesalius did, even when he believed he was doing so. I believe the way he treated muscular anatomy in both image and text proves how much artistic interest dominated him. Anatomy never became an end in itself for him at all; he studies the structure of the human body primarily as an artist; as a human being, he especially studies the function of the organs. He seeks a science of life. His notes contain magnificent plans for a complete physiology: even today, his program could hardly be expanded. The methods Leonardo employs to provide a precise, clear, and all-encompassing graphic representation of the various parts of the body—detached from one another and connected together, even functioning—are strokes of genius. The famous French anatomist M. Mathias Duval says in his introduction to the Sabaschnikoff edition of the Vincian anatomy that even today we have hardly progressed further in these methods. Professor Holl believes that Leonardo must have understood how to create anatomical preparations in the modern sense for his illustrative purposes, for example, by injection of the mesentery <note>The fold of membrane attaching the abdominal organs to the body wall.</note> and the blood vessels.

That Leonardo was the first to practice <term>comparative anatomy</term> <note>The study of similarities and differences in the anatomy of different species.</note>; that he perceived the common type in the animal body; that he, as a matter of course, regarded man as an organized living being as nothing more than a highly placed animal, and the...

That Leonardo intended to develop his biological works into a kind of anthropology is proven by the passage (p. 92): "and so may it please our Author <note>Leonardo often uses "the Author" or "the Creator" to refer to God or the formative power of Nature.</note> that I may be able to represent the nature of men and their customs in the same manner as I describe their figure," and for this purpose, he had already collected notes such as the following: "Long nails are held in contempt by Europeans, while by the Indians they are held in great veneration; they have them colored with penetrating waters, and they adorn them with various perforations, saying that this is a mark of noble people and that short nails are the mark of laborers and mechanics in various trades" (S. P., W. An. B. Fol. 3r.).

In botany, Leonardo was the first to see and explain the lawful arrangement of branches, twigs, and leaves; he was the first to determine the age of trees by the rings in the trunk; yet he occupied himself with the plant world far more as an artist.

Leonardo actually pursued zoology only in connection with anatomy and biology.

All the more remarkable, then, is a work by Leonardo contained in a notebook that was apparently written between the years 1493–1494: I mean his book of animals, his *Bestiarius* <note>A Bestiary; a descriptive or anecdotal treatise on various real or mythical animals, often accompanied by moralizing explanations.</note>. Here, a wonderful piece of the Middle Ages comes to light. The archetype of the book was the old *Physiologus* <note>A didactic Christian text, likely written in the 2nd century AD, which used descriptions of animals to illustrate religious and moral lessons.</note>, "a compilation of existing and fabulous animals, plants, and stones, whose properties were typologically explained in a section following the natural history narrative..."

placed before the genus of apes; that he recognized the functions of his body and the movements of his limbs as being subject to the laws of mechanics—these are but a few contributions that illustrate the freedom and greatness of this towering genius from a new and striking perspective.

That Leonardo intended to develop his biological works into a kind of anthropology is proven by the passage: "and so may it please our Author <note>Leonardo often uses "the Author" or "the Creator" to refer to God or the formative power of Nature.</note> that I may be able to represent the nature of men and their customs in the same manner as I describe their figure," and for this purpose, he had already collected notes such as the following: "Long nails are held in contempt by Europeans, while by the Indians they are held in great veneration; they have them colored with penetrating waters, and they adorn them with various perforations, saying that this is a mark of noble people and that short nails are the mark of laborers and mechanics in various trades" (S. P., W. An. B. Fol. 3r.).

In botany, Leonardo was the first to see and explain the lawful arrangement of branches, twigs, and leaves; he was the first to determine the age of trees by the rings in the trunk; yet he occupied himself with the plant world far more as an artist.

Leonardo actually pursued zoology only in connection with anatomy and biology.

All the more remarkable, then, is a work by Leonardo contained in a notebook that was apparently written between the years 1493–1494: I mean his book of animals, his *Bestiary* <note>original: "Bestiarius"</note> <note>A Bestiary; a descriptive or anecdotal treatise on various real or mythical animals, often accompanied by moralizing lessons.</note>...

<page-num>CXLIX</page-num>

interpreted or, in other words: explained as a <term>type</term><note>A "type" or "typus" refers to a symbolic figure or event in the natural world or Old Testament that foreshadows a spiritual reality, such as Christ or the Church.</note> for Christ, the Devil, the Church, or Man"—(see the works of Goldstaub and Wendriner and of Anton Springer)—thus, products of nature were used for the purpose of religious symbolism. The animals, plants, and stones were originally those mentioned in Holy Scripture and were thereby already emphasized and distinguished. Soon, plants and stones were dropped; writers unhesitatingly went beyond the Bible; instead of ecclesiastical symbolism, moral symbolism moved to the forefront, and every animal became an image and a lesson of virtue and vice: in this form, as a <term>Bestiary</term><note>A Bestiary (Bestiarius) was a popular medieval compendium of animals, combining natural history with moral lessons and religious allegories.</note>, the book became the most widespread and popular textbook and reader of the Middle Ages. Its versions are translated into all languages of the Christian world; there exist Icelandic and Syrian versions as well as Dutch and Provençal, yet the content, the circle of animals, and the interpretation remain almost the same in all of them. Leonardo's work joins these countless adaptations as one of the last. He borrows the material and the method of treatment—indeed, the arrangement itself—from the older works: otherwise, it would not have become a Bestiary. His sources are the "Flowers of Virtue" <note>original: "Fiori di virtù"</note>, a widely read, often printed book with small excursions that always treat a virtue and its opposite vice, with examples from antiquity, the Gospels, Church Fathers, and the book of animals—full of the most graceful naivety, comparable in mood to Fra Angelico: a third of Leonardo's work is extracted from this book and is recognizable by the paired arrangement of "Virtue-Vice"; only the delicate ornamentation of the language belongs to the artist Leonardo. The other sources are Cecco d'Ascoli's "The Acerbic One" <note>original: "L'acerba"</note> (a work I have not seen) and especially the Natural History of the younger Pliny, in addition to Brunetto Latini and Albertus Magnus, whose encyclopedias also contained moral-allegorical animal books—works that Leonardo knew and partially

<sig>CL</sig>

he himself possessed (for details see Goldstaub and Wendriner, "A Tosco-Venetian <term>Bestiary</term><note>original: Bestiarius; a medieval treatise on animals.</note>," Halle a. S., Niemeyer’s Publishing, 1892). — Nothing indicates for what reason Leonardo undertook this work — the least original and yet the only one that can be called finished. With its fabulous content and its reliance on authority, it seems doubly to contradict Leonardo’s very nature. At the beginning of the nineties of the <term>Quattrocento</term><note>The 1400s, or the 15th century in Italian art and culture.</note>, the critical thinker Leonardo certainly still had a long path of development ahead of him. We have, in general, a few fragments—very few passages—which, in light of what Leonardo was capable of believing (even if only as a youth), have a staggering effect. And why not! What contemporary travelers reported as eyewitnesses of distant lands and things was not much less wonderful than the stories of the tiger and the phoenix, and everyone swore by their words. The fantastic element, the bizarre nature of this "natural history," corresponded perfectly to one side of that era, a side of Leonardo’s genius, just like the penchant for symbolism: the stranger, the better; one need only read the mottos and allegories he devised at that time, the texts for his designs and drawings. I believe that we must be careful not to rationalize Leonardo in a modern way, and his book of animals is as good as a warning sign against doing so. Let us keep in mind: Leonardo comes to us; we never fully go to Leonardo. The past is dead; it is in vain to try to imagine today how those brains and hearts, now crumbled into decay, once felt.

That is the great, melancholy lesson one draws from any unbiased study of vanished times and things. Do we ever truly understand a complete <term>Renaissance man</term><note>original: Renaissancemensch; the ideal of a "universal man" (homo universalis) skilled in many fields.</note> in his mixture of the monstrous and the most delicate! Traces of both are found in the very greatest, even in a Leonardo. They provide the <term>chiaroscuro</term><note>original: Helldunkel; the treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting.</note> that sculpts his appearance into a three-dimensional form. Lomazzo <note>Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo (1538–1592), an Italian painter and art theorist.</note> relates that Leonardo sometimes took peasants from the market home with him and entertained them with wine and stories so that they laughed themselves full and mad: and when they had departed afterward with thanks, he drew their grotesque faces from memory. Among his manuscripts, he preserved beautiful jests, "<term>belle facezie</term>" <note>Italian for "beautiful witticisms" or "clever jokes."</note>, which he heard and collected in order to utilize them—jests, certainly, intended to make peasants laugh. For us, they are without wit, barely intelligible, and impossible to render in German <note>The translator notes that these jokes do not translate well into the target language of the original manuscript.</note>; yet in Leonardo’s time, Bandello <note>Matteo Bandello (c. 1480–1562), an Italian novelist known for his witty and sometimes bawdy tales.</note> told such things and worse still in the circle of the most educated, virtuous, and delicate women of the Renaissance, at Mantua, in the studio of the beautiful Marchioness Isabella Gonzaga, Princess of Este. And outside, the fountains splashed lovely accompaniment, while from every wall gazed the sweet poetry of Perugino and Mantegna, and grave and grand in a corner stood the marble Cupid of the young Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564).</note>, a gift from Cesare Borgia, Duke of the Romagna. Leonardo also knew how to enchant princes and princesses. For another half-century, people in Florence and Milan spoke of the seductive brilliance of his being. He was an improviser without equal and had the good taste not to write his improvisations down. His best verses and songs he left to us painted and drawn. Yet his fables, the fragments of stories, with their so modern mixture of scientific exactness and poetic flight, already give us a concept of what he used to tell beautiful ladies while he [painted] them—

<page-num>CLII</page-num>

portrayed them, so that he would not have to immortalize the bored mourning of their features. The novelistic fragments, fables, descriptions—everything that Leonardo left to us in writing has such a distinct conversational tone that a legend arose suggesting these texts served as the basis for lectures Leonardo gave in his Milanese Academy—an academy, parenthetically, that never existed except in the heads of a few over-clever gentlemen and as an inscription on some artistically intertwined ornaments. Leonardo’s writings are, however, certainly intended for speaking, destined for the ear, for which emphasis and pauses provide structure and grouping; intended for the long-winded speech of that era, which allowed one to slip over violations of syntax and cover them up again through compensating errors: a wild-blooming style of speech, such as flourishes wonderfully in every early age and in the mouths of the common people at all times. The pedants in Florence and Milan likely reproached him for this style, lacking as it was in grammatical schooling, against whom he knew how to defend himself so often and so proudly.

A most remarkable production are Leonardo’s "Prophecies." What we can date of them was compiled in 1497, precisely at the time when Savonarola <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), a Dominican friar and preacher active in Renaissance Florence, known for his prophecies of civic glory and calls for Christian renewal.</note> was regarded as a prophet in Florence and as far away as France. I am merely putting these facts together; I am not making a theory out of it. I only mean that Leonardo, faced with the man who wanted to transform the world into a joyless monastery, could hardly have felt differently than Goethe did a few centuries later, who called him a grotesque, fantastic monster and an impure enthusiast: only Leonardo was even more accustomed than Goethe to seeing the worst horrors from the perspective of eternity <note>original: "sub specie aeternitatis"</note> and to approving them in resignation as a mysterious necessity. He put on the Savonarola mask; what he said beneath it, while he

<sig>CLIV</sig>

often brought forth. There is no gift in him that does not have its counterpart, and if they disturb one another, they do not paralyze each other, his gifts, but rather draw strength from one another. A monstrous intellect that criticizes, dissects, decomposes; a monstrous imagination that combines, forms, and envisions. A heart that overflows, which embraces all of life, every creature, in a tenderness without equal; a character that holds everything together, bends everything in one direction, and forces it into the work with strict economy. So perfect, and thereby enclosed as if in inaccessible silver armor, Leonardo moves through his time. He is related to everything in love like the Saint of Assisi <note>St. Francis of Assisi, known for his love of all living creatures.</note> and yet a stranger to everything like the messenger of an entirely different world, because he does not mix with the lowly earthly one and has very little in common with it. With that great <term>Sophrosyne</term> <note>A Greek philosophical term for excellence of character and soundness of mind, characterized by temperance, moderation, and self-control.</note>, the serene balance of the outward being which is the hallmark of the highest superiority of human nobility, he is still considered today to be indifferently cool, like Goethe. Napoleon had recognized this differently. "He is a man who has had great sorrows," <note>original: "C'est un homme qui a eu de grands chagrins"</note> he said of him. Leonardo's wonderful self-portrait tells the same story. "Dig but deep enough, and under all earth runs water and under all life runs grief." If Leonardo's own words have not already betrayed it: "where there is the greatest feeling, there is the greatest martyrdom." The martyrdom of his own, truly greatest feeling, eventually turned the man—who once walked unmoved through blood and horror at the side of a Borgia <note>Cesare Borgia, the ruthless Italian nobleman whom Leonardo served as a military engineer.</note>—almost into a Buddhist, to whom all life was sacred, even to the point of abstaining from eating meat, so that for his sake not the slightest creature should have to suffer pain and death. And in him who said: "he who does not value life does not deserve it," there lies right alongside it the deep longing for rest, the longing for death. "Night" he calls the proverb: "just as a day's work well spent brings a good sleep, so a life well applied

Now see, the hope and the desire to return again to one’s homeland makes it like the butterfly with the light...” <note>Leonardo often used the metaphor of the moth or butterfly drawn to light to describe the soul's longing to return to its source.</note>
Such words lift the final veil from Leonardo’s essence. The great <term>Positivist</term> <note>A philosopher who recognizes only that which can be scientifically verified or logically proved.</note> was, in the deepest depths of his beauty-thirsty soul, a <term>pantheistic mystic</term> <note>One who finds the divine in all aspects of the natural world rather than in a distant, personified deity.</note>.

**W**hoever has taken the trouble to read through the preceding pages will already sense what immeasurable difficulties the understanding, the selection, and the translation of the great master’s works present. I set out years ago, as non-judgmental as a child, to scoop out an ocean with the nutshell of my skill and knowledge; and as it is with water: I did not become master over it, it became master over me and would not let me go. What I have gathered of the precious liquid in my shell, I now offer to the reader for the second time, to see if it pleases his palate. For me, all the treasures of the world glisten within it.

So much I had to leave aside. I could give no concept of the impulsive immediacy of these seemingly personal outpourings of Leonardo, which are at the same time nothing but the formulation of a physical truth, the calculation of <term>conic sections</term> <note>Curves obtained by intersecting a cone with a plane, such as circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas.</note>, the draft of an <term>icosahedron</term> <note>A three-dimensional geometric shape with twenty faces.</note>; yet next to these stands: “false! not right! erred!” or “this is a beautiful doubt and worthy of being considered!” or so amiably cheerful: “Tell me if anything was ever made...” “Bodies, emerged from the perspective of <term>Leonardo da Vinci</term>, disciple of science.”

The translation is neither elegant, nor is it very good German; it is only entirely faithful. It would be very easy

<meta>Continuing from the translator's reflection on the immense difficulty of translating Leonardo da Vinci's manuscripts and her decision to offer this second edition to the reader.</meta>

<page-num>CLVI</page-num>

been possible to make them differently—much more convenient for me, much more pleasant for the reader; however, I felt I had to reproduce Leonardo, not allow myself to improve him in any way. Where he is unclear, he remains unclear: my interpretation might perhaps have become a forgery. I have treated the texts as one treats documents; every rearrangement of a word could obscure the meaning. I did not want to place myself under the law of grammar and thus efface Leonardo. So I sacrificed, perhaps, a degree of clarity and easy readability—for grammar is not an end in itself, but a means to an end—yet I gained, I believe, without seeking out archaic words, an ancient, weathered tone of language: the naive circumstantiality, the sincere simplicity, and, with bold unconcern, something of the beautiful imagery—a piece of that which I wanted to preserve at all costs. In my heavy struggles of conscience, it often reassured me that Paul Ernst <note>A German neo-classicist writer and translator known for his rigorous approach to historical texts.</note> proceeded in the same way in his masterful translation of old Italian novellas, and that I had already dared something similar with J. P. Jacobsen <note>Jens Peter Jacobsen, a Danish author whose complex, atmospheric prose Herzfeld had previously translated.</note>.

In closing, I would like to express my warm gratitude to the high administration of the Imperial and Royal Court Library in Vienna <note>original: "k. k. Hofbibliothek in Wien." This is now the Austrian National Library.</note> for generously making the precious material for my difficult work available to me for years; I would like to thank the gentlemen who took so much trouble for me, specifically Dr. Othmar Doublier, Dr. Friedrich Egger von Möllwald, Dr. Franz Schöchtner, Dr. Doernhöffer, Dr. Egger, Dr. Weixelgaertner, and finally Dr. Beer, all of whom assisted and accommodated me in the most gracious manner in the Library and in the Print Collection <note>original: "Kupferstichsammlung"</note> of the Most High Imperial House.

September 1906

MARIE HERZFELD

The notes by Leonardo which are compiled in this collection were taken from the following publications:

1. From the beautiful, exemplarily arranged edition of the manuscripts in 6 folio volumes held by the library of the Institut de France in Paris (*The manuscripts of Leonardo da Vinci, published in phototypic facsimiles, with literal transcriptions etc. by Mr. Charles Ravaisson-Mollien, Paris, Maison Quantin, 1881—1891* <note>original: "Les manuscrits de Léonard de Vinci..."</note>). The individual manuscripts bear the signatures: A., B., C., D., E., F., G., H. (I, II, III), I., K., L., M.; additionally, the two manuscripts from the collection of the Lords Ashburnham, which are designated as Ash. I, Ash. II.

2. From the large luxury edition of the Codex Atlanticus of the Ambrosian Library (*The Atlantic Codex of Leonardo da Vinci in the Ambrosian Library of Milan, reproduced and published by the Royal Academy of Lincei etc. Diplomatic and critical transcription by Giovanni Piumati. Ulrico Hoepli, Milan 1894—1903* <note>original: "Il codice atlantico di Leonardo da Vinci..."</note>). This codex is designated as CA.

3. From the Codex of the House of Trivulzio (*The Codex of L. d. V. in the Library of Prince Trivulzio in Milan. Transcribed and annotated by Luca Beltrami etc. Milan 1891, Fratelli Dumolard* <note>original: "Il Codice di L. d. V. nella Biblioteca del Principe Trivulzio..."</note>). Signature Ms. Tr.

4. From the highly meritorious two-volume work by J. P. Richter (*Literary works of L. d. V. compiled and edited from the original manuscripts by Jean Paul Richter etc. in two volumes etc. London, Simpson Low, Matson, Searle & Rivington, 1883*). This work, which was published by subscription, remains extremely important to us today as a source for the treasures of the English libraries, which unfortunately for the most part still await publication. One can raise objections against the selection Richter made—no selection is flawless; he also occasionally errs in the reading and interpretation of the texts; the translation of the texts, which he did not perform himself, is certainly in excellent English but shows insufficient knowledge of Italian; nevertheless, it would be a mistake to fail to recognize or to underestimate the immense value of this great labor. SINCE I SEE THAT I CANNOT
SEIZE UPON ANY SUBJECT OF GREAT
UTILITY OR PLEASURE, BECAUSE THE MEN
WHO WERE BORN BEFORE ME HAVE TAKEN
FOR THEMSELVES ALL USEFUL AND
NECESSARY TOPICS, I SHALL DO
AS ONE WHO, OUT OF POVERTY, COMES LAST TO
THE FAIR AND, BEING UNABLE
TO PROVIDE HIMSELF WITH ANYTHING ELSE,
GATHERS UP ALL THOSE
THINGS WHICH HAVE ALREADY BEEN SEEN BY THE
OTHERS AND NOT ACCEPTED,
BUT RATHER REJECTED BECAUSE OF
THEIR LOW VALUE. I—THESE
LOWLY AND DISDAINED WARES, THE LEFTOVERS
FROM THE MANY BUYERS—I SHALL LOAD UPON
MY WEAK BEAST OF BURDEN <note>original: "Saumtier"; a pack animal used for transporting goods</note> AND WITH
THIS—NOT THROUGH THE GREAT CITIES,
BUT THROUGH THE POOR VILLAGES—I SHALL
GO DISTRIBUTING THEM AND RECEIVE SUCH REWARD
AS THE THING DESERVES, WHICH
WAS GIVEN BY ME. <term>MS. CA. FOL. 119 r.</term> <note>Refers to the Codex Atlanticus, folio 119 recto; Leonardo's largest collection of drawings and writings.</note>

# I. ON SCIENCE

<margin>Theory and Practice.</margin>
<margin>R. 110, MS. BR. M. FOL. 171 r. <note>Refers to the British Museum Manuscript (Codex Arundel), folio 171 recto.</note></margin>
**Y**ou must first describe the theory and thereafter the practice.

---

<margin>The leadership that belongs to knowledge.</margin>
<margin>MS. J. FOL. 130 r. <note>Refers to Manuscript J of the Institut de France.</note></margin>
## II.

->Science is the captain, and practice, those are the soldiers.<-

---

<margin>Let the artist not believe that they can dispense with science.</margin>
<margin>MS. G. FOL. 8 r. <note>Refers to Manuscript G of the Institut de France.</note></margin>
## III.

### Of the error of those who apply practice without science

Those who fall in love with practice without science are like the pilot who boards a ship without a rudder or a compass: who then never possesses certainty as to where they are going.

Practice must always be built upon good theory, for which perspective is the guide and the gateway; and without it, one achieves nothing well in the occurrences of painting.

---

<margin>Difference between theory and practice; the danger of pure theorizing.</margin>
<margin>MS. CA. FOL. 93 v. <note>Refers to the Codex Atlanticus, folio 93 verso.</note></margin>
## IV.

### Where the science of weights is deceived by practice

The science of weights is deceived by its practice, and in many parts, the latter is not in harmony with the former science, nor is it possible to bring them into accord; and this is produced by the poles of the balance, by means of which one draws science from such weights, which poles at <note>The text breaks off here, likely continuing the technical discussion of mechanics on the following page.</note>

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci argues that artistic and mechanical practice must be governed by scientific theory, specifically citing perspective and mechanics as essential foundations. He uses the metaphors of a captain and a pilot to illustrate that action without intellectual guidance is directionless and prone to error.</summary>

# I. ON SCIENCE (Continued)

<page-num>3</page-num>

the ancient philosophers were assumed as poles of the nature of the mathematical line, and in some places as mathematical points, which points and lines are incorporeal <note>Lacking physical substance; existing only in the mind.</note>: and practice sets them as corporeal <note>Physical or material.</note>, because necessity so commands it, if they are to support the weight of the same scale, together with the weights that are judged upon it.

<meta>This page continues the previous discussion on the necessity of mathematical certainty by establishing the "Experiment" as the bridge between nature's laws and human understanding, shifting from theoretical mechanics to the scientific method.</meta>

MS. CA. FOL. 86 r.

# X.

<margin>The Experiment: a systematic imitation of nature's process in order to find the lawful connections which constitute science.</margin>
The experiment, an interpreter <note>original: "Dolmetsch"</note> between ingenious nature and the human species, teaches us what that same nature applies among mortals; that one, constrained by necessity, cannot act otherwise than as reason, her rudder, teaches her to act.

---

MS. E. FOL. 55 r.

# XI.

<margin>From the investigation of effects, you will recognize the causes.</margin>
(In a definition regarding the compound balance) . . . But first I will make some trials before I proceed further, because my intention is to first put forward the experiment, and then to show with the cause why said experiment is constrained to act in such a manner. And this is the true rule of how the seekers of nature's effects must proceed; and although nature begins with the cause and ends with the experiment, we must follow the opposite path—that is, begin, as I said above, with the experiment and with this investigate the cause.

---

MS. A. FOL. 47 r.

# XII.

<margin>Only from a series of experiments can one draw certain conclusions.</margin>
. . . Before you make a general rule out of this case, try it two or three times and see whether the experiments produce the same effects.

---

MS. CA. FOL. 154 r.

# XIII.

<margin>Not experience, but our judgment deceives us.</margin>
The experiment never errs; rather, it is only your judgments that err, which promise themselves an effect from the experiment that is not grounded in our experiences. For, once a beginning is given, it is necessary that what follows is the true consequence of such a beginning, if it has not already been (disturbed and) hindered; and even if a hindrance were present, the effect which should have proceeded from the aforementioned beginning takes on more or less of the named <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

<term>Experiment (Experiment)</term>: In this context, it refers to a physical trial or observation used to test a theory.
<term>Cause (Ursache)</term>: The underlying physical law or reason why something happens.
<term>Effect (Wirkung)</term>: The observable result of a cause in the physical world.

<summary>This page defines the scientific method as an inductive process, arguing that while nature works from cause to effect, humans must work from experimental effects back to their underlying causes. It emphasizes that "experience" is reliable, but human interpretation of that experience is often where error occurs.</summary>
<keywords>scientific method, empiricism, cause and effect, logic, nature, experimental proof, human judgment</keywords>

...part in the obstruction, as the same is more or less powerful than the already mentioned beginning.

Experience does not err, but only our judgments err, promising themselves things from her that are not in her power. Men wrongly complain about experience, accusing her with the highest reproaches of being deceitful. But let that same experience alone and turn such lamentation against your own ignorance, which causes you to be over-hasty, promising yourselves with your vain and foolish desires those things which are not in her power, saying she is deceitful.

Men wrongly complain about innocent experience, frequently accusing her of false and lying demonstrations.

<margin>As in mathematics, one must ascend in all sciences from the known to the unknown.</margin>
### XIV. MS. F. FOL. 23 r.

To deepen a canal: do this in the book "On Practical Applications," and while you are testing them, refer to the proven propositions, and this is the true order; for if you wanted to show the application of every proposition first, you would have to make tools now to prove such utility, and so you would disrupt the order of the forty books among one another, and likewise the order of the illustrations; that is, you would have to mix practice with theory, which would be a confused and entirely fragmented matter.

<margin>Besides the experimental method, logical reasoning is also permissible.</margin>
### XV. R. 6, MS. BR. M. FOL. 32 v.

It is not to be blamed if, within the order of the development of a science, some general rule is shown that is born from a preceding conclusion.

<margin>The experiment is only an aid to knowledge.</margin>
### XVI. MS. CA. FOL. 147 v.

No effect in nature is without a cause; understand the cause, and you have no need for the experiment. <note>Leonardo suggests that once the underlying laws of nature are fully grasped through reason, the physical test becomes a confirmation rather than a discovery.</note>

<summary>Leonardo defends the reliability of experience against human error and outlines his methodology for organizing scientific treatises by separating theory from practical application. He concludes that while experiments are necessary for discovery, the ultimate goal of science is to understand the underlying causes of natural effects.</summary>

## XVII. MS. E. FOL. 54 r.

<margin>One must always strive to ascend to the ultimate causes if one wishes to ground their knowledge well.</margin>
In order to provide the true science of the flight of birds through the air, it is necessary first to provide the science of the winds, which we shall prove by means of the motions of water within itself; and this same rational science <note>original: "vernünftige Wissenschaft"</note> will of itself become a ladder, in order to reach by it the knowledge of flyers within the air and the wind.

## XVIII. MS. CA. FOL. 119 r.

<margin>All true knowledge teaches us to recognize the limits of our spirit and to demand nothing impossible.</margin>
. . . . These rules are the cause of making you distinguish the true from the false, which matter in turn ensures that men only promise themselves possible things and with more moderation, and that you do not shroud yourself in ignorance, which would result in you achieving no effect and having to surrender yourself to melancholy in despair.

## XIX. MS. M. FOL. 58 v.

<margin>The recognition of truth is a work of millennia.</margin>
Truth was always only the daughter of time. <note>A common Renaissance proverb, "Veritas filia temporis," suggesting that truth is revealed gradually through history.</note>

## XX. MS. G. FOL. 47 r.

<margin>One does not wrest all secrets from nature.</margin>
O you seeker of things, do not boast of knowing the things which nature leads through herself according to her own order. But rejoice to know the purpose and end of those things which are designed by your own mind.

## XXI. MS. CA. FOL. 223 r.

<margin>The value of knowledge for character and judgment.</margin>
The acquisition of any knowledge is always useful to the intellect, because it will be able to drive out the useless things from itself and retain the good. Because one can neither love nor hate a thing unless one first has knowledge of it.
