<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s reflections on the acquisition of knowledge, specifically criticizing those who seek intellectual shortcuts or "abbreviations" rather than studying the intricate details of nature, such as the human body.</meta>

<margin>To consider the presentation and derivative proof as superfluous.</margin>
...owledge was always the daughter of such knowledge; love is all the more inward as the knowledge is more certain, which certainty arises from the integral knowledge of all those parts which, united together, form the whole of the things that are to be loved. Of what use, then, is he who—in order to shorten the parts of those things of which he makes it his trade to give an exhaustive account—leaves out the greater part of the things from which the whole is composed? It is true that impatience, the mother of folly, is she who praises brevity: as if these same people did not have enough life remaining to them so that it might serve them to be able to acquire the complete knowledge of a single such detail as a human body is. And afterwards, they wish to encompass the spirit of God, in which the universe is enclosed, by weighing it in carats <note>original: "Karate"; a unit of weight, here used to mock the attempt to measure the infinite</note> and hacking it into infinite particles, as if they had to anatomize it.

O human stupidity! Do you, who have spent your whole life with yourself, not perceive yourself? And do you have no knowledge of that which you possess most of all—namely, your foolishness? And do you then wish to deceive yourself and others with the majority of the Sophists <note>term: Sophists; here referring to those who use clever but fallacious arguments rather than empirical truth</note>, despising the mathematical sciences in which truth dwells and all knowledge of the things contained within them? And do you then wish to run off to wonders and write that you have knowledge of things of which the human spirit is not capable, and which cannot be proven by any example from nature? And you believe you have performed a miracle when you have destroyed the work of some speculative genius <note>term: Ingenium; the innate creative power or talent of an artist or scientist</note>, and you do not notice that you fall into the same error as he who strips the tree of the ornament of its branches, which are full of foliage interspersed with fragrant blossoms and leaves... as Justinus did, the abbreviator of the histories that Trogus Pompeius wrote. <note>Justinus was a Roman historian who famously condensed the massive "Philippic Histories" of Trogus Pompeius, a process Leonardo views here as a destructive mutilation of knowledge.</note>

<summary>Leonardo critiques the "abbreviators" who seek brevity at the expense of depth, arguing that true love for a subject springs from an exhaustive knowledge of its parts. He warns against the arrogance of trying to define the divine or the supernatural while remaining ignorant of one's own nature and the mathematical truths of the physical world.</summary>

**XXIV.**                                         MS. CA. FOL. 119 r.

### XXV. Codex Atlanticus Folio 117 r.

<margin>Against certain humanists.</margin>
Although I might not know how to cite authors as they do, a much greater and more worthy thing to read is the citation of experience, the mistress of their masters. Those people walk about puffed up and pompous, clothed and adorned not with their own labors, but with those of others, and they do not grant me my own; and if they despise me as an inventor <note>term: inventor; in Leonardo's time, this referred to a discoverer of new truths or original creator, rather than just a mechanical tinkerer</note>, how much more can they be blamed—they who are not inventors, but rather trumpets and reciters of the works of others.

### XXVI. Codex Atlanticus Folio 76 r.

<margin>Against the book-scholars, the scholastics, and other unfree spirits.</margin>
Whoever disputes and relies on authority does not use his intellect, but rather his memory.

### XXVII. Codex Atlanticus Folio 76 r.

<margin>Spiritual gifts are to be valued higher than intellectual training.</margin>
Good sciences are born from a good nature; and because one must praise the cause more than the effect, you will praise a good nature without learning more than a good scholar without nature.

### XXVIII. Codex Atlanticus Folio 117 r.

<margin>Against the overestimation of the book-scholar and the underestimation of the researcher of nature and the inventor.</margin>
Men who are inventors and mediators between nature and humanity must be judged and esteemed differently than the reciters and trumpets of the works of others; just as an object outside of a mirror is far superior to the image of that object appearing in the mirror; for the one is something in itself, and the other is nothing. These are people little indebted to nature, for they only have clothing by chance, and without it, you could group them with the herds of cattle.

### XXIX. Manuscript F Folio 27 v.

<margin>Against the parasitism of those who live by criticizing great spirits.</margin>
**Of the five regular bodies.** <note>term: regular bodies; the five Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron) which were central to Renaissance geometry</note>
Against certain commentators who [criticize] the ancient inventors

### XXX. MS. CA. FOL. 91 v.

<margin>*He who closes his eyes to nature and to knowledge harms himself.*</margin>
To the ambitious, who are not satisfied with the gift of life nor with the beauty of the world, it is given as a penance that they themselves tear this life apart and that they do not possess the utility and beauty of the world.

### XXXI. SP., MS. V. U. FOL. 12 r.

<margin>*Concerning Truth.*</margin>
Lie is of such contemptibility that, even if it spoke of great things concerning God himself, it would rob His divinity of grace; and Truth is of such excellence that, even if it praises the most trivial things, they become noble.

Without doubt, such a distance exists between Truth and Falsehood as there is between light and darkness; and Truth in itself is of such excellence that even when it spreads over modest and lowly matters, it surpasses without comparison the uncertainties and lies that hold forth on grand and most sublime subjects. This is because, even if our spirit possessed the Lie as a fifth element <note>The "fifth element" refers to the quintessence or ether, which ancient science believed filled the universe beyond the four earthly elements</note>, it nevertheless remains that the truth of things is the highest nourishment of fine intellects, but not of wandering wits <note>original: "Ingenien"; refers to restless or undisciplined minds</note>.

<margin>Marginal note</margin> But you, who live on dreams, are better pleased by the sophistical arguments and the trickery of "ball-blowers" <note>original: "Ballaufbläsern"; a derogatory term for those who inflate their own importance with hot air or empty words</note> in grandiose and uncertain matters, than by those things that are certain, natural, and not of such lofty height.

<summary>Leonardo critiques the "ambitious" who ignore the beauty of the natural world and argues that even a small truth is superior to a grand lie. He asserts that the pursuit of natural reality is the only proper nourishment for a refined mind.</summary>

## XXXII. <meta>MS. CA. FOL. 79 r.</meta>

<margin>
*We must hold fast to appearances.*
</margin>
What an element is; the definition of the very essence <term>essence: the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing</term> of the elements is not within the power of man; but a great part of their effects is known.

## XXXIII. <meta>MS. J. FOL. 18 r.</meta>

<margin>
*Nature is deeper than our experience.*
</margin>
Nature is full of countless reasons <note>original: "ragioni"; in this context, Leonardo uses "reasons" to mean the underlying laws or causal principles of the natural world</note> that never entered into experience. <note>original: "La natura è piena d'infinite ragioni che non furono mai in isperienza." Leonardo often wrote in Italian even within German-compiled manuscripts; he argues here that the laws of physics exist whether or not humans have observed them yet.</note>

<summary>Leonardo reflects on the limitations of human understanding, noting that while we cannot define the true essence of the elements, we can observe their effects, and that nature contains infinite laws yet to be discovered by human experience.</summary>

# XI.

->**What is Force?**<-

<margin>Drafts for a comprehensive explanation of force as the cause of motion, and thus of all processes in nature.</margin>
Force I call a spiritual energy, an invisible power, which is brought forth through motion by means of accidental external violence and is inherent in and fused with bodies that have been torn from their natural habit and diverted from it. It gives them an active life of remarkable power, compels all created things to change their form and position, rushes with fury toward its longed-for death, and transforms itself according to the cause. Delay makes it great and speed makes it weak. It is born from violence and dies through freedom. And the greater it is, the more rapidly it consumes itself. It drives away with vehemence whatever opposes its destruction, desires to conquer and kill its own foundation and its opposite, and in conquering, it kills itself. It becomes mightier where it finds greater resistance. Every thing gladly flees death. Being itself constrained, it conquers everything. No thing moves without it. The body in which it is born grows neither in weight nor in form. No motion that it makes is permanent. It grows great through labor and vanishes in rest. The body into which it is forced is outside of freedom. And it frequently generates new force by means of motion.

Force is caused by motion and linked with weight. And likewise, impact <note>original: "Stoß"</note> is caused by motion and linked with weight.

Force is the cause of motion, and motion is the cause of force; motion fuses with force.

### XVIII.

### On Weight, Force, Motion, and Impact

Weight always presses upon its support and, by its very nature, penetrates and passes from the support to its base, and from each through every support and entirely through every base of said support, and entirely through every support of the base, and penetrates from support to support until it reaches the center of the world <note>The "center of the world" refers to the center of the Earth, which in pre-Copernican physics was considered the universal center toward which all heavy things strive.</note>.

Weight always presses upon a support; force fails the body in which it arises.

Motion weakens and consumes itself in its course; impact <term>impact <note>original: "Stoß"; can also be translated as percussion or shock</note></term> dies as soon as it is born, and leaves its cause tarnished.

Weight, which acts eternally in its pressure, is of lesser power than the three other <term>passions <note>original: "Passionen"; here meaning physical properties or "suffered" states of matter</note></term> that are within it, namely force, motion, and impact. The second thing of lesser duration is force, less powerful than weight, and its function lasts but a little while; the third permanence would be motion, of greater power than force and generated by it; the fourth, of shorter duration, is impact, which is a son of motion and grandson of force, and all of them are born from weight.

<margin>The straightness of the fall.</margin>
## XXI. On the motion of the arrow shot by the bow

The arrow, shot from the center of the world toward the highest part of the elements <note>The "elements" refers to the four spheres of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire that were believed to surround the globe.</note>, will ascend and descend upon one and the same straight line, even though the elements are in a circular motion around the center of those same elements.
A heavy object, which descends through the rotating elements, always has its motion according to the straightness of the line that extends from the beginning of the motion to the center of the world.

<margin>The line of the fall, determined by gravity and by the rotation of the earth on its axis.</margin>
## XXII. On a heavy object falling through the air while the elements are in a circular motion, with a total rotation time of 24 hours

The <term>moving body <note>original: "mobile"</note></term>, which descends from the highest part of the sphere of fire <note>The "sphere of fire" was considered the outermost shell of the terrestrial world, located just below the moon.</note>, will make a straight-line motion down to the earth, even though the elements are in constant circular motion around the center of the world. This is proven: let *B* be the load which moves from *A* through the elements to descend to the center of the world *M*. I say that such a load, although it makes a curved descent in the manner of a <term>spiral line <note>original: "Schraubenlinie"; literally a screw-line or helix</note></term>, will nevertheless never deviate from its straight-line course, which load is in constant progression between the place from which it [originated...]

When the <term>moving body <note>original: "Mobile"; refers to an object in motion</note></term> descends from *C* to *F*, *D*—the beginning of the motion—has moved toward *E* in that same time; and when *F* goes toward *H*, *E* rotates toward *G*. If the moving body descends from the highest part of the elements to the lowest in 24 hours, its motion is composed of the straight and the curved. I say straight, because it will never deviate from the shortest line extending from the place it left to the center of the elements, and it will come to rest at the lowest end of such rectilinearity, which, according to the zenith <note>The point in the sky directly above the observer</note>, is always located beneath the place from which such a <term>moving body</term> separated. And this motion is in itself curved, in all parts of its line, and is consequently also curved at the end with the whole line; and from this it follows that the stone thrown down from a tower does not strike the side of said tower until it reaches the very ground.

### XXIII.
<note>MS. M. FOL. 44 v.</note>

<margin>The law of the regularly increasing speed of the fall.</margin>
This occurs in air of uniform density. — The weight which moves downward acquires, in every degree of time, one degree of forward motion more than the degree of the preceding time, and likewise one degree of speed more than the degree of the prior motion. Therefore, in every doubled quantity of time, the length of the descent (the path) and the speed of the motion are doubled.

### XXIV.

<margin>Weight and Motion.</margin>
Every heavy thing exerts pressure in itself according to the direction of its motion, toward the place to which it moves.

---

### XXV.

<margin>Force is proportional to speed; impact, path, and time.</margin>
It is necessary that every motion, produced by force, should follow a course that is equal to the ratio between the thing moved and that which moves it. And if it finds a resisting obstacle <note>original: "opposizione"</note>, it will complete the length of its due journey through a circular motion and through all sorts of other leaps and bounds which—when the time and the total course are taken into account—will be equal in length as if the course had taken place without opposition.

---

### XXVI.

<margin>First intuition of the Law of Conservation of Energy <note>The author is describing how momentum is preserved through bounces rather than being lost.</note>.</margin>
Every spherical body with a dense and unyielding surface, set in motion by an equal <note>original: "pari"</note> force, covers as much distance with its bounces—produced by the hard and smooth ground upon which it strikes—as if it had been thrown freely through the air.

O admirable justice of the First Author of all motion, who did not wish to deny any force the full order and quality of its necessary effects! Therefore, if a force is to drive an object it has overcome a hundred cubits <note>original: "Ellen"; a historical unit of length based on the forearm</note> away, and this object finds an obstacle in its motion, He has ordained that the force of the impact should cause new motion again, which through various leaps recovers the whole sum of its due path. And if you then measure the path made by said leaps, you will find it to be of such length as it would be if, with the same force, an identical object were drawn freely through the air.

<summary>This page outlines early physical principles regarding the relationship between force and distance, specifically arguing that the total path of a moving object remains constant whether it travels in a straight line or is diverted into bounces by an obstacle.</summary>

## XXVII. MANUSCRIPT J. FOLIO 103 v., 102 r., 101 v.

<margin>In calculating the ratio between mass and speed, one must not forget the resistances <note>Referring to air resistance or friction, which the author argues prevents infinite speed.</note>.</margin>
If some have said that the smaller the moved body becomes, the more the moving force chases it—in proportion to its reduction, into infinity, always acquiring new speed—it would follow from this that an atom would be almost as swift as the imagination or as the eye, which suddenly runs to the height of the stars. Consequently, its journey would be limitless, because a thing which can be infinitely reduced would become infinitely fast and move in an infinite course, since every continuous quantity is divisible into infinity. This is an opinion rejected by reason, and consequently also by experience.

->(Now follows the application to bombards <note>A "bombard" is an early type of large-caliber cannon used for throwing heavy stone balls.</note>.)<-

<margin>A warning against researchers who neglect critical thinking during observation.</margin>
Therefore, O researcher, do not trust those writers who have sought to make themselves interpreters between Nature and man using only their imagination, but trust only those who have exercised their minds not on the hints (<term>cenni</term> <note>original: "cenni"; meaning signs, gestures, or subtle indications</note>) of Nature, but on the effects of their own experiments. These experiments deceive those who do not know their essence; for those things which frequently appear to be one and the same are often of great diversity, as is proven here.

## XXVIII. MANUSCRIPT M. FOLIO 57 v. AND 57 r.

<margin>Only repeated experiments provide certainty.</margin>
If many bodies of equal weight and equal shape are dropped one after another at the same tempo, the increases of the intervals between them will be equal to one another.

### Demonstration

By the 5th [proposition] of the 1st [book], which states how a thing that descends acquires equal degrees of speed with every degree of motion (downward).
Therefore, for this reason, the motion of the last (ball) at the bottom becomes much faster than that of the first at the top (etc.).

The experiment for the preceding conclusion regarding motion must be conducted in this manner, namely: one takes two balls, equal in weight and shape, and lets them fall from a great height so that at the beginning of their movement they touch each other; the experimenter stands on the ground below to see if their fall has kept them in contact or not. And this experiment should be performed several times, so that no accident hinders or falsifies the trial, because otherwise the experiment would be incorrect and would deceive the researcher—or perhaps not.

### XXXIII.

<margin>Against the music of the spheres.</margin>
## On the Friction of the Heavens

Every sound is created by air striking a dense body; and if it is produced by two heavy bodies against one another, it happens by means of the air that surrounds them, and this kind of friction consumes the bodies being rubbed. Therefore, it would follow that the heavens, in their course—because they have no air between them—would produce no sound. And even if such friction were a reality, in the many centuries that these heavens have been turning, they would have been consumed by such infinite speed every day. 

And even if they did produce a sound, it could not spread; for even the sound of a collision under water is barely heard, and it would be heard little or not at all in solid bodies. Furthermore, with smooth, polished bodies, friction makes no noise; the same would happen—namely, producing no noise—at the contact or rather the friction of the heavens. And if these heavens have not been polished by the contact of their friction, it follows that they have a rough and grainy surface; therefore, their contact is not continuous, and if that is the case, a vacuum <note>original: "Vakuum"</note> is created, which it is concluded does not exist in nature. 

Thus, it is concluded that friction would have already consumed the boundaries of every heaven; and by as much faster as it moves in the middle than toward the poles, so much more would it be consumed in the middle than at the poles; and then it would no longer rub at all, and the sound would cease, and the dancers would stand still—

<summary>The author dismisses the possibility of perpetual motion and uses physical principles of friction, acoustics, and the vacuum to disprove the Pythagorean idea of the 'music of the spheres.'</summary>
<keywords>perpetual motion, music of the spheres, celestial friction, vacuum, acoustics, celestial mechanics, alchemy</keywords>

# XLV. SP., MS. V. U. FOL. 6 r. AND 6 v.
<note>original: "V. U." refers to the Codex sul volo degli uccelli (Codex on the Flight of Birds)</note>

<margin>Flying with and without wing-beats — steering and turning.</margin>
When the bird wants to turn to the right or the left side while beating its wings, it will beat the wing lower on the side toward which it wishes to turn; thus the bird will turn its movement according to the <term>impetus</term> <note>original: "impeto" — a Renaissance physical concept referring to the force or momentum an object acquires through motion</note> of that wing which moved more, and it makes the reflected movement under the wind from the opposite side. When the bird wants to rise with its wing-beat, it lifts its shoulders and beats the tips of its wings toward itself, and so causes the air to compress—the air which lies between the ends of the wings and the bird's breast—and the tension of this air lifts the bird into the sky.

The vulture and other birds that beat their wings very little always seek out the <term>course</term> <note>original: "corso" — the path or flow of the wind currents</note> of the wind; and if the wind prevails high up, then they are seen at a great height, and if it prevails low down, they remain deep below.

When the wind prevails in the air, the vulture beats the air several times in its flight in such a way that it lifts itself high and acquires <term>impetus</term>, with which impetus it then—descending a little—travels a long distance without a wing-beat; and when it has sunk, it does the same thing again, and so it continues successively. This sinking without a wing-beat justifies itself by allowing the bird to rest in the air after the effort of the aforementioned wing-beating.

All birds that fly in bursts lift themselves with their wing-beats, and when they sink, they come to rest, because they do not beat their wings while sinking.

<vocab>Bird, wing, air, compression, impetus, vulture, course, wing-beat, drive/momentum</vocab>

<header>Wind and Flight. XLVI. SP., MS. V. U. FOL. 7 r.</header>

### ->On the 4 movements of reflection and incidence<-
### ->according to the various directions of the wind,<-
### ->which the birds perform<-

The slanted downward flight (<term>discenso</term> <note>original: "discenso" — descent or downward glide</note>) of birds, when made against the wind, will always be performed under the wind, and its <term>movement of reflection</term> <note>The "reflexionsbewegung" refers to the upward bounce or ricochet-like ascent a bird makes after a descent, similar to a ball bouncing off a surface</note> will be performed on top of the wind. But if such a <term>movement of incidence</term> <note>The "Einfallsbewegung" is the initial downward strike or entry into a current of air</note> is made toward the <term>Levante</term> <note>The East, where the sun rises</note> while a <term>Tramontana</term> (North-northeast wind) is blowing, the wing on the Tramontana side will be under the wind, and it will do the same during the movement of reflection; therefore, at the end of said reflection, the bird will find itself with its head facing toward the northeast. And if the bird goes downward after midday, with a north wind prevailing, it will make such a descent on the wind and its movement of reflection under the wind; but here a long dispute arises, which will be spoken of in its proper place, because here it seems to happen that a movement of reflection cannot be made.

When the bird makes its movement of reflection against the upper wind, it will then rise much higher than its natural impetus allows, since the favor of the wind is added to it, which, by getting under the bird, performs the office of a wedge. But when the bird is at the end of its ascent, it will have exhausted its impetus and only the favor of the wind will remain, which would overturn and turn it around because it strikes against the breast, were it not that the bird lowered the right or the left wing, which will make it fly to the right or to the left and come down in a half-circle.

XLVIII.
The movement of the bird should always be above the clouds, so that the wing does not become soaked, and to discover more land, and to escape the danger of the wind's revolutions within mountain gorges, where there are always gatherings and eddies of winds. XLIX.
The aforementioned bird <note>Leonardo frequently refers to his flying machine as an "artificial bird."</note> must rise to a great height with the help of the wind, and let this be its safety; for even in the event that all the previously mentioned rotations should befall it, it has time to return to a state of equilibrium, provided its limbs are of great resistive strength so that they can withstand the <term>furor</term> <note>original: "Furor" — the rage or violent force of the elements</note> and violence through the mentioned means of defense and through their joints (<term>giunture</term> <note>original: "giunture" — the mechanical hinges or articulations of the machine</note>) made of strong tanned leather and their "nerves" <note>In this context, "nerves" refers to the tension-bearing cables or cords of the machine.</note> made of the strongest raw silk ropes. And let no one drive themselves mad with ironwork, because it would soon break in its twists or wear itself out, for which reason one must not concern oneself with it.

The great bird will take its first flight from the back of its giant Swan <note>Mount Ceceri, or "Swan Mountain," near Fiesole, where Leonardo tested his flight theories.</note>, filling the universe with amazement, all writings with its fame, and bringing eternal glory to the nest where it was born.

<margin>On Water.</margin>
**LII. MS. C. FOL. 26 v.**

### What sort of thing water is

Water is the second of the four elements, less heavy and of a secondary mobility. This element never has rest until it unites with its maritime element <note>The sea or ocean</note>, where, unmolested by the winds, it reaches equilibrium and rests with its surface everywhere equidistant from the center of the world. This water is the increase and the life-blood <note>original: "Saft" — sap or vital fluid</note> of all living bodies; nothing retains its former shape without it; it binds and enlarges bodies during growth. No thing that is lighter can penetrate it without force; it readily rises by virtue of heat as fine vapor into the air; cold makes it freeze, and immobility spoils it (that is: heat moves it, cold freezes it, and rest corrupts it). It takes on every odor, color, and taste; of itself it has none; it penetrates all porous bodies. Against its fury no human defense is of use, and if it were, it would not be forever. In its swift course, it makes itself the sustainer of things which are heavier than it.

<summary>Leonardo describes the pilot's need for physical mobility to maintain balance in flight and offers a poetic prophecy of his machine's success before pivoting to a scientific treatise on the properties and power of water.</summary>

The primacy <note>original: "Das Prinzipat" — the dominant force or main characteristic</note> of its course lies sometimes at the surface, sometimes in the middle, and at times on the bottom. One mass rises over the transverse course of another, and were this not so, the surfaces of flowing waters would remain without spherical ripples <note>original: "Kugelungen" / Italian: "globosità" — Leonardo's term for the rounded, globular shapes formed by water movement</note>. Its parts do not press at all upon the parts subjected to them. No river will ever maintain its course even at any single place between its embankments; its upper portions do not weigh upon the lower ones.

## LVI.

Let the earth move in whatever direction it wishes, the surface of the water will never depart from its spherical form <note>original: "spera" — referring to the geometric perfection of a sphere</note>, but will always remain equidistant from the center of the world <note>original: "Mittelpunkt der Welt" — in the Aristotelian sense, the center of the Earth is the center of the universe</note>.

## LVII.

No part of the watery element will rise or move further away from the common center, unless by force. — No force has permanence.

<header>MS. CA. FOL. 75 v.</header>

<margin>The double sphericity of water and magnetism.</margin>
## LVIII.

Why, when two spherical liquids of unequal quantity come to the point of contact, the larger will draw the smaller to itself and immediately incorporate it, without destroying the perfection of its spherical shape?

This is a difficult answer; but for that reason, I shall not hesitate to state my own opinion. Water, clothed by the air, desires by nature to remain united within its own sphere, because in such a position it relieves itself of its own weight. This weight is double: namely, that its whole has weight in relation to the center of all elements; the second weight relates to the center of that same spherical shape of the water <note>Leonardo is distinguishing between global gravity (the Earth's center) and a form of surface tension or local attraction within the drop itself</note>; were this not so, it would form only a half-sphere, which would be the part rising upward from its (own) center. But I do not see in the human mind the possibility of providing knowledge (or an explanation) for this, except perhaps to say, as one says of the magnet, that it attracts iron: namely, that such a virtue is an occult property <note>original: "okkulte Eigenschaft" — a hidden or mysterious quality not yet explained by the laws of mechanics</note>, of which there are countless in nature.

<summary>Leonardo explores the spherical nature of water, arguing that it maintains its shape relative to the Earth's center and possesses an "occult" internal attraction similar to magnetism. He distinguishes between the weight of water in relation to the planet and the internal forces that allow droplets to merge and maintain symmetry.</summary>

# LX.

## On the Heat in the World

Where there is life, there is heat, and where there is vital heat, there is movement of the humors <note>original: "Säfte" — referring to the bodily fluids or "humors" believed to govern health and life in Renaissance physiology</note>. This proves itself by observing the effects: that the heat within the element of fire always draws moisture to itself—vapors and dense mists and frequent clouds, which it takes from the seas and other pools and rivers and wet valleys. By drawing these gradually up into the cold region, that first part comes to a halt because the warm and moist do not harmonize with the cold and dry <note>Leonardo is applying the Aristotelian theory of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. Where the first part stopped, the other parts join it, and thus, adding part to part, thick and dark clouds arise. These are often moved and carried by winds from one region to another, where through their density they constitute such great weight that they fall down as heavy rain. And when the heat of the sun unites with the power of the element of fire, the clouds are drawn even higher and encounter even greater cold, in which they freeze, and stormy hail-weather arises. Now, that same heat which holds such a great weight of water, as one sees raining from the clouds, also tears it from below out of the depths of the mountains and carries it and holds it within the summits of the mountain range, where the waters, finding any sort of crevices, run away and, emerging, cause rivers.

### LXX.

->On the Strike<-

<margin>The sympathetic resonance of identical and related tones.</margin>
The strike given to one bell is answered by and slightly moves another bell identical to it; and the plucked string of a lute finds an answer and slightly moves another identical string of the same pitch on another lute. You shall see this if you place a piece of straw upon the string that is identical to the one being played.

### LXXI.

<margin>The power of sound.</margin>
Whether many small voices joined together make a noise as great as one large one? — I say no; for if you took ten thousand voices of flies united, they will not be heard from as far away as the voice of a man. This voice of a man, if divided into ten thousand parts, would not in any of those parts be equal to the magnitude of the voice of a fly.

### LXXII.

<margin>The propagation of sound in liquid and solid bodies.</margin>
If you stop your ship and place the head of a speaking tube <note>original: "Sprachrohr"; likely referring to a primitive hydrophone or acoustic tube.</note> into the water and the other end to your ear, you will hear ships that are quite far away from you.

And you shall do the same if you place the said head of the tube upon the earth; you will hear whoever passes by at a great distance.

### LXXIII.

<margin>Sound and light spread in waves.</margin>
Just as a stone thrown into the water makes itself the center and causes various circles, so the sound produced in the air spreads in circles; likewise, every body placed within the luminous atmosphere

### LXXIV.

The voice that strikes an object will return to the ear on a line of the same inclination as the line of incidence was—namely, the line which carries the voice from its origin to the place where this voice is able to reform itself (where it is caught). ### LXXVIII. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; CODEX ATLANTICUS FOL. 121 r.

<margin>A similar thought.</margin>
The movement of the lightning born within the cloud is curved, because it bends from the dense into the thin, which density is created by the fury of its aforementioned movement. This same lightning, because it cannot expand with the straightness it began with, swerves toward the swiftest passage of the path, which it then continues until it has generated the next closest obstacle for itself; and in such a manner, according to this rule, it continues until its end. <note>Leonardo is attempting to explain the jagged, non-linear path of lightning as a result of the bolt meeting resistance in the air, forcing it to seek the path of least resistance.</note>

<margin>On the propagation of light.</margin>
### LXXIX. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; MANUSCRIPT A. FOL. 2 v.

Every body fills the surrounding air with its image, which image is complete in the whole and complete in the part.

The air is full of countless straight and luminous lines, which intersect and interweave with one another without mutual displacement: they present to everything that stands opposite them (the object, <term>obbietto</term> <note>original: "obbietto"; Leonardo uses this to mean the physical thing being perceived or the target of the light rays.</note>) the true form of their cause.

<margin>The same.</margin>
### LXXX. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; MANUSCRIPT ASHBURNHAM I, FOL. 6 v.

The body of the air is full of countless pyramids, composed of luminous and straight lines, which are caused by the superficial ends (boundaries) of the shaded bodies, thus placed in said air; and the further they move from their cause, the more pointed they become. Although their course is intersected and interwoven with others, they do not become confused with one another, and with diverging courses they go, spreading through all the surrounding air which they fill. They are of equal power among themselves, and all are as one and one as all; and through them the image of the body is carried, and carried as a whole everywhere and entirely in every part; and every pyramid for itself receives in every smallest of its parts the whole form of its cause. <note>This is a foundational concept in Leonardo's optics: the idea that light travels in "pyramids" or cones, allowing the eye to reconstruct a complete image from any vantage point because the information of the "whole" is present in every "part" of the air.</note>

# III. SUN/MOON AND EARTH

->Praise of the Sun<-

<margin>The Sun.</margin>
**W**hen you look at the stars without their rays—as one does when looking through a small hole made with the extreme tip of a fine needle and placed so that it almost touches the eye—you will find those same stars to be so tiny that nothing seems smaller: and truly, the vast distance lends them a rational diminution, although there are many that are many times larger than that star which is the Earth with its water. Now consider what this star of ours must seem at such a distance, and then reflect how many stars could be placed, in both length and breadth, between those same stars which are sown in the dark space.

## IV.

Measure how many Suns could be placed within its 24-hour path.
Make a circle and face it toward the south, as sundials are made; fix a rod in the center in such a way that its length moves around the center of said circle; mark the shadow that the Sun casts from this rod onto the circumference of this circle, and let that shadow be, shall we say, the width of *a n*. Now measure how many times such a shadow fits into the circumference of the circle, and that will be the number of times the body of the Sun fits into its 24-hour path. And there one will be able to see whether Epicurus spoke correctly when he said that the Sun is as large as it appears—for if the diameter of the Sun appears to be the measure of one foot, and that same Sun fits a thousand times into its 24-hour path, it would have traveled a thousand feet, that is, 500 cubits <term>Ellen: a traditional unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm</term>, which is one-sixth of a mile. Thus, it would follow that the Sun's journey through day and night would have covered only a sixth of a mile, and that this venerable snail of a Sun would have traveled 25 (20¹⁰/₁₂) cubits per hour.

<margin>Further proofs that the sun is warm.</margin>
### VII.

It is proven that the sun is warm by its nature, and not cold, as has already been said.

<margin>Heat rays reflected by concave mirrors.</margin>
The concave mirror <note>A curved mirror used to focus light</note>, which is cold—when it receives the rays of the fire, it throws them back hotter than the fire itself.

The glass sphere, filled with cold water, sends out from itself the rays that are taken from the fire, even much hotter than this fire.

<margin>Heat rays passing through a sphere with cold water.</margin>
From these two aforementioned experiments, it follows that the same heat of the rays that came from the mirror or from the sphere with cold water is warm by its own power and virtue <note>term: virtue <note>original: "Tugend" / "virtù" - referring to an inherent power or natural property</note></note>, and not because the same mirror or sphere was warm; and the same in this case happens to the sun, which passes through these bodies, which it warms by its own power. And therefore it has been concluded that the sun is not hot, while one proves through these same indicated experiments that the sun is extraordinarily hot—through the aforementioned experiment of the mirror and the sphere, which, being cold in themselves, seizing the rays of the heat of the fire, return them as warm rays because their first cause is warm. And the same happens with the sun, which, being warm itself, passing through cold mirrors, reflects great heat.

...of that luminous body, we perceive as much as it sees of us. And its night receives as much radiance as our waters lend to it, by reflecting back to it the image of the sun, which is mirrored in all those waters that see both the sun and the moon. The skin, or rather the surface of the water that composes the sea of the moon and the sea of our earth, is always wrinkled, a little or a lot, or more or less; and these wrinkles are the reason for expanding the countless phantom images <note>original: "Scheinbilder" - referring to the specular reflections or "glitter" of the sun on a moving surface</note> of the sun, which are mirrored on the hills and eminences and sides and fronts of the innumerable wrinkles. That is to say, they appear in as many different places on each wrinkle as there are different positions occupied by the eyes that see them. This could not happen if the sphere of water, which for the most part clothes the moon, were of a uniform roundness; for then the phantom image of the sun would be a single one for every eye, and its reflection would be individually isolated and would always be a spherical radiance, as is clearly shown to us by the gilded balls placed on the tips of high buildings. But if those same golden balls were wrinkled and bumpy, like mulberries—black fruits composed of tiny round globules—then every part of that sphericity, seen by the sun and the eye, would show to that same eye the radiance produced by the phantom image of the sun. Thus, one would see in one and the same body many tiny suns, which often, due to great distance, unite and appear fused together...

## XV.

### Concerning the Moon

<margin>How Leonardo explains to himself that the moon maintains its equilibrium.</margin>
No dense thing is lighter than the air.
After we have proven that that part of the moon which shines is water, which mirrors the body of the sun and reflects the radiance received from it; and that if said water were without waves, it would have to appear small, but in radiance almost equal to the sun; — so now it must be proven whether said moon is a heavy body or a light one. For, were it heavy—even granted that from the earth upwards, with every degree of height, one acquires degrees of lightness, which is why water is lighter than earth, and air than water, and fire than air, and so on in sequence — it would seem that the moon, if it possessed density, as indeed it does, would also have weight. And if it has weight, the space in which it finds itself could not support it, and therefore it would have to sink toward the center of the universe <note>In the Aristotelian/Ptolemaic worldview, the center of the Earth was considered the center of the universe, toward which all heavy things naturally fall.</note> and unite with the earth. And even if the moon itself did not fall, at least its waters would have to fall and strip it bare, falling toward the center and leaving the moon deprived of them and without radiance. Therefore, since that which reason promises us does not happen, it is a manifest sign that the moon is clothed by its own elements, that is, by water, air, and fire, and thus <insert>it sustains itself in that space as our earth does with its elements in this part of the air.</insert>

<summary>Leonardo argues that the moon must be a solid body surrounded by its own elements (water, air, and fire) to explain why it remains suspended in space and retains its reflective oceans without falling to Earth.</summary>
<keywords>moon, gravity, equilibrium, elements, reflection, density, celestial mechanics, water</keywords>

--- Page 237 ---
<meta>Continuing from page 56, where Leonardo argued that the moon must have density and weight, questioning how such a heavy body remains suspended in space without falling toward the center of the universe.</meta>

<page-num>57</page-num>

...is contained within itself by itself in that space, maintaining itself just as this our Earth with its elements does in this other space; and that the heavy things within its elements perform the same service as the other heavy things do within our elements.

<margin>Explanation of the ashen light <note>original: "lumen cinereum." This refers to "Earthshine," where the dark part of the moon is faintly visible due to light reflected from Earth.</note>.</margin>
When the eye in the east beholds the moon in the west near the sunken sun, it sees the shadowed part surrounded by a luminous portion. Of this light, the side and upper parts originate from the sun, while the lower part originates from the ocean, which likewise receives the sun's rays and reflects them back upon the lower seas of the moon. This gives as much radiance over the entire shaded part of the moon as the moon gives to the Earth at midnight. Therefore, that part does not remain entirely dark; because of this, some have believed that the moon has a light of its own in addition to what the sun gives it. However, for the reason stated above, this light originates from our seas which the sun illuminates...

**XVI.**                                    R. 906, MS. BR. M. FOL. 19 r.

<margin>The spots of the moon.</margin>
If you keep the details of the spots of the moon under observation, you will often find a great difference in them; I have made tests of this myself by drawing them. This comes from clouds that rise from the waters of that moon, which place themselves between the sun and those same waters. With their shadow, they rob those waters of the sun's rays, whereby that water happens to remain dark because it cannot mirror the body of the sun.

### XXII. MS. F. FOL. 41 v.

<margin>The Earth is not the center of the universe; it is not in the middle of the solar circle.</margin>
Just as the Earth is not in the middle of the solar circle <note>The orbit of the sun</note>, nor in the center of the universe, but is indeed in the center of its elements, which are its companions and connected with it; and anyone standing on the moon—insofar as the moon, together with the sun, is beneath us—would see this Earth of ours with the element of water appearing and performing the same service for them that the moon does for us.

## XXVIII. MS. A. FOL. 55 v. AND MS. CA. FOL. 80 r.

### Beginning of the Treatise on Water

<margin>The Earth is like an organic living being.</margin>
Man is called by the ancients a world in miniature <note>original: "Welt im kleinen" - the concept of the Microcosm</note>, and surely the application of this name is rightly placed; for just as man is composed of earth, water, air, and fire, the body of the Earth is the same. If man has bones within him, the supports and framework of the flesh—the world has its stones, the supports of the earth; if man has within him the lake of the blood, where the lungs expand and contract in breathing, the body of the Earth has its oceanic sea, which also expands and contracts every 6 hours with the breathing of the world; if from the said lake of blood veins arise which, branching out, go through the human body, likewise the oceanic sea fills the body of the Earth with countless veins of water. The body of the Earth lacks nerves (tendons), which are not there because nerves are made for the purpose of movement; and since the world is in constant equilibrium, movement does not occur there, and since no movement is present, nerves are not necessary here. But in all other things, there are many similarities.

### XXX.

<margin>Living things arise only from the living; therefore the Earth must be a kind of animal-like being.</margin>
No thing of any kind arises in a place where sensitive, vegetative, and rational life is not present: feathers emerge upon birds and change every year; hair grows upon animals and changes every year except in some parts, such as the hair of the beard in lions, cats, and the like; herbs arise in the meadows and leaves upon the trees, renewing themselves every year in great numbers; <margin>Vegetative soul, bodily soul, as the Platonic Academy in Florence assumed—the "life force" of later times.</margin> thus we can say that the Earth has a vegetative soul, and that its flesh is the soil; its bones are the arrangements of the connections of rock from which mountains are composed; its cartilage is the tuff <note>A type of rock made of volcanic ash</note>; its blood is the veins of water; the lake of blood that lies around the heart is the oceanic sea; its breathing and the increase and decrease of blood through the pulses is, in the case of the Earth, the ebb and flow of the sea; and the warmth of the soul of the world is the fire that dwells within the Earth, and the dwelling-place of the vegetative soul are the fires which breathe out from various places of the Earth into baths, sulfur mines, and volcanoes—into Mongibello <note>The local Sicilian name for Mount Etna</note> in Sicily and enough other places.

## XXXII.

<margin>Water is the blood of the Earth.</margin>
The water that wells up in the mountains is the blood which keeps that same mountain range alive. And if it is bored into, or if a vein is cut across—Nature, the helper of her living beings, abundant in increase to overcome the loss of the spilled juices, overflows there in a wonderful influx. This is similar to when a person has been struck in some place, and one sees the blood increase there under the skin in the form of a swelling to assist the injured part; likewise, because the life at the high peak has been cut off, Nature sends her juices from the deepest roots to the highest height of the severed place. And when these are spilled, she never leaves it lacking in the sap of life until the end of its existence.

# XXXIII.
## On the Confirmation of Why Water is Found on the Summits of Mountains

<margin>Heat as the motor of the water cycle.</margin>
I say that, just as natural heat holds the blood in the veins high up within a human being, and when the human is dead, this blood—having become cold—retreats to the lower parts; and just as when the sun warms a person's head, the blood increases and overcomes them with fluid so that it overwhelms the veins and produces a headache; — so, in the same way, the veins branch through the body of the Earth. Through the natural heat which is spread throughout the entire body of the Earth, the water is lifted through the veins up to the high peaks of the mountains. And this water, which flows through the body of this mountain like a dead thing through a masonry pipe, would not emerge from its original lowliness if it were not warmed by the vital heat of the primary vein. Furthermore, the heat of the element of fire <note>In the Aristotelian system, the "sphere of fire" sat above the air; Leonardo here links geothermal and elemental heat</note> and, by day, the heat of the sun, has the power to draw it upward.

# XXXIV.

<margin>The water cycle in the body of the Earth resembles the circulation of blood.</margin>
It is indeed water that is destined to be the vital juice <note>original: "Lebenssaft" - referring to the "protoplasm" or essential fluid of life</note> of this dry Earth, and that force which moves it through the branched veins, against the natural course of heavy things <note>Leonardo is grappling with why water defies gravity to reach mountain tops</note>, is the very same that moves the juices in all species of animal bodies. Thus the water, to the greatest wonder of its observers, rises from the deepest depths of the sea to the highest peaks of the mountains, and pouring out through the burst veins, it returns to the low sea. And anew, with speed, it ascends and returns to the aforementioned descent, thus turning from the innermost parts to the outer, and from the lowest back to the upper, when it in the natur— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "natürlichen" (natural)</note>

### XLIII.
<margin>Why seawater is salty.</margin>
### Why the water is salty

Pliny says in his 2nd book, chapter 103, that the water of the sea is salty because the heat of the sun browns and parches the moisture and sucks it up, and this gives the sea, which spreads out so widely, the taste of salt; but this is not conceded; for if the saltiness of the sea had its cause in the heat of the sun, there is no doubt that the lakes, ponds, and marshes would be so much more salty, as their waters are less mobile and of shallower depth: and experience shows us the opposite; such marshes show us their waters entirely deprived of saltiness. Pliny also cites in the same chapter that such saltiness could arise because, being deprived of every sweet and subtle part which the heat easily draws to itself, only the more bitter and coarse part remains, and therefore the water that is on the surface is sweeter than at the bottom. This is contradicted with the same reasons stated above, namely, that the same would happen to marshes and other waters which were dried up by the heat. It has also been said that the saltiness of the sea is the sweat of the earth: to this one answers that all the veins of water <note>term: "Wasseradern" (water veins) refers to the Renaissance belief in subterranean channels that functioned like blood vessels in the human body.</note> which penetrate the ground would have to be salty. But one concludes well that the saltiness of the sea is born from the many veins of water which, in
<margin>Dissolved salt mines.</margin>
penetrating the earth, encounter salt mines and partially [dissolve] those.

<summary>Leonardo critiques Pliny the Elder's theories on the salinity of the sea, arguing instead that salt is dissolved from underground mines by subterranean water veins. He also notes the physics of wave velocity during impact and ascent.</summary>

### XLVII. R. 1085, MS. LEIC. FOL. 10 v.

The Mediterranean basin, as an inland sea, receives the principal waters of Africa, Asia, and Europe that are turned toward it; its waters (once) reached the shore of the mountains that surrounded it and formed a coast for it, and the peaks of the Apennines stood in that same sea in the form of islands, surrounded by salt water. Likewise, Africa, inland by its Atlas Mountains, did not show the soil of its great plains—about 3000 miles in length—exposed to the sky; and Memphis <note>The ancient capital of Egypt</note> lay on the coast of such a sea, and on the plains of Italy, where today birds fly in flocks, fish used to wander in great schools.

<header>XLVIII. R. 984, MS. LEIC. FOL. 31 r. / XLIX. MS. E. FOL. 4 v.</header>

<margin>It is not documents, but things themselves that tell the history of the earth.</margin>
Since things are much older than the sciences, it is no wonder if in our day no writing exists to record that the aforementioned seas had covered so many lands; and even if any such writing had appeared, wars, conflagrations, floods, and changes in languages and laws have consumed all antiquities. But for us, the testimony of things is sufficient—things which, born in salt water, are found on high mountains far removed from the seas of that time.

---

<margin>The fossils bear witness.</margin>
->Concerning the sea, which changes the weight of the earth<-

The shells, oysters, and other similar creatures which are born in the sea-slime bear witness to us of the change of the earth around the center of our elements. This is proven thus: the principal rivers always run turbid because of the earth which they lift away from the bottom and the banks by the friction of their waters. This erosion <note>original: "Verzehrung," literally consumption or eating away</note> exposes the face of the strata <note>original: "Stufen," steps or layers</note> which were formed in layers from those shells living on the surface of the sea-slime, and which were born in those places when the salt water still covered them. And these same strata were covered from time to time by mud of varying density, such as is carried into the sea by rivers during floods <term>diluviums: great floods or inundations of water</term> of various sizes. Thus, these shells remained walled in and killed beneath such mud, piled one above the other at such a height that this seabed became exposed to the air. Now, these same grounds are of such a height that they have become hills or high mountains, and the rivers, the consumers of the sides of these same mountains, lay bare the strata of these shells; and so the lightened side of the earth rises.

<note>Leonardo is arguing against the Great Flood of the Bible as the sole cause of fossils, suggesting instead a slow, cyclical geological process of sedimentation and tectonic uplift.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains that fossils found in mountains are physical proof that those peaks were once seabeds, arguing that geological history is recorded in the earth itself rather than in lost human documents.</summary>

## Concerning the Shells in the Mountains

And if you were to say that the shells in the mountains were produced by nature through the constellations of the stars, in what way, would you show, does such a constellation produce shells of different sizes and different ages and different <term>species</term> <note>original: "Gattung"</note> in the same area?

weight of such mud, they necessarily had to die, because they lacked the animals <note>referring to the microorganisms or smaller prey</note> upon which they were accustomed to feed. As the sea sank over time and the salt water flowed away, that mud began to turn into stone, and the shells of those same mollusks—whose living animals had already vanished—were now filled anew with mud instead of flesh. And so, during the transformation of all the surrounding mud into stone, that mud which had remained inside the slightly opened shells and was connected to the rest of the mud through that opening, also began to turn into stone. Thus, all the casings of such shells remained between two stones: that is, between the stone that enclosed them and the stone which they enclosed. This is how they are still found in many places. And almost all the <term>petrified</term> <note>original: "versteinerten"; turned to stone</note> shells in the blocks of the mountains still have their natural coating around them, especially those that were old enough to preserve themselves through their hardness; while the young ones, already largely calcified, had been permeated by a viscous and <term>petrifying</term> <note>original: "petrifizierenden"; stone-making</note> juice.

## LVIII.

### Refutation directed against those who claim that shells were carried many days' journey from the seas by the Deluge, so high that it surpassed all heights.

<margin>Refutation of those who consider the Deluge to be the reason for the occurrence of petrified <term>fossils</term> <note>original: "versteinerter Muscheln"; literally "petrified shells"</note> in the mountains.</margin>

I say that the Deluge could not have carried things born in the sea onto the mountains, unless the sea, swelling, created floods up to the aforementioned places; which swellings could not occur because a vacuum would result. And if you said the air fills in there—we have concluded that the heavy cannot sustain itself upon the light, from which by necessity one further concludes that this flood was caused by rainwater. And if this is so, these same waters all run toward the sea and the sea does not run toward the mountains; and as they run toward the sea, they push the shells away from the shore.

<margin>And the corals in the middle of Lombardy?</margin>
And if you wish to say that such a Deluge was the one which carried such shells hundreds of miles from the seas—this cannot be, since the same Deluge was created by rainstorms; because, naturally, rainstorms drive the rivers toward the sea along with the things carried by them, and do not pull dead objects from the seashore up toward the mountains. And if you said that the Deluge then rose with its waters above the mountains, the movement of the sea was so sluggish in its progress against the flow of the rivers that it could not have kept floating those things which were heavier than itself; and even if it had kept them afloat, in rising it would have left them scattered in various places. <margin>And the stationary species of shells?</margin>
We know that they do not move, but always remain attached to the rock with one of their shells, opening the other shell to feed on tiny creatures that swim through the water; these creatures, believing they have found good grazing for themselves, become the food of the aforementioned shells. ### LXII. **MS. CA. FOL. 155 r.**

<margin>Was the Deluge in the time of Noah actually universal?</margin>
A doubt arises here, and it is this: whether the Deluge that occurred in the time of Noah was universal or not; and here it will appear not, for the reasons that will be cited. We have it in the Bible that the aforementioned flood consisted of forty days and forty nights of continuous and universal rain, and that such rain rose six cubits <note>a measurement of about 18-22 inches</note> above the highest mountain in the world. And if it were the case that the rain was universal, it would have clothed our earth in a spherical shape with its waters; and a spherical surface has every one of its parts equidistant from the center of its sphere. Therefore, if the sphere of water existed in the manner of the described circumstance, it is impossible for the water upon it to move, because water does not move within itself unless it descends; therefore, the water of such a flood—how did it go away, if it is proven here that it had no movement? And if it did go away, how did it move, if it

LXV.

<margin>The earth will become waterless and parched and end in fire!</margin>
The element of water remained enclosed within the up-grown banks of the rivers, and one sees the sea between the risen earth and the surrounding air, which has to wrap and bound the increased (enlarged) machine of the earth. --- Its density, which stood between the water and the element of fire, will then likely have greatly diminished and remain deprived of the necessary water; the rivers will be without their waters, the fertile earth will no longer send forth light foliage, the fields will no longer be adorned by overhanging trees; all animals, finding no more fresh herbs to graze upon, will die, and food will be lacking for the predatory lions and wolves and other animals that live by prey; and for men, after many expedients, it will be necessary to leave their lives, and the human race will not be there. In this way, the productive and fruit-rich earth will become deserted, parched, and barren; and through the enclosed moisture of the water, which is locked in its belly, and through living nature, it will remain for a little while longer in its growth, until the cold and thin air
<margin>Leonardo wrote this, according to the character of the handwriting, before his first Milanese period.</margin>
has entirely passed away and it is forced to end with the element of fire: then its surface will become burnt ashes, and this would be the end of earthly nature.

<margin>Anatomy—a profitless science.</margin>
**I** shall perform wonders;—may I have less than other, calmer men, and those who wish to enrich themselves in a single day; may I live for a long time in great poverty, as happens and will eternally happen to the alchemists, who seek to create gold and silver, and to the engineers, who wish for dead water to give itself moving life through perpetual motion, and to those chief fools, the necromancers and sorcerers.

<margin>Regarding his figurative anatomy.</margin>
And if you say that it is better to perform anatomy yourself than to look at such drawings, you would speak correctly, if it were possible to perceive all these things, which are shown in such drawings, in a single figure; in which <insert>the actual body</insert> you will see nothing with all your understanding and will have no idea of anything except for a few veins. To obtain a true and full conception of these, I have dissected more than ten human bodies, destroying all other members and consuming with the tiniest particles all the flesh that was found around these veins, without making them bloody, except perhaps for the imperceptible bleeding of the <term>capillaries</term> <note>Leonardo uses the term 'capillaries' to describe the hair-like, finest vessels of the circulatory system</note>; and one body did not suffice for so long a time, so that it was necessary to proceed in sequence with so many bodies, in order to complete the full knowledge; which I repeated twice to see the differences.

And if you had the love for such a thing, you would perhaps be prevented by the stomach, and if <note>The text breaks off here, likely leading into a description of the physical horrors of dissection, such as the stench and the fear of spending the night with flayed corpses</note>

### II. SP., MS. W. AN. A. FOL. 14 v.

<margin>Description and drawing must complement each other in anatomy.</margin>
And you, who wish to demonstrate the figure of man in all aspects of his structure with words alone, cast such an opinion far from you; for the more minutely you describe, the more you will confuse the mind of the reader and the more you will lead him away from the knowledge of the things described; therefore, it is necessary both to draw and to describe.

### VII. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; SP., MS. W. AN. A. FOL. 18 r.

<margin>Plans for the anatomical plates.</margin>
You will first draw the <term>bones</term> <note>German: Knochen</note> separately, and lifted slightly out of the <term>joint</term> <note>German: Gelenk</note>, so that one may better distinguish the shape of each <term>piece of bone</term> for itself. Then you will join them together in such a way that they do not deviate at all from the first demonstration, except for the parts that are hidden by their contact. When that is done, you will make the third demonstration with those <term>muscles</term> <note>German: Muskeln</note> which bind the <term>bones</term> together. After this, you will make the fourth, of the <term>nerves</term> <note>German: Nerven</note>, which are the carriers of sensation. Afterward follows the fifth, of the <term>nerves</term> that move or rather give reason (<term>senso</term>) <note>original: "senso"; Leonardo often uses this to mean the sensory-motor connection or "feeling" that directs movement.</note> to the first segments of the fingers (toes). And in the sixth, you will make the upper <term>muscles</term> of the foot, in which the sensory nerves are distributed. And let the seventh be that of the <term>veins</term> <note>German: Venen</note>, which nourish those same <term>muscles</term> of the foot. The eighth shall be that of the <term>nerves</term> that move the tips of the toes. The ninth of the <term>veins</term> and <term>arteries</term> <note>German: Arterien</note> that lie between the skin and the flesh. The tenth and last must be the finished foot with all sensations (<term>sentimenti</term>) <note>original: "sentimenti"; referring here to the full functional and sensory apparatus of the limb.</note>. You could make an eleventh, in the manner of a transparent foot, in which one would be able to see all the things mentioned above.

### XI. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; SP., MS. W. AN. A. FOL. 14 v.

<margin>How the layered arrangement of the muscles can be represented through drawing.</margin>
Perform a demonstration with lean and thin <term>muscles</term> <note>Leonardo suggests using a "wasted" or thin subject so the underlying structures are not obscured by fat</note>, so that the space created between one and the other forms a window to show what is located beneath them.

### XII. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; SP., MS. W. AN. FOL. 18.

<margin>How the muscles are to be drawn and named.</margin>

->Note<-

You will create utter confusion with your demonstrations of <term>muscles</term> and their positions, origins, and ends, if you do not first provide a representation of the <term>muscles</term> as thin as the threads of twine; in this way, you will be able to draw one (<term>muscle</term>) over the other as nature has placed them. Then you will be able to name them according to the limb they serve—that is, the mover of the tip of the <term>middle finger</term> and its <term>middle bone</term> <note>the medial phalanx</note>, or of the <term>thumb</term>, and so on. And assuming you have such knowledge, you will draw alongside this the true form, quantity (size), and position of each <term>muscle</term>. But remember to represent the threads, which teach the <term>muscles</term>, in the same position as the central lines of each <term>muscle</term>; thus, such threads will demonstrate the shape of the leg and its (<term>muscle</term>) distances, detached and clear.

### XIII. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; SP., MS. W. AN. B. FOL. 10 r.

<margin>How an arm is to be represented in correct outline with the <term>bones</term>, <term>musculature</term>, <term>nerves</term>, and <term>veins</term> drawn in.</margin>
Draw the arm of Francesco, the miniature painter, which shows many <term>veins</term>.

In this type of demonstration, you will draw the true outlines of the limbs with a single line, and in their center place their <term>bones</term> at the correct distances from their skin—namely, the skin of the arms. Then you will add the <term>veins</term>, which should be situated entirely within a transparent field; in this way, one will provide clear knowledge of the position of the <term>bones</term>, <term>veins</term>, and <term>tendons</term> (<term>nervi</term>) <note>original: "nervi"; in Leonardo's time, this term was used for both nerves and tendons</note>.

<summary>Leonardo describes his innovative "transparent" method of anatomical drawing, using thread-like lines to represent muscles and layering them to show depth without losing clarity. He also notes the importance of using a lean model, specifically mentioning a painter named Francesco, to better observe vascular and muscular structures.</summary>

Wonderful instrument, invented by the Supreme Craftsman.
The heart, cut through in the "vessel of the spirits," namely in the artery; and at **M** it seizes—or rather, it gives—the blood to the artery, and at the mouth **B** it refreshes itself with the wind of the lungs, and from **C** it fills **S**, the <term>atria</term> <note>the upper chambers</note> of the heart. **N**, a hard muscle, contracts and is the primary cause of the movement of the heart; in contracting it thickens, and in thickening it shortens, drawing back all the smaller and larger muscles, closing the gate **M**, and reducing the space situated between the base and the apex of the heart, by which means it is able to empty itself and draw fresh air into itself. <note>Leonardo’s mechanical view of the heart often compared its action to a bellows or pump, though he still adhered to the contemporary belief that the lungs provided "air" or "coolness" directly to the heart.</note>

<margin>*Blood heat and heart movement.*</margin>
**XVIII.** ->SP., MS. W. AN. B. FOL. 12 r.<-

### **On the Cause of the Heat of the Blood**

The heat is generated by the movement of the heart, and this reveals itself in that the more rapidly the heart moves, the more the heat multiplies, as the pulse of those with fever, moved by the beating of the heart, teaches us.

<margin>The liver in old people.</margin>
The liver loses the moisture of the blood that was carried to it, whereby this same liver dries out and becomes like frozen bran, both in color and in substance; so much so that with very little friction applied to it, this same substance falls apart into tiny particles, like sawdust, leaving behind the veins and arteries. And the vessels of the gall and the navel, which enter into the liver through the <term>portal vein</term> <note>original: "Pforte der Leber"</note>, remain entirely stripped of the substance of this liver, looking like broomcorn or sorghum when the grains have been removed.

<margin>Aneurysms and phleboliths.</margin>
The large intestine <note>the colon</note> and the other entrails narrow significantly in old people, and in their veins that pass under the breastbone, I have found stones as large as chestnuts, with the shape and color of truffles—or better yet, like lava or iron slag. These stones were extremely hard, like said slag, and had formed sacs attached to the aforementioned veins, like goiters.

<margin>Old age and frailty.</margin>
And such an old man, a few hours before his death, told me that he was over 100 years old and that he felt no deficiency <insert>failing</insert> <note>original: "mancamento"</note> in his person, except perhaps for a lack of strength. And so, sitting on a bed in the Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence, without any other movement or sign of any accident, he passed away from this life.

<margin>Leonardo dissects a marasmic old man and a two-year-old boy.</margin>

I describe this anatomy very diligently and with great ease, because it was devoid of the fat and moisture that so greatly hinder the recognition of the parts.

<margin>Blood circulation and nutrition.</margin>
(On the margin of the leaf). Old people who live in good health <note>original: "vivono con sanità"</note> die from a lack of nourishment. This happens because the passage into the veins of the <term>mesentery</term> <note>the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall; original: "Gekröse"</note> is constantly restricted by the gradual thickening of the walls <note>original: "pelle" or "tunica"</note> of the vessels, down to the capillary vessels, which are the first to close up entirely. From this it arises that the elderly fear the cold more than the young, and those who are very old have skin the color of wood or dry chestnuts, because such skin is almost completely deprived of nourishment.

<margin>Constant renewal of the blood.</margin>
And this <term>vascular tunic</term> <note>the coat or covering of the veins; original: "Adernhülle"</note> behaves in man as it does in <term>bitter oranges</term> <note>original: "Pomeranzen"</note>, whose skin thickens and whose flesh diminishes the older they become. And if you were to say that the thickening of the blood prevents it from flowing through the veins, this is not true, because the blood does not thicken in the veins at all, for it is incessantly dying and being reborn.

The eyes of the lion species <note>original: "Löwengattung"</note> have a large part of the lion's head as their socket, and the optic nerves connect directly with the brain: which is found to be the opposite in humans; for the housing for the eyes is only a small portion of the head, and the optic nerves are thin and long and weak, and they see with weak effect by day, and worse by night, while the aforementioned animals see in the night as in the day; and the sign of this is perceived because they go out for prey at night and sleep by day, as the nocturnal birds also do.

The light—or rather the pupil—of the human eye grows and shrinks by half its size, and in nocturnal creatures, it decreases and grows by more than a hundredfold its size; and this could be seen in the eye of the owl by bringing a lit torch near the eye, and even more if you let it look into the sun; for then you would see the pupil, which previously occupied the whole eye, shrink to the size of a grain of millet, and in this reduction, it resembles the eye of man, and bright things and glimmers of light appear to it in the same color as they appear to man at the same time, and all the more so as the brain of such an animal is smaller than that of man: therefore it happens that such a pupil, growing a hundred times more in the nighttime than that of man, beholds a hundred times more light than man, such that said visual power is not then overwhelmed by the nocturnal darkness; and the human light (pupil), which only doubles in its size, sees little brightness, almost like the bat, which does not fly in hours of too great darkness.

<margin>The pupil and the intensity of light.</margin>
XXXVI.
**The pupil of the eye transforms into as many different sizes as there are variations in the brightness and darkness of the objects presented before it.**

In this case, Nature has assisted the visual faculty: when it is offended by excessive light, it is able to constrict the pupil of the eye, and when it is harmed by various degrees of darkness, it can expand that same light-hole <note>the pupil; original: "Lichtloch"</note>, much like the mouth of a purse. Here, Nature acts just like a person who has too much light in their dwelling and closes half a window, more or less, according to need; and when night comes, they open the entire window to see better inside said dwelling. Here, Nature applies a constant equilibrium, with unceasing tempering and adjustment, increasing the opening and decreasing the pupil in proportion to the aforementioned darkness and brightness that continually present themselves.

<margin>The size of the pupil is variable.</margin>
XXXVII.
**In the open air, the pupil of the eye changes the degrees of its size with every degree of movement made by the sun.**

<margin>What follows from this.</margin>
And at every degree of size (of the pupil), the same object viewed will appear to be of a different size, although often the comparison with surrounding things does not allow one to perceive such a change in a single object being observed.
