thing moves toward it in such a way that it suddenly strikes fear into the person, they do not come to the aid of the heart—the source of life—with their hands, nor to the head—the container of the ruler of the senses—nor to the hearing, smell, or taste, but immediately to the frightened sense: it is not enough to close the eyes with their lids, which are pressed together with the greatest force so that they immediately turn in the opposite direction; since this does not yet secure them, the person places one hand over them and stretches out the other, thus forming a vanguard against their suspicion. Nature has also ordained that the human eye protects itself with the lid, so that, being unprotected while the person is sleeping, it cannot be injured by any thing.

## XL.

## On the muscles which move the tongue

<margin>On the tongue muscles.</margin>
No member requires such a great number of muscles as the tongue, of which 24 are known, besides those others which I have discovered; and of all the limbs that move voluntarily, this one surpasses all others in the number of its movements.

<margin>The tongue as the seat of taste.</margin>
And should you wish to say that it is the office of the eye to receive all the images of the infinitely many shapes and colors of the objects placed before it, and the smell the infinitely many mixtures of scents, and the ear those of sounds, we would say that the tongue also feels the infinitely many tastes, simple and compound; but that is not our purpose, since we have made it our task here to deal merely with the local movement of each limb.

<margin>The tongue as the organ of speech.</margin>
Consider well how, through the movement of the tongue, with the help of the lips and the teeth, the pronunciation (<term>pronunziazione</term> <note>Leonardo uses the Italian term for the physical act of articulating sounds</note>) of all the names of things has become known to us <note>original: "ci son note"</note>, and the simple words of a language and the compound ones reach our ear only by means of this instrument: which, if all the effects of nature had a name, would extend to infinity, together with the infinity of things which exist in reality and which lie in the possibility of nature; and this the tongue would express not merely in a single language, but in an extraordinary number of them, which also extend into infinity, because they...

And for this, the ancient alchemists will be my witnesses, who never, neither by chance nor by deliberate experiment, succeeded in creating the slightest thing that can be created by Nature herself. And this class of alchemists deserves infinite praise because of the usefulness of the things they have found for the benefit of men, and would deserve even more had they not been inventors of harmful things, such as poisons and other similar damages to life and mind, for which they are not to be acquitted. Yet with great study and effort, they wish to create that thing which is not the least noble: gold, the true child of the sun, namely, because it [is more] than any other creature...

My <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "gemeiner Sinn" / "sensus communis"; the central processing faculty of the brain.</note> is set in motion by the <term>faculty of impression</term> <note>original: "Impressivität" / "imprensiva"; the part of the mind that receives raw sensory data.</note>, which lies between it and the senses. Force is produced by deficiency or abundance; it is a child of material motion and a grandchild of spiritual motion, the mother and origin of weight; and this same weight is limited to the elements of water and earth, but force itself is unlimited, because through it infinite worlds could be moved, if one were merely able to make the instruments by which this force would be produced.

Force with material motion, and weight with impact, are the four external powers through which all the work of mortals has its existence and its death.

### XLIV.

<margin>The muscles and consciousness.</margin>

### On the Muscles

Nature has arranged the servant muscles in man, which are pulled by the nerves that can move the limbs, according to the desire and will of the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "allgemeinen Sinnes" / "sensus communis"; the central faculty that coordinates the five senses.</note>, in the likeness of officials who are distributed by a lord over various provinces and cities: who then, in those same places, represent and follow the will of that same lord. And that official who, in a specific case, has better obeyed the privilege given to him by the mouth of the lord, will later, in the same case, do nothing for himself that deviates from the will of that same lord. Thus one often sees the fingers—which, with the highest obedience, learn a task on an instrument that is commanded of them by the judgment—once they have learned it, they will play it without the judgment even noticing. Do not the muscles that move the legs also perform their service without the person knowing it?

### XLV.

<margin>Independence of the sensory nerves from one another.</margin>

See if you do not believe that such a sense (<term>touch</term> <note>original: "Tastsinn"</note>) is exerted in an organ player, while the soul at the same time attends to the sense of hearing.

<margin>Automatic movements.</margin>
### How the nerves sometimes act on their own, without command from the other officials and the soul

This appears clear; for you will see <term>paralytic</term> <note>Referring here to those suffering from palsy or tremors.</note> and freezing and shivering persons move their trembling limbs, such as the head and the hands, without the permission of the soul—which soul, with all its powers, cannot forbid those same limbs from trembling. The idea or imagination is the rudder and rein of the senses, since the imagined thing excites the sense.

Pre-imagining is the imagining of things that will be.

Post-imagining (remembering) is the imagining of past things.

<margin>Blood and heat.</margin>
## XLVIII.
<meta>MS. A. FOL. 56 v.</meta>

->**Why this blood flees through the crown of the head**<-

The spiritual parts have the power to move the material parts and to accompany them in their course. We see fire in the steaming smoke, by means of the spiritual element of heat, send elements of matter—earthly and heavy—up through the chimney, as is perceived in the soot, which, if you were to burn it, would turn back into ash. So the heat, mixed into the blood, desiring to unite itself with its element <note>In the Aristotelian worldview, heat/fire naturally seeks to rise to its "natural place" in the heavens.</note>, finds through the break [an opportunity] to evaporate and takes in its company the blood with which this heat is infused and mixed. — The reason that the smoke rises with such fury and carries earthly things with it is this: the fire, as it ignites in the wood, nourishes and satiates itself on a subtle moisture, and this moisture is too thick to be entirely consumed by the fire, by the heat of the fire found within it; the fire

<meta>MS. A. FOL. 57 r.</meta>

<margin>Mercury evaporation.</margin>
wishes to return to its element and takes the heated humors <note>original: "Säfte" - referring to the bodily fluids or "humors" in classical medicine.</note> with it, as can be seen if you were to distill <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note> in a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note>; you would see, if this silver—which is so heavy—were mixed with the heat of the fire, that it rises and, in the form of smoke in its second recipient, falls back to its first nature.

### LIII. SP., MS. W. AN. B. FOL. 28 r.

## **How the body of the animal dies and is reborn without ceasing**

The body of any thing whatsoever that takes in nourishment dies constantly and is constantly reborn; for nourishment can enter nowhere except into those places from which the past nourishment has been expelled; and once expelled, it is no longer with life; and if you do not provide them with such nourishment again—

--- Page 298 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 117 regarding the metabolic cycle of life and death, specifically focusing on the analogy of the candle flame. It then transitions into a systematic classification of mammals, concluding with a tribute to the perfection of Nature's designs.</meta>

<page-num>118</page-num>

...if you give back as much as has vanished, then life will decrease in strength; and if you take away that same nourishment, life will remain entirely destroyed. But if you give back to it as much as is destroyed of it in a day, then as much of life is reborn as was consumed, in the likeness of the light of a candle, with the nourishment provided to it by the fats of said candle; which light is also constantly restored with the swiftest <term>succor</term> <note>original: "Sukkurs"; meaning rapid aid or reinforcement</note> from below, replacing what is consumed from above in the act of dying, and which, in dying, transforms from a shining light into nocturnal smoke. This death is constant, just as the smoke is without ceasing, and the constancy of such smoke is equal to the continuous nourishment; in an instant, the light is dead and entirely reborn, simultaneously with the movement of its nourishment.

<margin>Classification of mammals, wherein man represents the genus of apes.</margin>

### LIV.

Man. The description of man, in which are also included those who are of approximately the same genus, such as the baboon, the ape, and similar creatures, of which there are many.

The lion and his followers, such as the panther, the ounce <note>A historical term for the snow leopard or similar medium-sized wild cats</note>, the tiger, the leopard, wolves, lynxes, wildcats, genets, and common cats, and others besides.

The horse and his followers, such as mules, donkeys, and the like, which have teeth both above and below.

The ox and his followers, horned and without upper teeth, such as the buffalo, stag, fallow deer, roebuck, sheep, goat, ibex, musk deer, chamois, and giraffe.

<margin>The inventive Nature.</margin>

### LV.

Though the human spirit makes various inventions, answering the same purpose with different tools, it will never produce an invention more beautiful, nor more effortless, nor more brief than Nature does.

<margin>The formative soul, the bodily soul.</margin>
...to invent, because in her inventions nothing is lacking and nothing is superfluous; she does not proceed with counterweights when she makes the limbs of animals suitable for movement. Rather, she places the soul into that very body—the formative soul, namely the soul of the mother, which first forms the shape of the human in the womb and, at the proper time, awakens the soul that is to be the inhabitant thereof. This inhabitant soul was previously asleep, under the guardianship of the mother’s soul, which nourishes and enlivens it through the umbilical cord with all its spiritual limbs. This continues as long as the said navel remains connected to the fetus and the <term>cotyledons</term> <note>original: "Keimblättern"; here referring to the placental attachments</note> through which the child is united with the mother. These are the reason why a wish, a strong desire, a fear felt by the mother, or any other mental pain, has even more power in the child than in the mother; for there are frequent cases where the son loses his life as a result, and so forth.

<margin>The higher soul and the friars.</margin>
This discourse does not belong here, but is necessary for the composition of animated bodies. And the rest of the definition of the soul I leave to the spirit of the friars, those fathers of the people, who know all secrets through inspiration.

<margin>The Holy Scriptures.</margin>
The "crowned books" <note>Likely referring to canonical or divinely inspired scripture</note> I leave as they are, because in them is the highest truth.

### On the attachment of leaves on their branches

The thickness of a branch decreases in the space from one leaf to the next by no more than the thickness of the "eye" <note>The axillary bud from which a new leaf or shoot grows</note> located above said leaf; this thickness is what the branch lacks as it continues to the next leaf.

<margin>The maternal role of the leaf, above which a branch sprouts.</margin>
### **LVII.** MS. G. FOL. 33 v.

Every branch and every fruit emerges exactly above the origin of a leaf, which serves as a mother to them by offering them the rainwater or the moisture of the dew which falls upon it at night; and it often shields them from the excessive heat of the sun's rays.

<margin>Thickening of the bark.</margin>
### **LVIII.** MS. CA. FOL. 76 r.

If a tree is stripped of its bark anywhere, Nature, providing for this, directs a much greater quantity of nourishing sap to that same stripping than to any other place, so that, because of the aforementioned lack, the bark grows much thicker there than at any other spot. And this sap is so impetuous that, having arrived at the place of <term>succor</term> <note>original: "Sukkurs"; meaning the point of emergency aid or relief</note>, it partly rises upward, in the manner of a bouncing ball, with various welling up or rather gurgling forth, no different than boiling water.

<margin>*The man who presumes to want to improve nature—!*</margin>

## IX. *Codex Atlanticus, Folio 76 r.*

The act of slitting the nostrils of horses is a thing worthy of laughter. And these fools observe this custom almost as if they believed that nature had neglected necessary things, for which men must be her improvers. She has made the two holes of the nose, each of which, by itself, is half the width of the lung's pipe <note>The trachea or windpipe</note> through which the breath exhales; and if these same holes did not exist, the mouth would suffice for abundant breathing. And if you said to me: — "Why has this nature made nostrils for animals if breathing through the mouth is sufficient?" — I answer you that the nostrils are made to be used when the mouth is occupied with chewing its food.

<margin>*Argument against the gold-seekers.*</margin>

## X. *Codex Atlanticus, Folio 76 r.*

The lying interpreters of nature claim that mercury is the common seed of all metals, without remembering that nature varies the seeds according to the diversity of the things she wishes to produce in the world.

### On Spirits

We have previously said on the other side how the definition of spirit is "a power united to the body," because it cannot maintain itself on its own, nor [can it have] any kind of local...

<summary>Leonardo argues that if necromancy were real, its immense power would have ensured its survival among greedy men; however, he concludes it is a physical impossibility because spirits lack bodies and nature abhors a vacuum.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s logical argument against the physical existence of spirits, specifically addressing why an incorporeal entity cannot remain stationary or move at will within the classical elements of air and water.</meta>

...make movement. And if you were to say that he <note>the spirit</note> sustains himself by his own power—that cannot be within the elements, because if the spirit is an incorporeal quantity, such a quantity would be called a vacuum, and a vacuum does not exist in nature; and assuming it did exist, it would be immediately filled by the ruin <note>the sudden rushing-in or collapse</note> of that element in which the vacuum was created.

Therefore, from the definition of weight, which says: — "Gravity is an external power, created by one element being drawn by another or pushed away by another," — it follows that, since no element has weight within its own element, it must have weight in a higher element that is lighter than itself. As one sees: one part of water has no more weight or lightness than the rest of the water; but if you pull it into the air, then it acquires weight, and if you pull the air under the water, then it <note>the air</note> acquires weight <note>buoyancy acting as "upward weight"</note>, which weight cannot maintain itself by itself; therefore its ruin is necessary, and so it falls through the water into that place which is empty of water. Such a thing would happen to the spirit if it were found within the elements: it would incessantly create a vacuum in whichever element it was in, for which reason a constant flight toward the heavens would be necessary for it, until it had emerged from such elements.

We have proven how the spirit cannot remain by itself without a body within the elements, nor move itself by its own will, unless it be upward. ### Whether the spirit can speak or not

<margin>Whether the spirit can speak.</margin>
<margin>Singing flame.</margin>
To show whether the spirit can speak or not, it is necessary first to explain what a voice is and how it is generated, and we shall state it in this manner: "the voice is a movement of air that rubs against a solid body, or a dense body rubbing against the air—which is the same thing—which friction of the dense with the thin <note>Leonardo uses "thin" (Dünnen) to refer to rare or gaseous substances like air</note> condenses the thin and thus creates resistance; also, when swift thin matter condenses within slow thin matter, they compress one another upon contact and create a tone or a tremendous noise. And the tone, or even a murmur, is produced by the thin moving within the thin with moderate motion, like a large flame, which is a generator of sounds in the air; and the tremendous noise is caused by the thin in the thin when the swift thin matter penetrates into the movable thin matter, like the flame of fire that comes out of a bombard <note>a primitive type of cannon</note> and strikes against the air, and furthermore the flame that comes out of a cloud and shakes the air in the generation of lightning." Therefore, we shall say that the spirit cannot produce a voice without movement of the air, and there is no air within it, nor can it expel air from itself if it does not have it; and if it wishes to move that air in which it is incorporated, the spirit must multiply (condense) itself, and it cannot multiply itself if it does not itself have quantity <note>physical dimensions or volume</note>, according to the fourth rule, which says: "No thin matter moves if it does not have a stable place from which it takes its motion, and especially when an element has to move within its own element, which does not move by itself,

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci argues that spirits cannot speak because sound requires the physical friction of air against a body, and an incorporeal spirit lacks the volume and density to move air.</summary>

### XIV. Manuscript B. Folio 4 verso.

> There can be no voice where there is no movement and percussion of the air; there can be no percussion of the air where there is no instrument; there can be no instrument that is incorporeal; this being so, a spirit can have neither voice, nor form, nor strength; and if it assumes a body, it will not be able to penetrate or enter where the entrances are barred; and if someone should say: "by means of condensed and compressed air, the spirit assumes bodies of various forms, and through this instrument it speaks and moves with strength," to this part I say: where there are no tendons and bones, there can be no strength exercised in any movement by these imaginary spirits.

Our judgment does not judge things that have happened at different distances of time in their proper and appropriate distances; for many things that occurred many years ago will appear close and neighboring, and many neighboring things will appear old, equal to the age of our youth; and the eye does the same between distant things which, because they are illuminated by the sun, seem close to the eye, and many close things seem far.

<margin>Pain and its role.</margin>
XIX. MS. H. II. FOL. 60 r.

If nature has ordained pain in vegetative living beings <note>i.e., animals capable of movement and growth</note> along with movement, for the preservation of the instruments <note>the limbs or organs</note> which might be diminished and destroyed by movement, then vegetative beings without movement do not have to run into objects placed against them; therefore, pain is not necessary in plants, so that if one breaks them, they do not feel pain as animals do.

<margin>The interaction of body and soul.</margin>

## XXII.

Whoever wishes to see how the soul dwells in its body should observe how this body employs its daily habitation; namely, if the latter is without order and confused, the body possessed by its soul will likewise be disorderly and confused. <note>Leonardo suggests that the physical state of one's living quarters reflects the internal spiritual state.</note>

<margin>People for whom the higher spiritual life is nothing.</margin>

## XXIII.

There are some here who can be called nothing other than a passage for food, producers of filth, and fillers of latrines, because for them there is nothing else in the world, nor does any virtue put itself to work; so that nothing remains of them other than full latrines.

## XXIV.

How you have described the king of animals—though I would speak better if I said king of beasts, since you are the greatest of them! For you have only refrained from killing them so that they might later give you their young for the sake of your palate, with which you have attempted to make yourself the grave of all animals; and I would say even more, if telling the whole truth were fully permitted to me. 

But let us remain within human affairs, naming a supreme wickedness which does not occur among the animals of the earth; for among them none are found who eat their own species, except for a lack of brain <note>original: "Mangel an Gehirn"; implying a lack of sense or instinctual error</note> [among a few of them and among mothers, as with humans, although they are not in such great numbers among the former], and this does not happen except among the beasts of prey, such as the genus of lions and leopards, panthers, lynxes, cats and the like, which sometimes eat their young. But you eat not only the young, but also the father, the mother, brothers, and friends; and these do not suffice for you, so that you go hunting on other islands, snatching away other men, and these, <note>Leonardo is likely referencing accounts of cannibalism reported by explorers like Vespucci or the travelogues of John Mandeville.</note>

### XXV. R. 1219, MS. BR. M. FOL. 156 v.

<margin>Why nature did not forbid one animal from living off another.</margin>
Why did nature not forbid that one animal should live by the death of another? Nature, being eager and finding pleasure in the creation and making of constantly new lives and forms—because she recognizes that herein is an increase of her earthly matter—is compliant and much faster in her creating than time is in destroying; and therefore she has ordained that many animals should be food for one another. And since this does not satisfy such a desire, she often sends down certain poisonous and pestilential vapors upon the great multiplications and gatherings of animals, and especially upon men, who have great increase because other animals do not feed upon them; and since the causes are removed, the effects are also lacking. Thus, this earth seeks to lose from its life while desiring constant increase; according to your indicated and proven reason, effects often resemble their causes; animals are the prototypical example of all earthly life.

<margin>On Nothingness.</margin>
**XXXI.** R. 1216, MS. BR. M. FOL. 131 r.

Every continuous **quantity** is intellectually divisible into infinity.

[Among the magnitudes of the things that are around us, the existence of Nothingness holds supremacy, and its office extends over the things that have no existence, and its essence dwells in the time between the past and the future and possesses nothing at all of the present. This Nothingness has its part equal to the whole, and the whole equal to the part, and the divisible to the indivisible, and has the same sum in the product, in division as in multiplication, and in addition as much as in subtraction, as is proved by the mathematicians in their tenth digit, which represents that same Nothingness (0); and its power does not extend to the things of nature.]

[That which is called Nothingness is found only in time and in words; in time it is found in the past and in the future, and holds nothing of the present; and likewise in the words of things of which one says that they are not or that they are impossible.]

In time, Nothingness resides in the past and in the future and possesses nothing in the present, and in nature it joins itself to impossible things, whence, according to what has been said, it has no existence. For where Nothingness were, the <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "Vakuum"; a space entirely devoid of matter, a concept Leonardo often debated in the context of Aristotelian physics.</note> would have to be present.

### XXXVIII.
<margin>Manuscript Codex Atlanticus, Folio 289 r. Point and Nothingness.</margin>

->On the Point<-

Nothingness is the absence of being or of the object. The point is the end of being or of the thing. <note>Leonardo distinguishes here between mathematical "nothingness" (zero) and the "point," which he views as the boundary where an object ends.</note>

### XXXIX.
<margin>Manuscript Codex Atlanticus, Folio 289 v. Zero.</margin>

Nothingness (Zero) has no center, and its ends are nothing (zero).

### XL.
<margin>Manuscript Codex Atlanticus, Folio 244 v. In the world there is no "negligible quantity."</margin>

Two weaknesses, leaning against each other, create a strength. Thus half the world, supporting itself on the other, maintains its equilibrium. <note>This is a classic Leonardesque observation on mechanics and architecture, likely referring to the principle of the arch.</note>

No divisible thing is so light that it would not move the world.

### XLI.
<margin>Sp., Manuscript Windsor Anatomy, Folio A. 2 r. Value of the slightest life (as a marginal note to anatomical drawings and explanations).</margin>

And you, O man, who in this work of mine observe the wonderful works of nature—if you should judge it a wicked thing to destroy my labor <note>Referring to his anatomical dissections and drawings</note>, then consider how it is the most wicked thing of all to take the life of a man; for if this, his composition, seems to you of wonderful craftsmanship, consider that this is nothing in comparison to the soul that dwells within such a structure. And truly, whatever that soul may be, it is a divine thing which she allows to dwell in her work according to her pleasure; and do not desire that your anger or malice should destroy such a life; for indeed, he who does not value it, does not deserve it.

<summary>Leonardo explores the definitions of nothingness and the geometric point before offering a powerful ethical defense of human life, arguing that the soul's "divine" residence in the body makes murder the ultimate sacrilege.</summary>

<margin>*Invocation.*</margin>
## Invocation (Prayer)

You, O Lord, sell us all good things at the price of labor. <note>original: "Oratio." Leonardo frequently expressed the idea that divine gifts are earned through human effort.</note>

<margin>*The Creative Impulse.*</margin>
II. ->R. 685, MS. W. P. FOL. 11 v.<-

Sooner be deprived of motion than grow weary of being useful.
Sooner death than weariness.
I am never sated by serving.
I do not tire of being useful — a carnival motto.
*Without weariness.* <note>original: "Sine lassitudine."</note>
No work is able to tire me.
Hands into which ducats and precious stones flutter down never tire of serving; but such service is only for one's own benefit and is not according to our purpose.
By nature, Nature has fashioned me so. <note>original: "natura cosi mi dispone, naturalmente." Leonardo reflects on his innate drive to create and serve through his art and science.</note>

<margin>*Wealth and Virtue.*</margin>
III. ->MS. ASH. I. FOL. 34 v.<-

Do not desire wealth that can be lost. Virtue is our true good and gives its possessor the true reward; it cannot be lost; it does not leave us unless life leaves us first. All property and external prosperity you guard with anxiety, and often they leave their owner behind with contempt and mockery as he loses them.

### XCVIII. R. 677, MS. OX. FOL. 2 v.

<margin>Envy (*Explanation for an allegorical drawing*).</margin>
This Envy is represented with the "fig" <note>original: "Feige." A vulgar or insulting hand gesture (the thumb thrust between the first and second fingers) directed toward the heavens.</note> toward heaven, because if he could, he would turn his strength against God; he is made with the mask of fair appearance over his face; he is made so that his eye is wounded by palms and olives; he is made with the ear wounded by laurel and myrtles, as a sign that victory and truth hurt him; many lightning bolts are shown coming from him to signify his evil speech; he is made lean and withered because he is always in constant sorrow; his heart is made gnawed by a swollen serpent; he is given a quiver with tongues as arrows, because he often wounds with these; he is given the skin of a leopard, because this animal kills the lion out of envy by means of deceit; he is made with a vase in his hand full of flowers, and let the same be filled with scorpions and toads and other poisonous things; he is shown riding upon Death, because Envy never dies and never tires of ruling; his bridle is made heavy with various weapons, because these are all instruments of death.

Hardly is Virtue born, before she brings Envy into the world against herself; a body is sooner without a shadow than Virtue without Envy.

Pleasure and Displeasure are made as twins, because one is never without the other, as if they were joined

<meta>This page continues Leonardo da Vinci’s series of allegorical descriptions and moral emblems. While the previous page detailed the grotesque iconography of Envy, this page moves to the dual nature of Pleasure and Pain, and the purifying power of Truth.</meta>

they are joined to one another; they turn their backs to each other because they are opposites. If you take a pleasure, know that it has something behind it that will bring you distress and repentance.

This here is Pleasure with Displeasure <note>original: "Mißvergnügen." Often translated in this context as Pain or Sorrow.</note>, and they are depicted as twins because one is never without the other, as if they were fastened together. They are made with their backs to one another because they are opposites; they are made founded upon a single body because they have the same foundation, since the foundation of all pleasure is the weariness of displeasure; the foundation of displeasure is the various and frivolous pleasures. And therefore they are represented here with a reed in the right hand, which is hollow and without strength; and the stabs one makes with it are poisonous. In Tuscany, this reed is used as a support in beds, to indicate that here one has vain dreams and that here a great part of life is consumed; here a great deal of useful time is thrown away, namely that of the morning, because the spirit is then sober and rested, and thus the body is fit to take upon itself new labors. Also, one snatches up a multitude of hollow pleasures there, both by hatching impossible things in the mind, and by creating those pleasures for the body which are often the cause of a failed existence; it is for this reason that the reed is used for such supports.

C. R. 684, MS. W. P. FOL. 11 r.

Fire destroys falsehood, that is <term>sophism</term> <note>A clever but false argument intended to deceive.</note>, and restores the truth by driving away the darkness.

Fire must be set as the consumer of all <term>sophism</term> and the discoverer and prover of truth, because it is the light, the driver-away of all darkness, which is the concealer of every essential thing.

# VII. ON ART

<margin>*Nature and Art.*</margin>
->R. 651, MS. S. K. M. III. FOL. 19 v.<-

**T**he beauty of mortal things passes, but not that of art <note>original: "Cosa bella mortal passa e non d'arte." A famous Italian aphorism attributed to Leonardo, emphasizing the immortality of artistic creation compared to the fleeting nature of physical life.</note>.

---

<margin>*Painting and Poetry.*</margin>
II.
->MS. ASH. I. FOL. 19 r.<-

*How painting surpasses all human works through the subtle contemplation that is its own*

The eye, which is called the window of the soul, is the principal way by which the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "allgemeine Sinn." In Renaissance psychology, the 'sensus communis' was the faculty that organized and interpreted data from all five senses.</note> can most abundantly and magnificently contemplate the infinite works of nature; and the ear is the second, which acquires nobility through the things recounted that the eye has perceived. If you, historians or poets or other mathematicians, had not seen things with the eye, you would report them poorly in your writings. And if you, poet, represent a story with the painting of the pen, the painter with his brush will make it with greater ease of satisfaction and less tedious to understand. If you call painting "mute poetry," the painter could say of the poet's writing: "blind painting." Now look: — which mockery is more biting: to be blind or to be mute?

### III. MS. ASH. FOL. 20 r. <note>Refers to the Ashburnham Manuscript, a collection of Leonardo's notes.</note>

<margin>He who disregards painting loves neither nature nor philosophy.</margin>
### How he who disregards painting loves neither philosophy nor nature

If you wish to disregard painting, which is the sole imitator of all the manifest works of nature, you certainly disregard a refined invention that, with philosophical and subtle reflection, considers all the qualities of forms: atmospheres and places, trees, animals, grasses, and flowers, which are surrounded by light and shadow. And truly, this is a science and the legitimate daughter of nature, because painting is born of that very nature. But, to speak even more correctly, we shall say it is the grandchild of nature, because all manifest things are produced by nature, and these produced things have given birth to painting; therefore, we shall correctly call it the granddaughter of nature and kin to God.

### IV. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 25 r.

<margin>Sculpture and Painting.</margin>
### How sculpture is of lesser spirit than painting and lacks many elements of nature within itself

Since I occupy myself no less in sculpture than in painting and practice the one as much as the other to the same degree, it seems to me that I can, with little presumption, offer a judgment on how one of them possesses more genius, difficulty, and perfection than the other. The perspectives of the sculptor never seem to possess truth; those of the painter lead hundreds of miles into the work. <term>Aerial perspective</term> <note>The technique of representing distance by modifying colors to simulate the effect of the atmosphere.</note> is foreign to the sculptor's work. What sculpture does possess is that it resists time better, although painting has just such a resistance when done on thick copper; covered with white enamel and painted upon with enamel colors, then placed once more into the fire and allowed to burn: in this way, it surpasses sculpture in eternity. One can also say that where they have made any error, it is not easily corrected. It is, however, a poor argument to wish to prove that an uncorrectable lack of foresight gives a work greater dignity. Rather, I say that to improve the mind of the master who makes such errors is much more difficult than to improve the work he has ruined.

### VIII. <note>original: "R. 658, MS. W. A. IV. FOL. 152 r."</note>

When the poet ceases to represent with words that which is a fact in nature, then the poet does not make himself the equal of the painter; for if said poet leaves aside such representation and describes the decorative and persuasive words of the one he wishes to have speak, then he makes himself an orator and is no longer a poet, nor is he a painter; and if he speaks of the heavens, he makes himself an astrologer; a philosopher and theologian if he speaks of the things of nature and of God; but if he returns to the representation of anything, he would make himself a competitor of the painter, if only he could satisfy the eye with words as the painter does.

## XIII. <note>original: "MS. ASH. I. FOL. 25 r."</note>

### On the sorry excuse offered by those who falsely and unworthily allow themselves to be called painters

There is a generation of painters who, because of their
scant study, eke out a living under the shield of the beauty of
gold and azure <note>Azure refers to lapis lazuli, an expensive blue pigment. Leonardo critiques those who rely on costly materials rather than artistic skill.</note>, and who claim with exquisite

They do not even know how to keep any work of quality,

price, and that one over there is scrap" <note>original: "Ausschuß"; referring to low-quality or rejected goods.</note>, showing
that they have work available at every price.

### XV. <note>original: "MS. ASH. I. FOL. 22 v."</note>

<margin>On the ten functions of the eye.</margin>
## On the ten functions of the eye, all concerning painting

Painting extends over all the ten functions <note>The "functions" or "offices" (Ämter) refer to the categories of visual perception that a painter must master to replicate reality.</note> of the eye, namely: darkness, light, body and color, figure and location, distance and nearness, motion and rest. My little work will be interwoven with these functions, as I remind the painter with what rule and method he should imitate all these things—the work of nature and the ornament of the world—by means of his art.

---

### XVI. <note>original: "MS. ASH. I. FOL. 27 r."</note>

<margin>Study of anatomy.</margin>
## How it is necessary for the painter to know the internal form of man

That painter who has knowledge of the nature of the nerves, muscles, and tendons will well know, when moving a limb, how many and what kind of nerves are the cause of it, which muscle by swelling is the cause of shortening that nerve, and which cords, transformed into the most delicate cartilage, surround and hold this muscle together. And so he will be a varied and versatile demonstrator of the muscles, which mediate all the different expressions of activity in the figures; he will not act like those who, in the most varied poses, always show the same features in the arms, legs, chest, and back, which must be counted among no small errors.

<margin>Against those who make a display of their anatomy.</margin>
## XVII.

O painter-anatomist, take care lest this excessive knowledge of bones, tendons, and muscles becomes the cause of making you a "wooden" painter <note>A "wooden" style refers to figures that appear stiff, unnatural, or overly rigid.</note>, in your striving to make your naked figures show all their sensations. Therefore, to remedy this, observe in what manner the muscles cover—or better yet, clothe—their bones in the elderly or the thin; and besides this, note the rule of how these same muscles fill the superficial spaces that lie between them. And which are the muscles of which one never loses perception, regardless of the degree of fatness, and which are the muscles of which one loses the knowledge of their points of contact at the slightest degree of plumpness. Many are the times when one muscle is made from many when one becomes fat, and many are the times when, through thinning or aging, several muscles are made from one. In due time, all the details of this discourse will be demonstrated, etc.

---

<margin>Order of study.</margin>
## XVIII.

I say that one must first learn the limbs and their functions, and when such knowledge is complete, one must follow the positions according to the accidents <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to the various spontaneous circumstances or chance movements a person might encounter.</note> in which a person finds themselves; and thirdly, learn to compose "histories" <term>histories: narrative paintings depicting a specific event or story</term>, the study of which will be made according to natural gestures, performed as they are appropriate for the events. Observe these gestures in the streets, marketplaces, and fields, and note them with a brief shorthand of lines: namely, making an "O" for a head, and a straight or bent line for an arm, and do similarly for the legs and the torso; and upon returning home, draw such memories in perfect form.

<summary>Leonardo warns painters against over-emphasizing anatomical details to the point of stiffness and outlines a three-step educational program: learning anatomy, observing spontaneous movement, and composing narrative scenes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the curriculum for the student painter, shifting from the study of anatomy and narrative composition to the fundamental methodology of learning: the debate between copying masters versus studying nature, and the necessity of a step-by-step approach.</meta>

<page-num>165</page-num>

If the opponent says that, in order to become practical and produce many works, it is better if the first period of study be spent in drawing various compositions made for paper or walls by various masters, and that in such a way one acquires quick practice and good habits. To which it is answered, that this habit would be good if based upon works of good composition and made by masters eager to learn; and because such masters are so rare that one finds few of them, it is safer to go to the things in nature than to those things imitated from that same nature with great deterioration, and thereby forming bad habits; for he who can go to the spring, let him not go to the water-pot. <note>This is a famous maxim of Leonardo's, emphasizing that nature is the primary source of truth, while copying other artists is like drinking stale water from a jar.</note>

---

<meta>XIX. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 28 r.</meta>
<margin>Instruction for beginners.</margin>
### This rule must be given to the painter's apprentices

We know clearly that sight is one of the fastest activities that exists, perceiving countless forms in a single point; nonetheless, it grasps no more than one thing at a time. Let us take the case that you, reader, might behold with a single glance this entire written page and judge at once that it is full of various letters; but you will not be able to recognize in that time which letters they are, nor what they intend to say; therefore you must take it word by word, line by line, in order to have knowledge of these letters. Likewise, if you wish to climb to the top of a building, it must suit you to climb step by step; otherwise, it would be impossible to reach the top. So I say also to you, whom nature inclines toward this art: if you wish to have true knowledge of the forms of things, begin with their details, and do not go to the second until you have the first well in your memory and in practice; and if you do otherwise, you will throw away your time.

<summary>Leonardo argues that students should study directly from nature rather than copying other artists' work, and insists on a disciplined, step-by-step approach to learning visual forms.</summary>

and truly lengthen the study considerably. And remember to value diligence in learning more than quickness.

<margin>Study, solitude, and inner peace.</margin>
## XX. <note>original: "MS. CA. FOL. 184 v." refers to the Codex Atlanticus, Leonardo's largest collection of drawings and writings.</note>

For the painter, mathematics is necessary—specifically that which pertains to painting—as is the avoidance of company that is foreign to his studies. He must possess a mind adaptable to the diversity of the objects that present themselves to him, and kept far from other worries.

And when it comes to the observation and definition of a case <note>Leonardo uses "case" or "instance" to describe a specific visual phenomenon or problem to be solved.</note>, as happens when an object sets the senses in motion, one must judge which of such cases is of the most difficult definition, and follow this until its final clarity, and only then pursue the definition of the next.

And above all, let his mind be like the surface of a mirror, which transforms into as many different colors as there are colors in its objects; and let his companions be similar to him in such studies, and, finding no such people, let him keep company with himself in his contemplations, because in the end he will find no more useful company.

---

<margin>Various instructions.</margin>
## XXI. <note>original: "MS. ASH. I. FOL. 17 v." refers to the Codex Ashburnham, a manuscript primarily focused on painting and optics.</note>

The youth should first of all learn perspective; then the measurements of all things; then he should draw from the hand of a good master, in order to accustom himself to good limbs <note>Meaning the correct anatomical proportions of the human body.</note>; then from nature, to confirm the reasons for the things he has learned; then for a time he should look at works by the hands of various masters; then finally accustom himself to putting things into practice <note>original: "mettere in pratica"</note> and mastering the art.

— If you wish to create a round sphere at a certain height, you must make it elongated, as shown here, and stand so far back that it appears foreshortened <term>foreshortening: the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually does to create an illusion of three-dimensional space</term>.

— That historical scenes <note>original: "Geschichten" (histories/narratives). In Renaissance art theory, the 'istoria' was considered the highest form of painting, depicting a significant narrative event.</note> should not be overcrowded or confused by too many people.

— That drapery must be drawn from nature; that is, if you wish to create a woolen garment, use the folds of such a fabric, or if it is to be silk, or fine cloth, or rustic fabric, or a veil, make the folds different for each according to its kind. Do not do as many do, who drape garments over models covered with paper or thin leather; in this, you would be greatly deceived.

— That the elderly must be depicted with sluggish and slow movements, the legs bent at the knees when they stand still, the feet parallel and slightly apart, the spine deeply curved, the head tilted forward and down, and the arms not stretched far away.

— How one must represent women: with modest gestures, the legs firmly closed, the arms gathered to themselves, the heads inclined and turned to the side.

— How old women must have violent, rapid, and angry movements, in the manner of hellish furies <note>original: "Furien." In classical mythology, the Furies were female deities of vengeance; Leonardo uses them here as a shorthand for intense, uncontrolled emotion.</note>, and the movements must appear faster in the arms and the head than in the legs.

Perspective is the bridle and the rudder of painting.

<margin>*On perspective and the doctrine of light.*</margin>
XXIII. MS. CA. FOL. 203 r. <note>CA refers to the Codex Atlanticus, the largest collection of Leonardo's drawings and writings.</note>
Among the studies of natural causes and reasons, light delights the beholder most of all; among the great things of the mathematical sciences, the certainty of demonstration most gloriously elevates the spirit of the investigator.

Perspective must therefore be placed before all treatises and human disciplines, in whose field the complex radiant line provides the means for demonstrations; in which is found the glory not so much of mathematics as of physics, adorned with the flowers of both. Their maxims—which, because they are extended with great digression, I shall draw closer in the following brevity—I will weave together, according to the nature of the material, using natural and mathematical demonstrations. Sometimes I shall conclude the effects from the causes, and sometimes the causes from the effects. To my conclusions, I shall add some that are not contained in those and yet nevertheless deal with them, just as the Lord, the light of all things, shall deign to enlighten me, the writer <note>original: "Traktator" (one who treats a subject/treatiser)</note> of light . . . .

People who have a desire only for physical riches and pleasures, and who are entirely devoid of that desire for wisdom, nourishment, and the truly secure wealth of the soul; for, by as much as the soul is worthier than the body, by so much will the riches of the soul be worthier than those of the body. And often, when I see someone of that sort take this work into their hand, I have no doubt that, just like a monkey, he will bring it to his nose and ask me if it is something to eat.

### XXV.

<margin>What is perspective?</margin>
Perspective is a subject of demonstration <note>A "demonstration" in this context is a logical or mathematical proof.</note>, through which experience confirms that all things send their image into the eye by means of pyramidal lines. By pyramidal lines, I mean those which originate from the surface edges of bodies and, by converging from a distance, lead themselves to a single point; which point, in this case, I intend to show as being located within the eye, the universal judge of all bodies. I say "point" referring to that which cannot be divided into any part; therefore, since this point located in the eye is indivisible, no body will be seen by the sight that is not larger than this point; since this is so, it is necessary that the lines coming from the body to the point be pyramidal. And if someone wished to prove that the power of sight does not lie in this point, but on the contrary in that black spot seen in the middle of the pupil, one could answer them that a small object could never become smaller through any distance—be it even a grain of millet or a fennel seed or other such things—and then any object larger than that spot could never be seen in its entirety, as shown by the following proof, etc.

<summary>Leonardo argues that intellectual wealth surpasses material riches before defining perspective as a mathematical system where objects project "pyramidal" lines to a single point in the eye. He defends the theory of a singular point of vision against those who believe sight occurs across the entire surface of the pupil.</summary>

<keywords>perspective, pyramidal lines, optics, geometry of vision, soul vs body, anatomy of the eye, mathematical proof</keywords>

<margin>Which is more difficult: to understand light and shadow or to draw well.</margin>
### XXVI.
### Which is more difficult: light and shadow or merely good drawing

I say that a matter which is constrained by a boundary is more difficult than one which is free. Shadows have their boundaries in certain degrees, and whoever is ignorant of them, his works are without that "rounding" <note>The term "rounding" (Rundung) refers to *chiaroscuro*, the technique of using light and dark to create the illusion of three-dimensional volume.</note>, which rounding is the most important thing and the soul of painting. Drawing is free, for when you see countless faces, they will all be different; one has a long nose or a short one; thus the painter can also take this freedom for himself, and where there is freedom, there is no fixed rule.

<margin>The study of nature.</margin>
### XXVII.

. . . . Therefore, O painter, you who have no such rules—in order to escape the criticism of those who understand—be diligent to draw all your subjects according to nature and do not despise study, as those who work only for profit <note>original: "Verdiener" - likely referring to "hack" artists or commercial painters who prioritize speed over observation.</note> do.

<header>MS. G. FOL. 5 v.</header>
<margin>Variety and richness.</margin>
### XXVIII.
### On the variety of figures

The painter must strive to be universal, because he lacks dignity if he does one thing well and another poorly, like many who study only the well-measured and proportioned nude and do not seek out its variations; for a man can indeed be proportioned and yet be short and fat, or long and thin, or average. And whoever does not take this variety into account always makes his figures as if from a mold <note>original: "im Abdruck"</note>, so that they all appear to be siblings, a thing which deserves great criticism.

---

When you have drawn an object so often that you believe you have it in your mind, try to recreate it without the example <note>original: "Vorbild" - the reference model or original work being copied</note>. To check your progress, trace your example onto a thin, flat piece of glass, and place this over the drawing you made without a model. Note carefully where the tracing does not align with your drawing and where you find you have erred; remember these spots so as not to err again. You should even return to the model to redraw that mistaken part so many times that you have it well-fixed in your imagination. If you do not possess a flat glass for tracing, take a very thin sheet of goat parchment <term>goat parchment: a translucent writing surface made from animal skin, often treated to be clearer for tracing</term>, well-oiled and then dried. Once you have used it for your drawing, you can erase it with a sponge and use it a second time.

## XXX. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 26 r.

### On studying when you wake up, or before you fall asleep, in bed, in the dark

<margin>Memory exercise.</margin>
I have experienced in my own life that it is of no small utility when you are in bed in the dark to go over in your imagination the superficial outlines <note>original: "Lineamente"</note> of the forms you have previously studied, or other noteworthy things grasped by subtle reflection. This is a praiseworthy and useful act for fixing things in the memory.

<margin>Application of the mirror.</margin>

### XXXII.

## How the mirror is a teacher to painters

If you wish to see whether your picture as a whole corresponds with the thing you have made from nature, then take a mirror and let the living subject be reflected in it; compare the reflected subject with your painting and look carefully to see whether the object of the one and the other image are in agreement with each other. And above all, the mirror. One must take the mirror as a master—that is, the flat mirror—because on its surface, things possess a similarity to a picture in many respects. That is to say, you see a picture made on a surface showing things that appear raised <note>original: "erhaben" - meaning three-dimensional or in relief</note>, and the flat mirror does the same; the painting has a single surface and the mirror likewise. The painted image is not tangible, in the sense that what appears round and detached within it cannot be grasped with the hands, and it is the same with the mirror; the mirror and the painting show similarities of things surrounded by light and shadow; in both cases, they—

## XXXV. MS. A. FOL. 23 r.
## On the deception to which one is subject in judging limbs

<margin>Bias of judgment within the limits of one's own nature.</margin>
That painter who possesses clumsy hands will make them the same in his works, and this same thing will happen to him with every limb, unless long study prevents him from it. Therefore, O painter, look well at that part of yourself which you have most ugly on your whole person, and upon this, through your study, apply good improvement; for, if you are beastly, your figures will be the same and without reason, and likewise every part of good and bad that you have within you will show itself in part in your figures.

<margin>Be selective!</margin>

### On the Selection of Beautiful Faces

It seems to me no small grace in a painter if he gives his figures a good appearance. This is a grace which, if one does not possess it by nature, may be acquired through occasional study in this manner: seek to select the good features from many beautiful faces, whose beauty is confirmed more by public reputation than by your own judgment, because you could deceive yourself by choosing faces that have a resemblance to your own. For it often seems that such resemblances please us; and were you yourself ugly, you would not choose beautiful faces but would create ugly ones, like many painters whose figures frequently resemble the master. Therefore, take beauties as I describe them to you, and impress these upon your mind.

### On the Sinuous Movement and Balancing of Figures and Other Living Beings

Whatever figures or graceful living things you create, remember to flee from "woodenness"—that is, they should move in <term>contrapposto</term> <note>A pose where the weight is shifted onto one leg, creating a natural "S" curve in the spine.</note>, or better yet: walking in a balanced way so that they do not appear like a stick.

### XXXIX.
## On the Choice of Light that Gives Grace to Faces

<margin>Which atmospheric mood is most favorable for the expression of the human face.</margin>

If you had a courtyard that you could cover with a linen awning at will, this light would be good. Or if you wish to paint someone, paint them during bad weather or at the onset of evening twilight, by placing the person being painted with their back against one of the walls of said courtyard. Observe the faces of men and women in the streets as evening approaches when the weather is poor; notice how much grace and sweetness is perceived as belonging to them. Therefore, O painter, you shall have a courtyard prepared with walls tinted black, with a small roof overhang above the aforementioned wall. It should be 10 cubits <note>original: "Ellen" (ells/cubits). An old unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm.</note> wide, 20 long, and 10 high; and when the sun is out, cover it with an awning, or else paint an hour before the approach of evening, while it is cloudy or misty. And this is the perfect atmosphere.

---

### XL.
## On the Quality of Light

<margin>Good lighting.</margin>

### XLI.

<margin>How to render the limbs.</margin>

### XLII.
## On the Gestures of the Figures

You shall make the figures in such movement that it suffices to show what that figure has in its mind; otherwise, your art would not be praiseworthy.

<margin>Expression.</margin>

### **XLIII.**

How a figure is not praiseworthy if some gesture upon it does not express the passion of the soul.

That figure is most to be praised which, through its gesture, best expresses the passion of its being <note>The German "Wesen" here refers to the inner nature or character of the subject.</note>.

---

<margin>Mien and gesture as means of expression.</margin>

### **XLIV.**

. . . Painting, or rather: painted figures, must be made in such a way that the beholders are able to recognize with ease the intent of their minds from their positions. And if you have to make a virtuous man speak, ensure that his action is a companion to his good words; and likewise, if you have to fashion a bestial man, make him with wild movements, throwing his arms toward the listener, his head pressed against his chest, and his legs spread apart, which should accompany the hands of the speaker.

In equality with the mute (deaf-mute), who, seeing two speakers, although he is deprived of hearing, nonetheless understands the subject of their dispute through the effects and the gestures of those same speakers.

I saw in Florence a man who had accidentally become deaf, who, if you spoke loudly to him, did not understand you, but speaking softly, without the sound of the voice, he understood you solely through the guidance of the lips. Now you might say to me: — "does one not move the lips when speaking loudly just as when speaking softly? and if one moves them like the other, would not one be understood as well as the other?" — For this, I leave the judgment to be given by experience: have someone speak softly, and then loudly, and pay attention to the lips.

---

<margin>Smoke and air.</margin>

### **XLV.**

When the smoke from dry wood is located between the eye that sees it and another dark place, it appears blue.

Thus, the air becomes blue because of the darkness that lies behind it. And when you look toward the horizon of the sky, you will see that the air is not blue, and this arises from its thickness. And so, with every degree that you raise your eye from the horizon up to the sky that stands above you, you will see the air become darker; this is because a smaller quantity of air is pushed between your eye and that same darkness <note>Leonardo is describing the phenomenon of Rayleigh scattering and atmospheric perspective, observing that the "blackness" of space appears blue when filtered through illuminated air.</note>. And if you find yourself on a high mountain, the air above you will become all the darker as it has become thinner between you and the aforementioned darkness, and so it continues with every degree of height until, in the end, it remains dark.

That smoke appears more azure <note>original: "azurner"</note> which arises from the driest wood, and which is closer to its origin, and which is seen against a very dark field with the light of the sun falling upon it.

### XLVI.
<margin>Landscape and light.</margin>
## On Trees and Their Light

The true manner of the practitioner in representing a <term>Campagna</term> <note>An Italian term for the countryside or an open landscape.</note> or, I should say, a landscape with its plants, is to choose a time when the sun is covered by clouds. This allows said landscape to receive a general light rather than the specific light of the sun, which makes the shadows appear cut off and very starkly contrasting against the lights.

---

This shadow has definite borders and a decided darkness, and sometimes it is a half or a third part of that leaf which is in shadow, and

<margin>On Coloring.</margin>

### XLVIII.

Because white is not a color, but possesses a receptive power for every color, all its shadows—when it is located in an open field—are blue; and this comes from the fourth proposition, which says: "The surface of every opaque body participates in the color of its opposite." Therefore, if this white is deprived of the light of the sun by the intervention of an object placed between the sun and this white, then all that white which sees the sun and the air remains a participant in the color of the sun and the air; and that part which does not see the sun remains in shadow, participating in the color of the air. And if such white did not see the green of the landscape all the way to the horizon, without doubt, the white would then appear to be of the simple color which the air shows itself to be.

---

<margin>Value of the rules.</margin>

### XLIX.

. . . These rules are only to be used for the verification of figures, since everyone makes some kind of error in the first composition, and he who does not recognize them (the errors) does not correct them; therefore, in order to know the errors, you shall verify your work, and where you find said errors, correct them and keep it present in your mind never to fall into them again. But, if you wished to use the rules while composing, you would never reach a beginning and would bring confusion to your works.

These rules ensure that you have a free and good judgment, since good judgment comes from a good understanding, and good understanding stems from an object treated according to good rules, and good rules are the children of good ex— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "experience" (Erfahrung).</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains how white surfaces absorb the colors of their environment, specifically turning blue in shadows due to the sky, and argues that artistic rules should be used for correcting work rather than as a restrictive guide during the initial creative process.</summary>

### L. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 28 r.

<margin>To form the judgment.</margin>
#### On judging your painting well

We know well that one recognizes mistakes better in the works of others than in one's own, and often, while you scold the small faults of others, you are unaware of your own large ones. To escape such ignorance, see to it above all that you are a good <term>perspectivist</term> <note>A specialist in the science of perspective, which Leonardo considered the "rudder" of painting.</note>; thereafter, have complete knowledge of the measurements of man and other animals, and furthermore, be a capable architect—that is, as far as is necessary for the form of buildings and other things that are found upon the earth, whose forms are countless. The more knowledge you have of them, the more praiseworthy your work will be. And those things with which you are not familiar, do not disdain to draw them from nature . . .

And if we are able, regarding men, to truthfully [judge]...

### LII.

### Why in works of importance a man should not rely so much on his memory that he disdains working from nature

That master who would suggest he could keep all the forms and effects of nature stored within himself—certainly, it would seem to me that he is adorned with much ignorance, since the said effects are countless, and our memory is not of such capacity that it would suffice. Therefore, O painter, see to it that the greed for profit does not overcome in you the honor of art, for the gain of honor is much greater than the honor of riches. So that for these and other reasons that could be cited, you will strive first to show to the eye, through a drawing in a suggestive form, the intention and the invention that first arose in your imagination; then proceed by taking away or adding so much that it satisfies you; thereafter, see to it that you improve the people—clothed or naked—in the manner you have arranged them in your work, and ensure that, in proportions and in size, they are subjected to <term>perspective</term> <note>The mathematical system for representing three-dimensional space on a flat surface.</note>,

### LIII. MS. CA. FOL. 122 v. <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 122 verso.</note>
<margin>Resting the eye.</margin>

Just as the body, with great hesitation caused by the length of its contrary movement, returns with a longer path and then gives a stronger blow, while that which is of continuous and short movement has little power; — so in the study of one and the same matter, conducted at long intervals of time, the judgment has perfected itself and better recognizes its error. And the eye of the painter does the same when it moves away from its painting. <note>Leonardo suggests that taking breaks and stepping back physically or mentally allows the artist to see flaws that become "invisible" through constant exposure.</note>

### LIV. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 16 r. <note>Ashburnham Manuscript I, folio 16 recto.</note>
<margin>Which rooms serve the painter best.</margin>

Small rooms or dwellings gather the spirit, and large ones scatter it.

### LV. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 27 v.
<margin>How the painter should live.</margin>

->**On the life of the painter in his studio**<-

So that the comfort of the body does not perhaps damage the prosperity of the spirit, the painter or draftsman <term>Zeichner: one who creates drawings or diagrams</term> should be solitary, and especially when he gives himself over to the observations and reflections which constantly present themselves to the eye and give material to the memory to be well-preserved therein. When you are alone, you are entirely your own, and if you were accompanied by even a single companion, you would belong to yourself only half as much, and even less so the greater the intrusiveness of his company is; and if you are with several, you fall even further into such inconveniences. And should you now wish to say: — "I will act according to my own way; I will keep myself apart in order to better behold the forms of things in nature" —, then I reply, that is simply not possible, because you cannot

And if you said: — "I will keep myself so far apart that their words cannot reach me and cannot disturb me" —, I answer you in this regard that you will be declared a madman. ### LVI. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 2 r. <note>Ashburnham Manuscript I, folio 2 recto.</note>

The mind of the painter should be like a mirror, which always transforms itself into the color of that thing which it has as its object, and fills itself with as many images as there are things placed before it. Therefore you, painter, well aware that you cannot be good if you are not a universal master <term>universaler Meister: an artist capable of depicting everything in the natural world</term> in your ability to imitate with your art all the qualities of the forms produced by nature—which forms you will not know how to create unless you see them and retain them in your memory—when you walk through the fields, strive to turn your judgment toward various objects. Look now at this thing, and then at that, weaving a bouquet, as it were, from the diverse choice things selected from among those of lesser quality. And do not do as many painters do, who, weary in their imagination <term>Phantasie: the creative faculty of the mind</term>, leave their work and go out for pastime to get exercise, yet still carry their mental weariness with them. Because of this, they can see nothing nor take various things into their minds; instead, frequently meeting friends and relatives and being greeted by them, they see and hear so little that it is as if they had encountered nothing but air.

<summary>Leonardo compares the painter's mind to a mirror that must reflect all of nature, emphasizing that a true master must be "universal" and maintain a constant, observant focus even when walking outdoors.</summary>

<header>LVII. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 29 v.</header>
<margin>Representation of Anger.</margin>
### How to represent a person in a state of anger

The person in anger you shall have seizing someone by the hair, turning their head toward the ground and bracing a knee into their flanks. With the right arm, let them shake their fist on high. Their hair should be bristling, the brows low and drawn together, the teeth pressed one against the other, and the two corners of the mouth curved sideways into an arch; the neck, thick and leaning forward as it bends over the enemy, should be full of wrinkles.

---

<header>LVIII. MS. ASH. I. FOL. 29 v.</header>
<margin>Representation of a desperate man.</margin>
### How to represent a desperate man

The desperate man you will have striking himself with a knife. Let him have his clothes torn, and be in the very act of tearing open the wound with one hand. And you will make him with his feet apart and legs somewhat bent, and the whole figure likewise bowed toward the earth, with disheveled and tangled hair.

---

### LX. &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; MS. ASH. I. FOL. 18 v.

# On the manner of representing a night

<margin>How one paints a night.</margin>
That which is entirely deprived of light is total darkness. Since the night is in these circumstances, and you wish to represent a story within it, you shall do it in such a way that, given there is a large fire in this night, everything that is closer to the vicinity of said fire is more clothed in its color; for the thing that is nearer to an object also participates more in its nature. And since you will make the fire lean toward a red color, you shall also make all things illuminated by it reddish; and those which are further removed from that fire must bear more of the black color of the night. The figures that are between you and the fire appear dark in the darkness of the night and not from the brightness of the fire, and those located on the sides should be half dark and half reddish. # LXI.
<margin>Manuscript Ashburnham I, Folio 21 recto. A storm.</margin>

### How one should represent a storm

If you wish to represent a storm well, observe and properly set down its effects when the wind, blowing over the surface of the sea and the earth, stirs up and carries with it whatever is not firmly fixed in the general mass. And to represent this storm rightly, you will first have the tattered and torn-apart clouds driven according to the course of the gale and accompanied by the sandy dust whirled up from the seashore, and by branches and leaves which the power of the wind's fury has lifted up and scattered far in the air, in the company of many other light things. The trees and the herbs, bent to the earth, seem almost to want to follow the direction of the wind, with branches twisted out of their natural position and their foliage ruffled and turned inside out. The people who are present, partly overturned and whirled about by their garments and the dust, should be almost unrecognizable; and those who remain upright may be behind some tree, which they embrace so that the storm does not carry them away; others, with hands before their eyes because of the dust, bent toward the earth, and clothes and

### LXIV.

## The Manner of Representing a Battle

You shall, above all, create the smoke of the artillery <note>original: "Artillerie" - referring to heavy cannons and firearms</note> mixed into the air, together with the dust stirred up by the movement of the horses and combatants. Regarding the mixture you apply: dust, being an earthy and heavy thing, even though it rises easily and mingles with the air due to its fineness, nevertheless tends to fall back down to the depths; the finest parts rise the highest, and therefore they are seen the least and appear almost the color of the air. The smoke, which mixes into the dusty air, appears more like a dark cloud the higher it rises to a certain height, and thus at the very top, one sees the gunpowder smoke more clearly than the dust. The smoke will lean slightly toward blue in its color, and the dust will retain its own color. On the side where the light comes from, this mixture of air, smoke, and dust will appear much more luminous than on the opposite side. The more the combatants are immersed in the midst of this turmoil, the less visible they are, and the smaller the difference becomes between their lights and shadows. You shall make the faces and figures, the cannons, and the arquebusiers <note>term: Arquebusiers - soldiers armed with an early type of long gun called an arquebus</note> together with their surroundings reddish, and this redness fades the further it moves from its cause. The figures that are between you and the light will, because they are distant, appear dark against a bright field; and their legs, the closer they approach the ground, will be seen less, because the dust there is coarser...

<margin>*Studies of the Deluge.*</margin>
### LXV.

### The Deluge and its Representation in Painting

One saw the dark and misty air combated by the course of opposing winds and enveloped by continuous rain and mingled with hail; which winds, now here, now there, carried countless branches of torn plants mixed with an immense quantity of leaves. All around, one saw ancient trees uprooted and shattered by the fury of the storm. One saw the ruins of mountains, their bases already laid bare by the course of their rivers, collapsing in ruins upon those same rivers and damming their valleys; which same rivers, swollen, overflowed their banks and submerged many lands together with their peoples.

Also, upon the heights of the numerous mountains, you could have seen many different species of animals huddled together, full of terror and now finally huddled together in familiarity, in the company of fleeing men and women with their children. And the plains covered with water showed their floods for the most part covered with tables, bedframes, boats, and other various implements which necessity and the fear of death had produced, upon which were women and men together with their mingled children, with the most diverse lamentations and tears, terrified by the

One perceives the movement of the air through the movement of the dust stirred up by the running of the horse; the movement of this dust is as fast in refilling the void it left in the air—which clothed itself in the dust—as the speed of that same horse was in fleeing through said air. And it will perhaps seem to you that you could blame me for having depicted the paths which the movement of the wind made through the air, because the wind in itself is not seen in the air. To this part, it is to be countered that it is not the movement of the wind, but rather the movement of the things it carries, which alone is what one perceives in the air.

### Divisions:

Darkness, wind, sea storm, flood, burning forests, rain, lightning strikes from heaven, earthquakes and landslides, cities leveled to the ground.

### LXVI.

## Description of the Deluge

First, let there be represented the summit of a steep mountain, with several valleys situated around its base, and on its sides, one sees the crust of the earth rising up with the finest roots of small bushes, exposing large portions of the surrounding rocks; the devastating descent of such a landslide; in the fury of its course, let it shake and strip bare the winding and gnarled roots of the great plants and bury them over and over. And the mountains, laid naked, reveal the deep crevices which former earthquakes have produced; and let the base of these mountains be largely covered and clothed with the ruins of the shrubs that have tumbled down from the sides of the high peaks of said mountains, which are mixed with mud, roots, and tree branches, with various leaves mingled into the mud, and earth and stones.

And let the ruins of any mountains have descended into the depths of any valley and formed themselves into a dam for the swollen waters of its river, which dam has already broken, so that it flows out with extraordinarily large waves, the largest of which shake and destroy the walls of the cities and villas of that same valley. And let the ruins of the high buildings of the aforementioned cities stir up great dust; let the water rise in the form of smoke or enveloped clouds into the heights and move against the falling rain. The crests of the waves of the sea descend below their base, battling and rubbing themselves upon the **spherical bubbles** of the surface: and this friction churns the falling water into tiny particles which, transformed into thick mist, mix into the path of the winds in the manner of curling smoke and gathering clouds, and finally rise into the air and become clouds.
