LXVII. <margin>MS. G. FOL. 6 v. *The same.*</margin>

# Representation of the Deluge

The air was dark from the dense rain, which, in its slanted fall, curved by the cross-current of the winds, made waves through the air, no different than one sees the dust do, but with the only difference that such a flood is streaked with lines caused by the tiny drops of water as they descend. But its color was tinted by fire, produced by the lightning—splitters and quarterers of the clouds—whose flames flashed through and opened the great lakes of the filled valleys, which openings in their bellies revealed the bent tops of the trees. And <term>Neptune</term> <note>The Roman god of the sea, often used by Leonardo to personify the power of water.</note> was seen in the midst of the waters with his trident, and one saw <term>Aeolus</term> <note>The ruler of the winds in Greek mythology.</note> with his winds enveloping the floating, uprooted plants, mixed with the infinite waves. The horizon with the entire hemisphere was agitated and set aflame by the glow of the incessant lightning. One saw the people and the birds, who filled the great trees with themselves, left exposed by the receding waves, forming hills which the great <term>water-chasms</term> <note>original: "Wasserschlünde"; refers to deep, devouring whirlpools or abysses.</note> surrounded.

## II.

<margin>It is nowhere mentioned which damaged *Cathedral* *Leonardo* is meant to provide an expert opinion on here.</margin>

My Lords, delegated Fathers, just as it is necessary for doctors, guardians, and nurses of the sick to know what man is, what life is, what health is, and in what way a parity, a concordance of the elements maintains them, and likewise how a discordance of them destroys and annihilates them; and just as he who well knows the aforementioned natures will be better able to restore them than one who is devoid of this knowledge...
You know that medicines, well applied, restore health to the sick; this "well applied" will take place when the doctor, with an understanding of their natures, understands what man is, what life is, what the constitution of the body is, and thus what health is. Knowing these well, he will be well [able to...]

You know of medicines that, when well applied, restore health to the sick, and he who knows them well will apply them well, if he furthermore knows what man is, what life and the <term>constitution of the body</term> <note>original: "Körperbeschaffenheit"</note> are, and what health is; knowing these well, he will also know their opposite: if this is the case, he will be closer to restoring it than anyone else. This same thing is needed by the **ailing Cathedral**, that is, a **medical architect** <note>Leonardo uses the metaphor of the "medico architetto" to suggest that structural failures are like biological diseases.</note> who well understands what a building is, and from which rules correct building originates, and from where these rules are drawn, and into how many parts they are divided, and what the causes are that hold the building together and make it permanent, and what the nature of **weight** <note>original: "Schwere"</note> is, and what the desire of **force** <note>original: "Kraft"</note> is, and in what manner they must be interwoven and connected with one another, and, when united, what effect they will produce. Whoever has true knowledge of the aforementioned things will leave you satisfied by his **reason** <note>original: "rason" / "Vernunft"</note> and work.

Therefore, without disparaging or blackening anyone’s reputation, I shall strive to give satisfaction, partly through reasoning and partly through the work itself, sometimes demonstrating the effects from the causes, and sometimes confirming the reasons through experience, and adorning these with some authority of the **ancient architects**, whose buildings have stood the test and (show) what the reasons for their ruin and their preservation are, etc.

And with this, I shall demonstrate what the first task is, and what and how many the causes are that bring ruin to buildings, and what the nature of their immutability and permanence is.

But in order not to be too long-winded to Your Excellencies...

### III.

High President, recalling to myself often the offers which Your Excellence has made to me several times, I have gathered the confidence to be permitted to write and to recall to the same those promises which I received at the last departure: namely, the possession of those 12 ounces of water <note>original: "12 Unzen Wasser." A measure of water rights for irrigation or power, granted by the King.</note> which were given to me by the Most Christian King <note>Louis XII of France.</note>; Your Lordship knows that I never entered into possession of the same, because at that time when they were gifted to me, there was a lack of water in the canal, both due to the great drought and because of its outlets not yet being regulated; but I was promised by Your Excellence that when such regulation was made, I would have what I expected; hearing now that the canal is repaired, I wrote several times to Your Lordship and to Master <term>Messer<note>An Italian honorific title for a gentleman or person of high standing.</note></term> Girolamo da Cusano, who has the paper with the deed of gift with him; and likewise I wrote to the Corigero and never received an answer. Now I send Salai <note>Gian Giacomo Caprotti, Leonardo’s long-time pupil.</note> there, my student, the bearer of this, to whom Your Lordship will be able to say everything orally that has happened, regarding which matter I petition Your Excellence. I believe I shall be there (in Milan) this Easter, because I am almost at the end of my legal dispute <note>Referring to the inheritance lawsuit with his brothers in Florence.</note>, and I will bring two paintings of Our Dear Lady <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> with me, which I have begun, and in the time I have brought before me, I have brought them into a very good harbor <note>A metaphor meaning he has brought the paintings to a successful state of completion.</note>. Nothing else occurs to me.

His Majesty knows this; what he gives to me, he takes from himself.

But here nothing is taken from the King; rather, it is taken away from the one who has stolen it, because in regulating the mouths which they have widened, the robbers of the water . . . .

If it is said that this is to the detriment of many—this is nothing other than taking back from the thieves what they are obliged to return.

Which matter the <term>Magistrate<note>The governing body or administrative officials in Milan.</note></term> is constantly taking back, through no fault of mine, and it exceeds more than five hundred <term>ounces of water<note>A unit of measurement for the flow of water, used to determine irrigation rights and taxes.</note></term>, and only twelve ounces of water are stabilized for me.

## XV. MS. CA. FOL. 389 r.

I have one who, because he promised himself things from me that are far less than what is proper, and having remained deceived in his arrogant desire, has attempted to take all my friends from me; and because he found them wise and not easily bent to his will, he has threatened me that he would find such accusations that he would rob me of my benefactors; therefore I have informed Your Lordship of this, so that if that man wished to sow the usual scandals, he would find no suitable ground to sow and to harbor the thoughts and actions of his evil nature. So that, if he attempts to make Your Lordship the instrument of his treacherous and wicked nature, he may remain deceived in his wish.

I rejoiced so greatly, my most illustrious Lord, at the long-awaited recovery of your health, that my own ailment has almost fled from me. But I am very sorry that I have not been able to satisfy the wishes of Your Excellency, owing to the malice of that German deceiver, for whom I have left nothing undone that I believed would give him pleasure. And first, besides inviting him to lodge and live with me—by which means I could constantly see the work he was doing and easily correct any errors; and moreover, he would also learn the Italian language, through which he could speak with ease without an interpreter <note>original: "Dolmetsch"</note>; and above all, his money was always given to him ahead of time; in short, it was done. Upon this, his desire was to have the models finished in wood just as they were to be in iron, which he wanted to take back to his homeland. This I refused him, saying that I would give him in a drawing the width, length, thickness, and shape of what he had to make; and so we remained ill-disposed toward one another.

The second matter was that he set up another workshop for himself, with new <term>pincers</term> <note>original: "Kneipzangen," likely specialized metalworking tools</note> and instruments, in the chamber where he slept, and there he worked for others; furthermore, he went to eat breakfast with the Swiss of the Life Guard, where there are idle people, in which matter he surpassed them all; from there he would go away, and most times two or three of them went off with their guns <note>original: "Flinten," early firearms</note> to kill birds among the ancient ruins, and this lasted until evening.

And in this case, I know that I shall acquire not a few enemies, although no one will believe what I might say of him, because there are few of those who are displeased by his vices; on the contrary, such things displease only those men who are by nature against such vices; and many hate their fathers and destroy their friendships when they are rebuked for their vices, and they desire neither examples that are contrary to them, nor any kind of human advice.

And if anyone is found to be good and virtuous, do not drive him away from you; show him honor, so that he does not have to flee from you and confine himself to hermitages, or caves, or other deserted places; and if any such people are found, show them honor, for these are your earthly gods; these deserve statues and images from you. Yet remember well that their images are not to be consumed by you, as is still done in some parts of India; for as soon as these images perform any miracles, according to their opinion, the priests cut them into pieces—since they are made of wood—and give a portion to everyone in the land, not without payment; and each person grinds his share very fine and puts it upon the first food he eats;

Surely, in this case, the human species has reason to envy every other genus of animals; for even if the eagle conquers other birds through power, at least they are not defeated in the swiftness of flight: thus the swallows, with their speed, escape the predation of the thrush; the dolphins, with their rapid flight, escape the predation of the whales and the great sperm whales; but we wretches! ### Description of Mount Taurus and the River Euphrates

->To the Diodar <note>A title for a high-ranking official or lieutenant, likely from the Arabic "Dawadar"</note> of Syria <note>original: "Soria"</note>,<-
->Governor of the holy Sultan of Babylon<-

The new misfortune which has occurred in these western parts of ours—which, I am certain, will inspire horror not only in you but in the entire universe—shall be told to you successively in order, showing first the effect and then the cause.

Finding myself again in these regions of Armenia to carry out with love and zeal that commission for which you sent me, and to make a beginning in those parts which seemed to me best suited for our purpose, I entered the city of Calindra <note>The medieval port of Kelenderis, modern Aydıncık</note> in the neighborhood of our borders.

This city is situated on the shore of that part of Mount Taurus which is split by the Euphrates and looks upon the horns of the great Mount Taurus from the west.

These horns are of such height that it seems as if they touch the sky, because in the universe there is no earthly part that is higher than its summit; and always four hours before daybreak, the rays of the sun from the east strike upon it; and because it is of the whitest stone, it shines brightly and performs the service for these Armenians that a beautiful light of the moon would perform in the middle of the darkness; and by virtue of its great height, it exceeds the highest altitude of the clouds by the space of four miles in a straight line. This summit is [seen] from a great part of the West by...

### Form of the Taurus Mountains

I am not to be accused of laziness by you, O Diodar <note>original: "Diodario"; likely referring to the Devatdar or high official mentioned on the previous page</note>, as your reproaches seem to imply; but the excessive love created by the benefit I hold from you is what has compelled me to seek with the highest zeal and to research with diligence the cause of such a great and astonishing effect, a matter which could not be carried out without time. Now, in order to satisfy you well regarding the cause of such a great effect, it is necessary that I show you the form of the region, and then I will come to the effect, with which, I believe, you will be satisfied . . . .

The matters about which you questioned me are of such a nature that they cannot be well expressed without the passage of time; and mostly because, in order to show the reason for such a great effect, it is necessary to describe the nature of the region in good form, and by means of this, you will then with ease be satisfied regarding the aforementioned inquiry.

I will leave behind the description of the form of Asia Minor and which seas or lands they may be that limit the figure of its quantity <note>The "figure of its quantity" refers to the geographical dimensions and borders of the landmass</note>, because I know that the diligence and zeal of your studies have not left you deprived of such information; I shall only proceed to indicate the true shape of the Taurus, which is the cause of the so amazing and harmful wonder that serves the completion of our project.

This Mount Taurus is that which is described by many as the ridge of the Caucasus Mountains; but since I wished to be well informed, I wanted to speak with some of those who live by the Caspian Sea, who show that, although their mountains bear the same name, these are of greater height, and therefore they affirm that theirs is the true Mount Caucasus, because "Caucasus" in the Scythian language <note>original: "skythischer Sprache"; referring to the ancient nomadic peoples of Central Asia</note> means "highest height." And indeed, there is no report that the Orient <note>The East</note> nor the Occident <note>The West</note> has a mountain of such height; and the proof that this is so is that the inhabitants of the landscapes situated to the west of it see the rays of the sun illuminating a part of its summit until the fourth part of the longest night, and it does the same for those landscapes situated to the east of it.

### XXIX.

After I have often made you a participant through my letters in the things that have happened here, it did not seem right to me to remain silent about a new event that occurred in the past days, which . . . After I have often . . . .

After I have often rejoiced with you through letters over your prospering fortune, I know that you, as a friend, will now grieve with me over the miserable state in which I find myself; and that is, that in the past days I have been in so much worry, fear, danger, and harm, together with these miserable countryfolk <note>original: "Landleute"</note>, that we had cause to envy the dead; and certainly, I do not believe that, since the elements dissolved the great chaos <note>A reference to the classical creation myth where the world emerges from a state of disorder</note> through their separation, they ever united their power—indeed, their fury—to do as much harm to men as has now been seen and experienced by us, so that I cannot imagine what could yet increase such great evils as we have endured in the space of ten hours.

First, we were attacked and warred upon by the impetuosity and fury of the winds, and to this were added the ruins of the great mountains of snow <note>An evocative description of an avalanche</note>, which filled all these valleys and smashed a large part of our city. # IX. ALLEGORICAL NATURAL HISTORY (BESTIARY)

---

## Love of Virtue

<margin>A final revision of the bestiaries so beloved in the Middle Ages. Leonardo's sources are "The Flower of Virtue" <note>original: "Fiore di virtù," a popular 14th-century anonymous work</note>, "The Acerba" <note>original: "L'acerba," an encyclopedic poem by Cecco d'Ascoli</note>, and the Natural History of Pliny the Younger <note>The translator likely means Pliny the Elder, whose Naturalis Historia was the primary source for such lore</note>. However, his material is that which is common to most bestiaries. See Introduction.</margin>
**T**he lark is a bird of which it is said that if it is brought before a sick person, and said sick person is destined to die, this bird turns its head away from him and never looks at him; but if the sick person is to recover, this bird never lets him out of its sight and thus brings it about that every evil is taken from him.

In the same way, the love of virtue never regards a lowly or bad thing, but always joins itself only to honorable and virtuous things and makes its home in noble hearts, just like birds in green forests upon flowering branches. And this same love shows itself more in adversity than in prosperity, acting like light, which shines all the more brightly the darker the place it can find.

## II. Envy

One reads of the vulture that when it sees its young in the nest becoming too fat, it pecks them in the ribs out of envy and keeps them without food.

## III. Cheerfulness

Cheerfulness is attributed to the cock, who rejoices over every small thing and crows with diverse and playful movements.

<summary>This page introduces a series of moral allegories based on animal lore, a common medieval genre known as a bestiary, which Leonardo da Vinci used to illustrate human virtues and vices. It specifically covers the lark as a symbol of virtue, the vulture as envy, and the cock as cheerfulness.</summary>
<keywords>Bestiary, Allegory, Virtue, Leonardo da Vinci, Flower of Virtue, Cecco d'Ascoli, Pliny the Younger, Lark, Vulture, Envy, Cock, Cheerfulness</keywords>

### IV.
## Sadness

Sadness is compared to the raven, which, when it beholds its newborn children to be white, flies away out of great sorrow, abandoning them with loud lamentation; it does not feed them until it sees at least a few black feathers appearing upon them. <note>This reflects a common medieval belief that ravens were born white and only recognized as kin by their parents once their black feathers grew in.</note>

### V.
## Peacefulness

One reads of the beaver that when it is pursued, knowing well that this occurs for the sake of the virtue of its medicinal testicles <note>original: "Testikeln"; referring to castoreum, a secretion used in ancient medicine</note>, as soon as it can no longer flee, it stands still; and, in order to have peace from the hunters, it bites off its own testicles with its sharp teeth and leaves them for its enemies.

### VI.
## Anger

It is said of the bear that when it goes to the houses of the bees to take their honey, the bees begin to sting him; whereupon he leaves the honey and runs to seek revenge. And because he wishes to avenge himself on every one of them that bites him, he avenges himself on none, in such a way that his anger turns into a frenzy; he throws himself upon the ground and, only provoking them further with his hands and feet, defends himself against them in vain.

### VII.
## Gratitude

The virtue of gratitude is said to be especially present in the bird called the hoopoe <note>original: "Wiedehopf"</note>. Recognizing the benefit of life and nourishment received from its father and mother, when it sees them grow old, it makes a nest for them, cherishes them, and feeds them; with its beak, it removes their old and bad feathers and, with the help of certain herbs, restores their...

<summary>This page uses the legendary behaviors of the raven, beaver, bear, and hoopoe to illustrate the moral qualities of sadness, peacefulness, anger, and gratitude. It draws on the "bestiary" tradition where animal traits serve as direct metaphors for human ethics.</summary>

### VIII.
### Avarice

The toad nourishes itself on earth and always remains thin because it never satisfies itself; so great is the fear that this earth might one day fail it. <note>Avarice, or greed, is here depicted as a self-imposed starvation born of the irrational fear of future lack.</note>

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 7 recto</margin>
### IX.
### Ingratitude

Doves are compared to ingratitude; for when they are at the age where they no longer need to be fed, they begin to fight with the father, and this struggle does not end until they have driven the father out and taken his wife from him, making her their own.

### X.
### Cruelty

The basilisk <note>A mythical reptile, often called the king of serpents, said to kill with a single glance.</note> is of such cruelty that, if it cannot kill animals with its poisonous gaze, it turns toward the grasses or herbs and, fixing its gaze upon them, makes them wither.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 7 verso</margin>
### XI.
### Liberality

Of the eagle, it is said that it never has such great hunger that it does not leave a portion of its prey for those small birds that are around it; since these cannot nourish themselves, it is necessary that they be the companions of the eagle; for in this way, they find their bread. <note>Liberality refers to the virtue of being generous or giving freely.</note>

### XII.
### Chastisement

When the wolf prowls with caution around some stall with livestock and by chance sets one foot down wrongly, <note>The text breaks off here, likely continuing with the wolf punishing itself for its own noise or mistake to maintain stealth.</note>

### XIII.
## Flattery or Adulation

The siren sings so sweetly that she lulls the sailors into slumber; then she climbs onto the vessel and kills those who have been put to sleep. <note>The siren is a classical mythological figure used here to warn against the "sweet" but deadly nature of false praise.</note>

### XIV.
## Caution

The ant, by the counsel of its nature, provides for itself in the summer for the winter by killing the collected seed-grain so that it does not sprout again; and from this, when the time comes, it nourishes itself. <note>The "killing" of the grain refers to the ant's habit of biting off the germ of the seed to prevent it from growing in the damp nest.</note>

### XV.
## Folly

The wild bull has directed its hatred toward the color red; therefore, hunters clothe the trunk of a tree in red. That bull charges the trunk and, with great fury, nails its horns into it, whereupon the hunters kill it.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 8 verso</margin>
### XVI.
## Justice

One can compare the virtue of justice to the king of the bees, who arranges and assigns every matter with reason: some bees are commanded to go out for flowers, others are commissioned to work, others to fight with the wasps, others to clear away the refuse, and others to accompany and surround their king. And when he is old and without wings, they carry him; and if one of them neglects its duty, it is punished without mercy. <note>In the Renaissance, the leader of a beehive was thought to be a king rather than a queen.</note>

### XVII.
## Truth

### XVIII.
## Loyalty or Devotion

Cranes are so loyal and devoted to their king that at night, while he sleeps, some go out into the surrounding meadow to keep watch from a distance; others among them stand nearby, each holding a stone in its claw, so that if sleep should overcome them, this stone would fall and make such a noise that they would wake up again. There are others who sleep together in a circle around the king, and they do this every night, taking turns, so that their king may be preserved for them. <note>The image of the crane holding a stone—the "Crane of Vigilance"—was a popular medieval and Renaissance symbol for a watchful leader or guardian.</note>

### XIX.
## Falsehood

The fox, when he catches sight of a flock of magpies, crows, or similar birds, instantly throws himself upon the ground with his mouth open so that he appears dead. Those birds intend to peck out his tongue, and he snaps off their heads.

### XX.
## Deception

The mole has very small eyes and always remains underground; it lives only as long as it stays hidden. As soon as it comes into the light, it dies immediately because it becomes revealed to others. — Thus it is with deception. <note>The original German "Lüge" can mean both a specific lie and the general state of falsehood or deception.</note>

### XXI.
## Strength

The lion is never afraid, but fights with a strong heart in fierce battle against the multitude of hunters, always seeking to attack the one who attacked him first.

### XXII.

## Fear or Cowardice

The hare is always afraid, and the leaves that fall from the trees in autumn keep him constantly in fear and mostly in flight.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 10 recto</margin>
### XXIII.

## Magnanimity

The falcon does not hunt except for large birds, and he would sooner let himself die than nourish himself on small ones, or eat decayed flesh. <note>Magnanimity, or "Großherzigkeit," literally means "great-heartedness." In the chivalric tradition, the falcon represents a noble spirit that refuses to stoop to lowly or "easy" tasks.</note>

### XXIV.

## Vainglory

One reads that the peacock is subject to this vice more than any other animal, because he continually gazes upon the beauty of his tail, spreading it out in the shape of a wheel, and by his screaming draws the gaze of the animals in the vicinity to himself.

And this is the last vice that one can conquer. <note>The idea that pride or vainglory is the "last vice" to be overcome is a common theme in ascetic literature; even when one has conquered physical desires, the pride of having done so remains a trap.</note>

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 10 verso</margin>
### XXV.

## Constancy

The phoenix is compared to constancy, for by its nature it resolves upon its own renewal and steadfastly endures the seething hot flames that consume it, and out of which it is thereafter born anew.

### XXVI.

## Inconstancy

The swallow is set as the symbol for inconstancy, because she is always in motion, so as not to endure the slightest discomfort. <note>Swallows were often associated with the changing seasons and restlessness due to their migratory nature.</note>

### XXVII.

## Incontinence

The camel is the most lustful <note>original: "geilste," which in this historical context refers to being lecherous or driven by animal desire</note> of all animals that exist, and it would go a thousand miles behind a female camel...

XXVIII.

### Intemperance

The unicorn, because of its intemperance <note>original: "Unmäßigkeit," referring here to a lack of moderation or self-control regarding its desires</note> and inability to master itself—in the delight that it finds in young maidens, it forgets its shyness and wildness; setting every suspicion aside, it goes to the seated girl (*maiden*) and falls asleep in her lap; and the hunters, in such a manner they capture it.

XXIX.

### Humility

One sees the principal proof of humility in the sheep, which submits itself to every animal; and if one gives them (sheep) to imprisoned lions for food, they submit themselves to these as if to their own mother, so that, as has often been seen, the lions did not wish to kill them at all.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 11 verso</margin>
XXX.

### Pride

The falcon in its haughtiness and pride wants to rule over and surpass all other birds that go out for prey, and desires always to be alone; and often one has seen the falcon attack the eagle, the king of birds.

XXXI.

### Abstinence

The wild ass, when it goes to the spring to drink and finds the water clouded, will never have such great thirst that it would not abstain from drinking and wait until the water becomes clear.

## XXXII.

### Gluttony

The vulture is so enslaved to its gullet <note>original: "Schlund," referring to the throat or maw, symbolizing insatiable appetite</note> that it would travel a thousand miles to feed upon a corpse, and for this reason, it follows armies.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 12 recto</margin>
## XXXIII.

### Chastity

The turtledove never commits an offense against its mate, and if one of them dies, the other observes eternal chastity; it never again perches upon a green branch and never again drinks clear water. <note>This reflects a common medieval belief that the mourning turtledove seeks out dead branches and muddy water to mirror its grief.</note>

## XXXIV.

### Unchastity

The bat, in its unrestrained unchastity, observes no general rule of pleasure; instead, male with male, female with female, they mate just as they happen to be together by chance.

## XXXV.

### Temperance

The ermine, in its temperance <note>original: "Mäßigkeit," meaning moderation or self-restraint</note>, does not eat more than once a day; and it would sooner let itself be caught by hunters than flee into a filthy den, simply so as not to stain its loveliness <note>original: "Lieblichkeit," here referring to its pure white fur</note>.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 12 verso</margin>
## XXXVI.

### Eagle

The eagle, when it is old, flies so high up that it scorches its feathers, and nature consents that it should be renewed in youth when it falls into shallow water. And if its young cannot endure the sight of the sun, it does not feed them. Let no bird that does not wish to die approach its nest! As much as the animals fear it, it does not harm them; it always leaves them some of its prey.

### XXXVII.
## Lumerpa — Fame
<note>The "Lumerpa" appears to be a legendary bird, likely a corruption of "Lucerpa" or related to the "Ercinee" birds of the Hercynian forest mentioned in medieval bestiaries, which were said to have glowing feathers.</note>

This bird is born in the Near East and shines so brightly that it consumes its own shadows; even in death, it does not lose this light. Its feathers never fall out, yet a feather that is forcibly removed from it no longer shines.

---

### XXXVIII.
<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 13 recto</margin>
## The Pelican

This bird cherishes a great love for its young, and if it finds them killed in the nest by a snake, it likewise pierces its own heart. By bathing them with its flowing blood, it brings them back to life. <note>The pelican "in its piety" is a classic Christian symbol for the sacrifice of Christ and the Resurrection.</note>

---

### XXXIX.
## The Salamander

->The salamander refines its skin in the fire: — this signifies virtue.<-

It has no limbs capable of suffering and cares for no food other than fire; in the flames, it frequently renews its skin. <note>In medieval lore, the salamander was believed to be fireproof, representing the soul that remains unconsumed by the fires of temptation.</note>

---

### XL.
## Chameleon

This creature lives on air, and in this element, it is subject to all birds. To ensure greater safety, it flies above the clouds and finds air so thin that it cannot support any bird that might attempt to follow it. — No one rises to this height unless it is granted to them by heaven — that is to say, no one reaches the place where the chameleon still flies. <note>The author here treats the chameleon as a winged creature of the upper atmosphere, symbolizing spiritual transcendence.</note>

---

### XLI.
<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 13 verso</margin>
## The Fish Alep

The Alep <note>original: "Alep," likely referring to a specific fish or a corruption of a Greek name for a sea creature</note> does not live outside of the water.

### XLII.
## The Ostrich
This creature transforms iron into food; it hatches its eggs by means of its gaze alone. It is considered a symbol for weapons and the nourishment of captains. <note>Medieval lore often claimed the ostrich could digest iron, symbolizing strength and the ability to overcome hardship.</note>

---

### XLIII.
## The Swan
The swan is white, without any blemish, and sings sweetly as it dies, which singing brings its life to an end. <note>The "swan song" is a classic allegory for a peaceful or beautiful death after a virtuous life.</note>

---

### XLIV.
## The Stork
This bird drives evil away from itself by drinking salt water. If it finds its mate guilty <note>likely referring to infidelity</note>, it leaves her; and when the stork is old, its children tend to and nourish it until it dies.

---

### XLV.
<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 14 recto</margin>
## The Cicada
This creature, through its song, makes the cuckoo fall silent; it dies in oil and comes back to life in vinegar; it sings during the glowing heat of summer.

---

### XLVI.
## The Bat
The more light there is, the less this creature sees, and the more it looks at the sun, the blinder it becomes: this stands for vice, which cannot endure where virtue dwells.

---

### XLVII.
## The Partridge
This bird transforms from a female into a male and forgets its former sex; out of envy, it steals the eggs of others and hatches them; but the young birds eventually follow their true mother. <note>This reflects a common medieval belief about the deceptive nature of the partridge, often used as a warning against theft or the subversion of the natural order.</note>

# XLIX.

## The Oyster — stands for Treachery

This creature, when the moon is full, opens itself completely; when the crab notices this, it throws a stone or a splinter inside so that the oyster can no longer close itself. Thus, the oyster becomes the crab's food. So it happens to the mouth that speaks its secret: it becomes a prey to the indiscreet listener.

# L.

## The Basilisk — Cruelty

This creature is fled by all snakes; the weasel, by means of <term>Rue</term> <note>original: "Raute"; a bitter herb used in antiquity as an antidote to poison</note>, fights with it and kills it. — <term>Rue</term> stands for Virtue.

## The Viper

This creature carries sudden death in its teeth, and so as not to hear any magical charms, it stops up its ears with its tail. <note>This refers to the "deaf adder" motif from the Psalms, symbolizing those who refuse to hear spiritual truth.</note>

### LIV.

->The Scorpion<-

Spittle, spat while fasting upon said scorpion, kills it; this is an allegory for the temperance of the palate <note>meaning fasting or self-restraint in eating</note>, which takes away and kills the diseases that depend upon said palate, and opens a path for the virtues.

### LV.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 17 recto</margin>
->The Crocodile — Hypocrisy<-

This animal catches a man and kills him instantly. After it has killed him, it mourns him with a wailing voice and many tears, and when it has finished its lamentation, it cruelly devours him: so does the hypocrite, who fills his face with tears over every small matter, but in his heart shows the tiger, rejoicing in his soul at the misfortunes of others while wearing a compassionate face.

### LVI.

->The Toad<-

The toad flees the light of the sun, and if it is nevertheless held there by force, it bloats itself so much that it hides its head below and withdraws from those rays. So also does he who is an enemy of clear and shining virtue, who stands before it only by force and with a puffed-up spirit.

### LVII.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 17 verso</margin>
<margin>This allegory is likely without an older model.</margin>
->The Caterpillar<-
->Of Virtue in general.<-

The caterpillar, through its diligent study, full of wonderful craftsmanship and the most delicate labor to weave its new house around itself, then emerges from it with painted and beautiful wings and soars with them toward heaven. <note>Leonardo uses the metamorphosis of the caterpillar into a butterfly as a rare positive allegory for the soul's refinement through work and virtue.</note>

### LVIII. The Spider

The spider produces from itself the artistic and masterfully crafted web, which yields to it the captured prey as its profit.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 18 recto</margin>
### LIX. The Lion

This animal, with its thunder-like roar, wakes its young on the third day after their birth and instructs all their slumbering senses: and all the wild animals that are in the forest flee. <note>In medieval bestiaries, the lion cub was said to be born dead and brought to life after three days by the father's breath or roar, a common allegory for the Resurrection of Christ.</note>

This can be compared to the children of virtue, who wake up at the call of praises and promote those honorable studies through which they are raised ever higher. And all the wicked flee at this call, separating themselves from the virtuous.

Furthermore, the lion covers its tracks so that its journey may not be guessed by its enemies. This serves a commander well: to hide the secrets of his inner mind so that the enemies do not know his movements.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 18 verso</margin>
### LX. The Tarantula

The bite of the tarantula keeps a person fixed in their purpose—that is, in whatever they were contemplating when they were bitten. <note>A reference to the folk belief that the venom of the tarantula froze the victim's mental state or compelled them to a specific behavior, often cured by dancing.</note>

### LXI. The Long-eared Owl or the Little Owl

These punish those who fight with them by robbing them of their eyesight; for so it has been arranged by nature, so that they may feed themselves.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 19 recto</margin>
### LXII. The Elephant

The great elephant has by nature what is rarely found among men: namely honesty, prudence, and equity.

## LXIV.
## The Lindworm
<note>original: "Lindwurm." A legendary serpentine monster, often depicted as a wingless dragon or giant serpent.</note>

The Lindworm is a very large beast; if it sees any bird in the air, it draws its breath in so strongly that it pulls the birds into its mouth. Marcus Regulus, the consul of the Roman army, was attacked with his army by such a beast and almost destroyed. This beast, having been killed by a siege engine <note>likely a ballista or catapult</note>, was measured at 123 feet long, which is 64 and a half cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length based on the forearm</term>. It rose with its head above all the trunks of a forest.

## LXV.
## The Boa

This is a large adder that wraps itself around the feet of a cow so that she cannot move; it then milks her in such a way that it almost dries her out. Of this species, one was killed on the Vatican Hill <note>original: "Mons Vaticanus"</note> during the time of the Emperor Claudius,
<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 21 verso</margin>
which had an entire child in its belly, whom it had swallowed down.

## LXVI.
## The Elk is Caught in Sleep
<note>original: "Elentier." Historically referring to the Moose or Elk.</note>

This animal is born on the island of Scandinavia; it has the form of a large horse, except that the great length of its neck and ears differ from it. It grazes in the grass moving backward, because its upper lip is so long that if it grazed moving forward, the lip would cover the grass. Its legs are made of a single piece <note>A common medieval myth that elks had no joints in their legs and could not kneel</note>; therefore, when it wants to sleep, it leans against a tree. The hunters, foreseeing the accustomed place for sleeping, saw through almost the entire trunk; when the animal then leans against it while sleeping, it falls over because of its sleep. ### LXVII.
### The Bison harms through flight

This is born in Pannonia <note>A province of the Roman Empire, primarily in modern-day Hungary and parts of Austria</note>; it has a neck with a mane like a horse; in all other parts it is similar to a bull, except that its horns are curved backward in such a way that it cannot gore, and therefore it has no other recourse than flight, in which it flings its dung over a distance of 400 cubits <term>cubit: an ancient measurement of roughly 18 inches</term> along its path: which, wherever it lands, burns like fire.

### Lions, Leopards, Panthers, Tigers

These keep their claws in a sheath and never reveal them, except against prey or an enemy.

### LXIX.
### The Lioness

When the lioness defends her young against the hands of the hunters, she lowers her eyes to the ground so as not to be frightened by the spears, so that her children do not become captives as a result of her fleeing.

This animal, so fearsome, fears nothing so much as the rattling of empty wagons and likewise the song of the rooster; he also greatly fears the sight of it, and with anxious expressions he observes its comb and becomes very despondent if one covers his face.

### LXXII.

->Camels<-

Those from Bactria <note>An ancient region in Central Asia, modern-day Afghanistan and Uzbekistan</note> have two humps, the Arabian ones have one; they are nimble in battle and extremely useful for carrying loads. This animal is highly precise in observing rule and measure, for it does not move if it has more weight than usual, and if it is expected to travel further than its custom, it does the same; it stops immediately, thereby forcing the merchants to halt.

### LXXIV.
### Catoblepas (Gnu)

This is born in Ethiopia, near the source of the Niger <note>original: "Nigricapo", likely referring to the headwaters of the Niger River</note>; it is a creature of no great size, is sluggish in all its limbs, and has a head of such weight that it carries it only with great effort, so that it is always bent toward the ground: otherwise, it would be the worst plague for mankind, for whosoever is glimpsed by its eyes dies instantly.

---

### LXXV.
### The Basilisk

This is born in the province of Cyrenaica <note>An ancient Greek and later Roman province in modern-day Libya</note> and is no larger than twelve inches and has a white spot on its head like a diadem <note>a crown or headband</note>. With its hiss, it puts all snakes to flight. It bears a resemblance to the adder, but does not move in coils, but rather straight forward from its middle. It is said that if one is killed with a spear by someone on horseback, its venom runs up along the spear, yet it does not kill the man, but the horse. It harms the grain, and not only that which it touches, but also wherever it breathes; the grass withers, and the stones burst.

---

### LXXVI.
### The Weasel

This creature, when it finds the den of the basilisk, kills it by the scent of its sprayed urine; the odor of which urine even many times kills the weasel itself.

### LXXVII.

## The Horned Viper

These have four small, movable horns; therefore, when they wish to eat, they hide their entire person beneath the leaves, except for these little horns. They move these horns so that they appear to birds like little worms at play, which causes the birds to swoop down immediately to peck at them. Then, the viper suddenly entwines them in its coils and thus devours them.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 25 recto</margin>

### LXXVIII.

## The Two-Headed Serpent — <term>Amphisbaena</term> <note>From the Greek 'amphis', meaning both ways, and 'bainein', to go; a legendary ant-eating serpent with a head at each end.</note>

This creature has two heads, one in the correct place and the other in the tail, as if it were not enough for the venom to be sprayed from a single location.

### LXXIX.

## The Javelin-Snake

This snake perches upon the trunks of trees and hurls itself like a javelin <note>original: "Pfeilschlange", literally 'arrow-snake'</note>, piercing wild animals and killing them.

### LXXX.

## <term>Asp</term> (Uraeus Cobra) <note>The 'Aspis' was often identified in antiquity with the Egyptian Cobra, used as a symbol of royalty (the Uraeus) on the crowns of Pharaohs.</note>

The bite of this animal cannot be healed, except by the immediate cutting away of the bitten parts. This most pestilential animal has such an affection for its mate that they always travel in company; thus, if one of them is unfortunately killed, the other follows the killer with incredible speed. It is so zealous and intent upon revenge that it conquers every difficulty and overtakes every army. It seeks only to harm its enemy and overcomes any distance; one cannot escape it except by crossing water or by a most hurried flight. It has its eyes deep within, and large ears, and is guided more by hearing than by sight.

LXXXI. MS. H. I. FOL. 25 v.

## The Ichneumon <note>The Egyptian Mongoose, famous in antiquity for its supposed ability to slay crocodiles and cobras.</note>

This animal is a deadly enemy to the Uraeus snake <note>The Egyptian Cobra</note>; it is born in Egypt and, whenever it sees an asp near its dwelling, it immediately runs to the river sand or the mud of the Nile and smears itself entirely with it. Then, having dried in the sun, it smears itself with mud again, and so, drying one layer over the other, it makes itself three or four coats, like a suit of armor. Afterward, it attacks the asp and fights it well, so that, seizing the right moment, it leaps into its throat and kills it.

### LXXXII.

## The Crocodile

This creature is born in the Nile, has four feet, and does harm on water and on land; also, no earthly animal is found without a tongue except for this one, and it bites only by moving its upper jaw. It grows up to 40 feet, is provided with claws, and is armed with a leathery skin that resists every blow. During the day it stays on the land, and at night in the water. Feeding itself on fish, it falls asleep on the banks of the Nile with an open mouth, and the bird called

MS. H. I. FOL. 26 r.

<margin>The Trochilus, or hummingbird, is confused here with the Egyptian Plover, a bird of the plover genus that constantly hops around on the crocodile, picking maggots, leeches, etc., out of its skin, and even taking morsels from its mouth.</margin>
Trochilus, a tiny little bird, immediately runs into its mouth and, hopping around between its teeth, goes back and forth picking away the leftover food. While it thus picks at the teeth with pleasurable delight, it invites the crocodile to open its mouth fully, and so the beast falls asleep. When the Ichneumon sees this, it immediately plunges into the crocodile's gullet and, after it has pierced through the stomach and the intestines, it finally kills the same.

## LXXXIII.

### The Dolphin

Nature has granted animals such understanding that, besides knowing what is to their own advantage, they also possess knowledge of their enemy's disadvantage; therefore, the dolphin understands the value of a cut from the sharp fins located on its back, and how very tender the belly of the crocodile is. Thus, when they fight one another, it throws itself beneath its opponent, slices open its belly, and kills it in this manner.
The crocodile is terrifying to those who flee from it, and most cowardly toward those who hunt it.

<margin>Manuscript H. I. Folio 26 verso</margin>

## LXXXIV.

### The Hippopotamus

This creature, when it feels itself burdened <note>Likely referring to an excess of blood or "humors," a common medieval medical concept</note>, goes to seek thorns or places where the stumps of cut reeds are found, and rubs a vein against them until it cuts it open. After it has let out as much blood as is necessary, it smears itself with river mud and heals the wound. It has nearly the form of a horse, with a cloven hoof, a curled tail, and the teeth of a boar, with a mane upon its neck; its skin is impenetrable, except when it bathes. It feeds on grain; it enters the fields walking backward, so that it appears as though it has walked out.

## LXXXV.

### The Ibis

This bird bears a resemblance to the crane and, when it feels itself to be sick, it fills its crop with water and, with its beak, gives itself a clyster <note>An enema; a common myth in ancient natural history used to explain the bird's long, curved beak</note>.

## LXXXVI.

### The Stag

This animal, when it feels it has been bitten by the spider called the harvestman <note>original: "Weberknecht"</note>, eats crayfish and frees itself from such poison.

### LXXXVII.
->The Lizard<-

This creature, when it fights with snakes, eats the sow-thistle <note>original: "Saudistel"; Sonchus oleraceus, believed in folklore to be an antidote to venom</note> and frees itself from the poison.

### LXXXVIII.
->The Swallow<-

This bird restores sight to its blinded young using the juice of the Celandine <note>original: "Chalidonia"; from the Greek 'chelidon' for swallow. It was a common medieval belief that swallows used this yellow-flowered herb to heal their chicks' eyes</note>.

### LXXXIX.
->The Weasel<-

This animal, when it hunts rats, eats rue <note>original: "Raute"; a bitter herb used as a disinfectant and believed to protect against toxins</note> beforehand.

### XC.
->The Wild Boar<-

This creature heals its ailments by eating ivy.

### XCI.
->The Snake<-

This creature, when it wishes to renew itself, casts off its old skin, beginning at the head; it completes the change in one day and one night.

### XCII.
->The Panther<-

This animal, even when its entrails are already hanging out, continues to fight with dogs and with hunters.

<header>MS. H. I. FOL. 27 v.</header>

### XCIII.
->The Chameleon<-

This creature always takes on the color of the object upon which it sits; therefore, along with the foliage on which they sit, they are often consumed by elephants.

### XCIV.
->The Raven<-

This bird, when it has killed a chameleon, purges itself with laurel <note>original: "Lorbeer"; used here as a medicinal cleanser to counteract the perceived toxicity of the chameleon</note>.

# X. FABLES

<margin>Paper and Ink.</margin>
R. 1322, MS. S. K. M. III. FOL. 66 v. <note>Reference to the Forster Manuscript III in the South Kensington Museum, now the Victoria and Albert Museum.</note>
**T**he paper, seeing itself completely soiled by the dark blackness of the ink, complains about it; the ink, however, shows the paper that the words composed upon it are the very reason for its preservation. <note>A metaphor for how the "stain" of wisdom or art grants immortality to an otherwise fragile material.</note>

<margin>Of Water.</margin>
R. 1271, MS. S. K. M. III. FOL. 93 v.
II.
The water, finding itself in the proud sea, its own element, was seized by the desire to rise up into the air. Encouraged by the element of fire and raised up as a fine vapor, it seemed almost as thin as the air itself. Having risen to a great height, it reached the even thinner and colder air, where it was abandoned by the fire; and the tiny particles, pressed together, united and became heavy. As it fell, its pride turned into flight, and it dropped from the sky, only to be swallowed up by the dry earth, where, imprisoned for a long time, it did penance for its sin.

<margin>The Flame and the Candle.</margin>
MS. CA. FOL. 67 r. <note>Reference to the Codex Atlanticus.</note>
III.
The flames, which had already endured for a month in the glass furnace, saw a candle approaching in a beautiful and shining candlestick. They strove with great longing to reach it. Among them, one flame—leaving its natural course and drawing itself through a hollow firebrand from which it fed—emerged through a small crack at the other end. It threw itself upon the candle that was so near, and with the utmost greed and gluttony, began consuming it,

<term>Fables (Fabeln)</term>: Short stories, typically with animals or inanimate objects as characters, conveying a moral lesson.
<term>Glass furnace (Glasofen)</term>: A high-temperature oven used for melting the raw materials to make glass; a common sight in the workshops of Leonardo's time.
<term>Preservation (Erhaltung)</term>: Here referring to the survival of the physical object through the value of the information recorded on it.

<summary>This page presents three moral fables by Leonardo da Vinci concerning the vanity of elements and objects, specifically focusing on the relationship between paper and ink, the pride of water, and the destructive greed of a flame.</summary>
<keywords>fables, allegory, Leonardo da Vinci, morality, elements, pride, preservation, nature</keywords>

brought itself almost to its end; and while it wished to help prolong its existence, it strove in vain to return to the furnace from which it had departed, but was forced to die and waste away along with the candle, where finally, with weeping and remorse, it turned into insufferable smoke, while all its sisters remained behind in shining and long life and beauty.

# IV.

<margin>Those who humble themselves shall be exalted.</margin>
There was, fixed upon the peak of a rock, a very tiny bit of snow, which was placed upon the extreme height of an enormous mountain; and gathering its imagination within itself, it began to contemplate with that imagination and to say in its heart: "Now, must I not be judged as something haughty and proud, that I, a tiny little particle of snow, have set myself in such a high place? And is it to be endured that such a quantity of snow as can be seen from here below me should remain lower down? Surely, my small quantity does not deserve such height; for I may well have to experience, as a witness to my small stature, what the sun did yesterday to my companions, who were destroyed by the sun in a few hours; and that came upon them because they had placed themselves higher than was proper for them. I wish to flee the wrath of the sun and humble myself, and find a place that fits my smallness." — And after it had hurled itself down and begun the descent, rolling from the high banks over the other snow—the deeper the place it sought, the more its quantity grew, so that when it had finished its course, it found itself of almost no less size upon a hill than the hill that carried it; and it was the last which was dissolved by the sun in 그 summer. For those it is said, who humble themselves; they shall be exalted. <note>A reference to the biblical proverb from Luke 14:11: "For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted."</note>

<term>Vocabulary: Snow, Sun, Humility, Imagination, Rock, Exaltation, Humiliation, Parable</term>

<summary>This page concludes the fable of the greedy flame and presents a moral allegory about a snowflake that finds safety and greatness through humility. Leonardo uses these natural metaphors to warn against pride and advocate for a modest, self-aware life.</summary>

<margin>The Stone.</margin>
### V.

A stone, only recently uncovered by the water and of a beautiful size, was situated upon a certain elevated place where a delightful little grove ended, above a road strewn with fragments of rock, in the company of herbs which were adorned by various blossoms in manifold colors; and it saw the great multitude of stones that were gathered together on the road situated beneath it. The desire came upon it to let itself fall down there, saying to itself: "What am I doing here among these herbs? I wish to dwell in company with these, my siblings." — And, after it had let itself fall down, it ended the speed of its course among the desired companions. And having been there scarcely a little while, it began to be in incessant distress from the wheels of the wagons, from the feet of the iron-shod horses and the travelers; this one turned it over, that one ground against it; many a time it raised itself a little bit when it was covered by mud or by the filth of some animal, and in vain it gazed at the place from which it had come, the place of solitary and quiet peace. So it happens to those who wish to come away from the still and contemplative life into the city, among people full of infinite evils.

---

Certainly not! May it not please the gods that such brilliant beauty should fall into such lowli—

...pleasure the gods that I should fall back into such baseness of mind! What madness it would be that would lead me to shave the lathered beards of rustic village folk and perform such mechanical labor! Is this a body for such exercise? Truly not. I wish to hide myself in some secret place and there spend my life in quiet repose."
— And so, after it had been hidden for some months, it returned one day to the air, and leaving its sheath, it saw itself transformed into the likeness of a rusting saw, and its surface no longer reflected the shining sun. With vain regret, it wept in theater for the irreparable damage, saying to itself: — "Oh, how much better it was to practice my now-lost edge of such fineness at the barber's! Where is the shining surface now? Surely, the troublesome and loathsome rust has consumed it!"
— This same thing happens to those minds which, in exchange for exercise, surrender themselves to idleness: who, in likeness to the aforementioned razor, lose their cutting keenness, and the rust of ignorance spoils their form. <note>Leonardo uses the metaphor of the razor to warn that intellectual talents wither without constant use.</note>

# XVI.
->Codex Atlanticus, Folio 67 recto<-

<margin>The Laurel, the Myrtle, and the Pear Tree.</margin>
The Laurel and the Myrtle, seeing the Pear Tree being hewn down, cried out with a loud voice: “O Pear Tree! Where are you going? Where is that pride you possessed when your fruits were beautifully ripe? Now you will no longer provide us shade with your thick tresses!” — Then the Pear Tree answered: — “I go with the peasant who cuts me down and takes me to the workshop of an excellent sculptor; through his art, he will cause me to take the form of the god Jupiter, and I shall be dedicated to the temple and worshipped by men in place of <term>Jove</term> <note>original: "Jovis" - the Latin genitive or archaic form for Jupiter, the king of the gods</note>. But as for you, prepare yourselves to be frequently mutilated and stripped of your branches, which shall be wound all around me by men in order to honor me.”

# XVII.
->Codex Atlanticus, Folio 67 recto<-

<margin>False brilliance leads to destruction.</margin>
The vain and flighty moth, not content with being able to fly comfortably through the air and overcome by the charming flame of the candle, resolved to fly into it; and its joyful movement became the cause of sudden sorrow. When its delicate wings were consumed in said light, the butterfly, wretched and entirely burnt, fell to the foot of the candlestick.

<margin>The Chestnut and the Fig Tree.</margin>
### XVIII.

The Chestnut tree, seeing the man atop the Fig tree, how that man bent the branches toward himself and plucked the ripe fruits from them — which he then put into his open mouth and mangled and tore apart with hard teeth — shaking its long branches, said with an agitated rustling: — 
> “O Fig tree! how much less are you indebted to Nature than I! Do you see how she arranged my dear children within me, closed away, first dressed in a delicate shirt, over which the hard and lined rind is placed; and as if she were not satisfied with heaping such goodness upon me, she even built them a strong habitation and established sharp and dense thorns upon it, so that the hands of men cannot harm me?”

— Then the Fig tree, along with its children, began to laugh, and when the laughter ended, it said: — 
> “Know that man is of such a spirit that, with rods and stones and branches, he well understands how to pull you down from your boughs, to make you poor of fruit, and when these have fallen, he stamps upon them with feet and with stones, so that your fruits come out of their <term>armed house</term> <note>original: "gewappneten Hause" - referring to the prickly chestnut burr</note> torn and mutilated; whereas I am touched with all diligence by hands, and not like you, by sticks and by stones.”

### XXV. MS. CA. FOL. 67 r.

<margin>*The Donkey.*</margin>
The donkey, who had fallen asleep on the ice of a deep lake; his warmth caused that very ice to melt, and underwater, to his own detriment, he woke up and immediately drowned.

### XXVI. MS. CA. FOL. 67 r.

<margin>*The Ant and the Grain of Millet.*</margin>
When the ant found a grain of millet, the grain, feeling itself seized by the former, cried out: — "If you will grant me the great fortune of allowing me to fulfill my desire to be born <note>The grain refers to the process of germination and growth</note>, I will give back to you a hundred of my own self." — And so it also happened.

### XXVII. MS. H. II. FOL. 51 v.

<margin>*Oyster, Rat, and Cat.*</margin>
The oyster, which along with the other fish had been unloaded at the fisherman's house near the sea, begs the rat to lead it to the water. The rat, having formed the intention to eat it, causes it to open up, and as he bites it, the oyster clamps down on his head and holds him fast. Along comes the cat and kills them both.

### XXVIII. MS. CA. FOL. 76 r.

<margin>*The Falcon and the Duck.*</margin>
The falcon, unable to endure with patience the game of hide-and-seek that the duck plays with him when she flees from him and goes under the water, wanted to do as she did and pursue her beneath the surface; however, having soaked his feathers, he remained stuck in that same water, and the duck, rising into the air, mocked the falcon as he drowned.

### XXIX. MS. CA. FOL. 117 r.

<margin>*The Thrushes.*</margin>
The thrushes <note>original: "Krammetsvögel," specifically fieldfares or song thrushes</note> rejoiced greatly when they saw that the man caught the little owl and took away its freedom, binding it with strong ties by its feet. This owl then, by means of birdlime <note>A sticky substance spread on branches to trap birds</note>, became the cause for the thrushes to lose not just their freedom, but life itself. — Told for those regions that rejoice to see their masters lose their freedom.

<margin>The Dog and the Flea.</margin>
### XXX. MS. CA. FOL. 119 r.

The dog was sleeping on the skin of a wether <note>A castrated ram; the "fleece of a sheep."</note>. One of his fleas, sensing the smell of the oily wool, judged that this must be a place of better living and safer from the teeth and claws of the dog than feeding upon the dog himself; and without another thought, he left the dog. And, having entered between the thick wool, he began with the greatest effort to try to penetrate to the roots of the hairs; which investigation he found to be in vain after much sweat, because such hairs were so frequent that they almost touched one another, and there was no space where the flea was able to taste of that same skin. Wherefore, after long distress and plague, he began to want to return to his dog, who had already run away, so that he was forced, after long repentance and bitter tears, to die of hunger.

<margin>Cat, Weasel, and Mouse.</margin>
### XXXI. MS. CA. FOL. 67 r.

The mouse was besieged in her tiny dwelling by the weasel, who with constant vigilance was intent upon her destruction, and through a small crack she observed her great danger. Meanwhile, the cat came, and immediately she caught the weasel and had devoured it at once. The mouse hereupon, after she had offered a sacrifice to Jove <note>original: "Jovi," the Roman king of the gods</note> with several of her hazelnuts, thanked her deity exceedingly and went out of her hole to truly enjoy the freedom she had thought lost; of which she was immediately robbed, together with her life, by the cruel claws and teeth of the cat.

### XXXVI. MS. CA. FOL. 116 v.

<margin>The Flame and the Kettle (Draft).</margin>
A little fire, which remained in a small coal among the lukewarm ashes, nourished itself miserably and poorly from the little moisture <note>original: "Saft" (juice/sap); referring to the residual energy or volatile matter in the coal</note> that was left in it. When the kitchen maid <note>original: "Verwalterin der Küche" (manager of the kitchen)</note> appeared here to use it for her usual cooking duties, and after she had placed the wood in the hearth and—with a sulfur match <note>A "Schwefelfaden" or sulfur-thread was an early method of catching a spark to start a fire</note>—reawakened a small flame from that which was almost dead, and fanned this among the arranged logs and set the kettle over it, she went away again in full security without any other suspicion. The fire then, rejoicing in the wood lying above it, began to rise, chasing the air through the gaps of those same logs, between which it worked itself in a playful and joyful passage. It had already begun to shimmer out of the intervals of the wood, from which it had made for itself merry windows, and thrusting out glowing and reddish sparkling flames, it suddenly drove away the black darkness of the closed kitchen; and full of joy, the now-grown flames played with the air surrounding them, and singing with a gentle hum, it created a sweet sound . . .

## XLII.
<meta>MS. L. FOL. 72 v.</meta>

Flax is consecrated to death and to the decay of mortals—to death through the snares and nets for birds, beasts, and fish; to decay through the linen cloths in which one wraps the corpses when they are buried, and which rot within such linens.

And furthermore, flax does not separate from its fibers unless it begins to rot and decay; and with this, one should wreathe and adorn funeral processions. <note>Leonardo highlights the irony that flax, which provides the shroud for the dead, must itself undergo a process of "retting" or rotting in water to become usable.</note>

Now it happened that this friar, finding himself in the middle of the river, also remembered his own Rule <note>The monastic rules governing the conduct of friars, which often forbade the touching of money</note>, and stopping still like Saint Christopher, he raised his head toward the one weighing upon him: — “Tell me a little, do you have any money on you?” — “You know well that I do,” he answered; “how else do you think a merchant of my standing would travel about?” — “Oh dear!” said the friar; “our Rule forbids us from carrying any money on our person” — and he suddenly threw him into the water. When the merchant realized what had happened—namely, that the insult he had previously given had been avenged with a joke—he endured this revenge with an amiable laugh, peacefully, and half-blushing with shame.

## II.

<margin>A painter to a priest.</margin>
A priest, who was walking through his parish on Holy Saturday <note>The day before Easter</note> and, as is the custom, was sprinkling holy water in the houses, entered the room of a painter. When he splashed the water onto some of his pictures, the painter turned around somewhat angrily and asked why he was splashing his paintings so. To this the clergyman replied that it was the custom and his duty to do so, and that he was doing a good deed; and whoever does good should expect good and better in return, for so God promised, and that for every good thing one does on earth, one will receive a hundredfold from above. The painter, waiting for the priest to leave, went up to the window and poured a large bucket of water over the priest's head, saying: — “There, now you receive from above a hundredfold for everything, just as you said it would happen for the good you did me with your holy water, with which you have half-ruined my paintings.”

<note>Technical vocabulary from the original: Friar, wooden sandals, St. Christopher, merchant, Holy Saturday, holy water, painter, priest, hundredfold, revenge.</note>

### III. MS. CA. FOL. 76 r.

<margin>A quick retort.</margin>
A certain man said that his homeland produced the strangest things in the world. The other replied: — “You, having been born there, confirm this by the strangeness of your own ugly presence.”

### IV. MS. M. FOL. 58 v.

<margin>A Pythagorean outdone.</margin>
When a man wished to prove, by the authority of <term>Pythagoras</term><note>The ancient Greek philosopher who taught the doctrine of metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls into new bodies after death.</note>, how he had been in the world on other occasions, and someone would not let him finish his reasoning, the former said to the latter: — “And as proof that I am here for a second time: I remember that you were a miller back then.” — This man, feeling stung by these words, then confirmed that it was true, and that as a counter-sign he remembered in turn that this same fellow had been the donkey who carried the flour for him at that time.

### V. MS. M. FOL. 58 v.

<margin>A jest.</margin>
A painter was asked why, given that he made his figures so beautiful—which were but dead things—for what reason had he made his children so ugly. To this the painter replied that he made his paintings by day, but he made his children by night.

### VI. MS. CA. FOL. 306 v.

<margin>A true friend.</margin>
Someone ceased his association with one of his friends because the latter frequently spoke ill to him of his own friends. This man, having been abandoned by his friend, complained to him one day and, after much lamenting, begged him to say what the cause was that had made him forget such a great friendship. To which the other replied: — “I no longer wish to associate with you because I wish you well; and I do not want it to happen that, when you tell others evil things about me, your friend, these others should receive a bad impression of you as I have, because you [speak ill] of me, your friend...”

### XI. MS. CA. FOL. 76 r.

<margin>A ready-witted answer.</margin>
A man said to his acquaintance: — “Your eyes have changed into a strange color.” — The other replied that this happened to him often; “but you have paid no attention to it.” — “And when does it happen to you?” — The other retorted: — “As often as my eyes see your strange face; through the force that such great displeasure inflicts upon them, they turn pale and change into such a strange color.”

### XII. MS. TR. FOL. 40 v.

<margin>A fine lesson.</margin>
An old man publicly mocked a youth, boldly showing that he did not fear him, whereupon the youth replied to him that his advanced age was a better shield for him than his tongue or his strength. <note>The youth implies he refrains from violence only out of respect for the man's frailty, not out of weakness.</note>

### X.

### Of beaten walnut trees

Those who have done the best will be beaten the most, and their children will be taken away from them, or their skins will be peeled or torn off, and they will be broken and their bones crushed. <note>This refers to the harvesting of walnuts, where the tree is beaten with poles to drop the fruit, which is then husked and cracked.</note>

### Of sculptures

## XII.

### Of sold crucifixes

I see the crucified Christ being sold anew and his saints martyred. <note>Leonardo refers to the trade in religious art and icons, where the image of the passion is treated as a mere commodity.</note>

### Of the doctors who live off the sick

Men will fall into such wretchedness that they will take it as a grace when others triumph over their ills.

Or over the loss of their true wealth, which is health. <note>A cynical observation that a doctor's success and livelihood depend entirely on the misfortune and physical decay of their patients.</note>

### Of the religion of the monks who live off their long-deceased saints

Those who have died, after a thousand years, will be the ones who sustain many of the living. <note>Refers to the monastic orders supported by the legacies, relics, and reputations of saints who died centuries prior.</note>

### Of the stones that are turned into lime and from which prisons are built

Many things that were destroyed by fire before this time will rob many men of their freedom. <note>Lime is produced by burning limestone in a kiln; this lime is then used for mortar to build the stone walls of dungeons.</note>

<margin>Manuscript J. Folio 67 recto</margin>
## XIII.

### Of children who are nursed

Many a Francis, Dominic, and Benedict will eat that which was eaten by others nearby at other times, and will remain so for many months before he can speak. <note>A riddle describing infants named after great saints who consume breast milk—nutrients derived from the food their mothers have already eaten.</note>

### Of mussels and snails, which, rejected by the sea, will rot in their shells

How many are there who rot away dead in their own houses and fill the surroundings with a foul stench. <note>A comparison between the literal decay of shellfish on a beach and the isolation of people who die alone in their homes.</note>

### XXIV.

->Of the beaten donkeys<-

O thoughtless Nature, why have you made yourself so partial, being to some of your children a merciful and kind mother, but to others a most cruel and pitiless stepmother? I see your children given into the bondage of others without ever receiving any benefit; and instead of a reward for services rendered, they are paid with immense tortures, and they must always spend their lives for the profit of their oppressors. <note>Leonardo frequently expressed deep empathy for beasts of burden, viewing their exploitation as a violation of natural justice.</note>

### XXV.

->Of cats that eat mice<-

In you, cities of Africa, your own natives shall be seen torn to pieces in their own houses by the most cruel and rapacious animals of your country. <note>The "natives" are mice, and the "rapacious animals" are domestic cats; Leonardo uses the grand language of a traveler's tragedy to describe a common household occurrence.</note>

### XXVI.

->Of bees<-

And from many others, their stores and their food shall be taken away, and they shall be cruelly drowned and destroyed by men without reason. O Justice of God! Why do you not awake to see your creatures so ill-treated? <note>This refers to the practice of smoking out hives or drowning bees to harvest their honey.</note>

### XXVII.

->Of ants<-

There shall be many communities who will hide themselves and their children and their provisions within dark caverns; and here, in these gloomy places, they will feed themselves and their families for many months without any other light, whether artificial or natural.

### XXVIII.

->Of nuts, olives, acorns, chestnuts, and the like<-

Many children, beaten by wicked hands, shall be torn from the arms of their own mothers, thrown to the ground, and then mangled. <note>The "children" are the fruits or nuts, and the "beating" refers to the method of harvesting them by striking the tree branches with poles.</note>

### XXXII.
<meta>MS. CA. FOL. 145 r.</meta>

->Of food that becomes alive<-

A great part of animated bodies will pass through the bodies of other beings; that is, uninhabited houses will pass in pieces through inhabited houses, giving them something useful and carrying away their waste: that is to say, the life of man is sustained by the things he eats, which take with them that part of man which has died. <note>A philosophical observation on metabolism; the "uninhabited houses" are the carcasses of animals or plants (meat/vegetables) being consumed by the "inhabited houses" (living humans).</note>

### XXXVI. R. 1297, MS. BR. M. FOL. 42 v.

The water which has fallen from the clouds, while still in motion over the slopes of the mountains, will remain for a long time without moving in any way; and this will happen in many and various provinces.

<note>This riddle refers to snow or ice, which is water "in motion" as it falls, but becomes stationary once it settles on the peaks.</note>

The snow, which falls in flakes, and is water.

The great stones of the mountains will cast out fire, so that they will burn the wood of many and very large forests and many wild and domestic animals.

<note>The "stones" are flints used to strike sparks.</note>

The flint stone, which makes fire, which will burn all the loads of wood, and so devastate the forests. And with it, one will roast the meat of animals.

Oh, how many great buildings will be destroyed because of fire!

### On the fire of the bombards.
<note>A "bombard" is an early type of large-caliber cannon used in the 14th to 17th centuries.</note>

The oxen will be, in large part, the cause of the ruin of cities, and likewise horses and buffaloes. They pull the <term>bombards</term> <note>early heavy cannons</note>.

### XXXVII. R. 1310, MS. BR. M. FOL. 212 v.

### On grain and other seeds

Men will throw out from their own houses the very food which was intended to sustain their existence.

<note>This refers to the act of sowing seed in the fields.</note>

### On the trees that nourish the grafts

One will see fathers and mothers granting many more advantages to stepchildren than to their true children.

<note>A metaphor for grafting: the trunk (the parent) provides sap and life to the foreign branch (the graft) rather than its own original limbs.</note>

### On the censers

Those who will go about in white robes, with arrogant gestures threatening others by means of metal and fire, though these others have not done them the slightest harm . . . .

<note>A "censer" is a metal vessel used for burning incense in religious ceremonies; the "white robes" refer to the clergy.</note>

### On the Mowing of Grass

Unnumbered lives will be extinguished, and countless holes will appear upon the earth.

Men will pass through their own entrails when dead.

They live together in communities, yet are destroyed so that their honey may be taken from them. Many and great communities will be destroyed within their own houses.

There will be many who, with all diligence and eagerness, will pursue with fury that very thing which has always terrified them, without recognizing its malice.

## Of Metals

That which will emerge from dark and nocturnal caverns will bring great pain, danger, and death to the entire human race. To some of its followers, after many sufferings, it will provide pleasure; but whoever is not its partisan will die in misery and want. This thing will commit countless treacheries; it will multiply and entice all men toward murder, robbery, and base deeds; it will arouse suspicion in its partisans; it will take the state away from free cities; it will rob many of their lives; it will incite men against one another with many arts, deceits, and betrayals. O monstrous creature! How much better it would be for men if you returned to hell. For its sake, the great forests will be stripped of their trees; for its sake, countless animals will lose their lives. <note>Leonardo is describing gold and silver (money). The "caverns" are the mines, and the "monstrous creature" is the greed and warfare fueled by precious metals.</note>

---

<header>LXXVII. MS. CA. FOL. 370 r.</header>

## Of the beating of the bed to put it in order

Men will be found in such ingratitude that they will heap blows upon the one who gives them lodging, without any reward, so that large parts of its interior will be pushed out of their place and go through its body, turned over and over. <note>The "lodging" is the mattress or bed-bolster; the "blows" are the person fluffing the feathers or wool inside to make it comfortable.</note>

CV. <margin>Manuscript Codex Atlanticus, Folio 370 r.</margin>

### Of the Confessors

Unhappy women will go of their own free will to reveal to men all their excesses and their shameful, most secret deeds. <note>Leonardo refers here to the practice of auricular confession, framing it as a riddle where women voluntarily share their secrets with men (priests).</note>

CVI. <margin>Manuscript Codex Atlanticus, Folio 370 r.</margin>

### Of the Churches and Dwellings of Monks

Many shall be those who leave behind labor and toil, poverty of life and of possessions, and go to dwell in riches and in triumphant buildings, claiming that this is the means of making themselves friends of God.

CVII. <margin>Manuscript Codex Atlanticus, Folio 370 r.</margin>

### Of the Selling of Paradise

Infinite multitudes will publicly and peacefully sell things of the greatest value without license from the owner of the same, and which never belonged to them nor were ever in their power; and human justice shall not put a stop to this. <note>This is a critique of the sale of indulgences—remissions of temporal punishment for sin—which Leonardo views as selling something (salvation) that the clergy does not actually own.</note>

CVIII. <margin>Manuscript Codex Atlanticus, Folio 370 r.</margin>

### Of the Dead Whom One Goes to Bury

Simple folk will carry a great number of lights to provide illumination on the paths for all those who have completely lost the power of sight. <note>The "lights" are funeral candles, and those who have "lost their sight" are the dead being carried to their graves.</note>

->**Decorative Endpaper**<-

The page is covered in a repeating geometric pattern, a common feature in historical bookbinding to provide both aesthetic appeal and durability to the volume's interior.

The design consists of:
*   **Vertical stripes** in alternating orange and grey-brown tones.
*   **Wavy guilloche-style lines** <note>Guilloche is a decorative technique in which a very precise, intricate and repetitive pattern is mechanically engraved into an underlying material.</note> that create a sense of rhythmic movement across the page.
*   **Circular medallions** containing a stylized "X" or cross motif, centered within the geometric framework.

This style of printed paper was frequently used in the 18th and 19th centuries to protect the manuscript and hide the structural elements of the binding.

<summary>This page features a decorative printed endpaper with a repeating geometric and medallion pattern in orange and grey-brown, typical of historical bookbinding.</summary>
